3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Variational Aut.why_it_exists: Directly maximising the data likelihood p(x) = ∫p(x|z)p(z)dz is intractable (integral over all z). The ELBO is a tractable lower bound on log p(x) derived via variational inference — maximising it is a proxy for maximising the true (intractable) likelihood.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Variational Aut.how_it_works: ELBO = E_{q(z|x)}[log p(x|z)] - KL(q(z|x) || p(z)). The first term is the reconstruction log-likelihood (e.g. negative MSE for Gaussian likelihood, negative BCE for Bernoulli); the second term penalises the encoder's posterior q(z|x)=N(μ,σ²) for deviating from the prior p(z)=N(0,I), with a closed-form: KL = 0.5·Σ(σ² + μ² - 1 - log σ²). Total loss = -ELBO = reconstruction_loss + KL_term, minimised via gradient descent.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Variational Aut.use_when: Training any VAE — this IS the VAE training objective, not an optional component.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Variational Aut.avoid_when: N/A as a technique to apply/avoid — but the relative weighting of the two terms (see β-VAE) needs task-specific tuning.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Variational Aut.what_goes_wrong: If reconstruction loss dominates, the latent space isn't well-regularised (less smooth, harder to sample from); if KL dominates, posterior collapse occurs (decoder ignores latent code, all outputs become similar/blurry 'average' images) — this tradeoff is exactly what the β hyperparameter in β-VAE controls.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Variational Aut.real_example: Every VAE training loop computes `loss = recon_loss + kl_loss` (often with KL annealing — starting at weight 0 and ramping up — to avoid posterior collapse early in training, a technique from Bowman et al. 2016 for text VAEs).

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Variational Aut.what_it_is: A VAE variant that introduces a hyperparameter β multiplying the KL divergence term in the ELBO: loss = reconstruction_loss + β·KL_term. Setting β>1 over-penalises the KL term relative to standard VAE (β=1), encouraging more disentangled latent representations.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Variational Aut.why_it_exists: Standard VAEs don't guarantee that individual latent dimensions correspond to independent, interpretable factors of variation (e.g. one dimension = object rotation, another = color). β-VAE was proposed to encourage such disentanglement by more strongly enforcing the factorised Gaussian prior.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Variational Aut.how_it_works: By increasing β, the model is forced to represent information more efficiently/independently across latent dimensions (each dimension must justify its 'KL cost' by contributing meaningfully to reconstruction) — empirically, this tends to push the model toward representations where each latent dimension controls a distinct, semantically meaningful factor.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Variational Aut.use_when: Representation learning where interpretability/disentanglement matters — e.g. controllable generation (varying one latent dimension changes only one attribute, like face rotation independent of expression), scientific data analysis where you want to discover independent generative factors.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Variational Aut.avoid_when: When reconstruction fidelity is the priority — high β trades off reconstruction quality for disentanglement, so β>>1 can produce notably blurrier/lower-quality reconstructions; for pure generation quality, standard VAE (β=1) or other generative models are better.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Variational Aut.what_goes_wrong: Too high β can cause severe posterior collapse (most latent dimensions become uninformative, only a few 'active' ones carry information); disentanglement is not guaranteed even with high β — it's an empirical tendency, not a theoretical guarantee, and depends heavily on the dataset's true generative factors being somewhat independent.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Variational Aut.real_example: Higgins et al. 'β-VAE: Learning Basic Visual Concepts with a Constrained Variational Framework' (ICLR 2017) showed on datasets like dSprites (simple shapes varying in position, scale, rotation) that β-VAE learns latent dimensions that align with these individual factors, unlike standard VAE.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Variational Aut.what_it_is: Using a VAE trained only on 'normal' data to detect anomalies/outliers at inference time, based on the principle that the model reconstructs in-distribution data well (low reconstruction error) but reconstructs out-of-distribution/anomalous data poorly (high reconstruction error).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Variational Aut.why_it_exists: Many real-world anomaly detection problems (fraud, manufacturing defects, network intrusion, medical imaging) have very few labeled anomalies — VAEs provide an unsupervised approach that only requires 'normal' examples to train on.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Variational Aut.how_it_works: Train VAE on normal data only, minimising the ELBO loss. At inference, compute the reconstruction error (and/or the full ELBO, including KL term) for a new sample x: anomaly_score = ||x - x̂||² (or -ELBO(x)). Since the VAE has only learned to model the normal data distribution, anomalous x falls in low-density regions of the learned latent space, leading to poor reconstruction → high anomaly score. Threshold the score (e.g. via a validation set with known normal/abnormal examples, or a percentile of training reconstruction errors) to flag anomalies.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Variational Aut.use_when: Unsupervised/semi-supervised anomaly detection where labeled anomalies are scarce or nonexistent — manufacturing defect detection, fraud detection, network intrusion detection, medical scan anomaly flagging.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Variational Aut.avoid_when: When labeled anomaly examples ARE plentiful — a supervised classifier will likely outperform the VAE-reconstruction-error approach; when anomalies are subtle and don't manifest as large pixel/feature-level reconstruction differences (the VAE might reconstruct them just as well as normal data).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Variational Aut.what_goes_wrong: If the VAE is too powerful/expressive, it might generalise too well and reconstruct anomalies accurately too (reducing detection power); choosing the anomaly threshold is non-trivial and dataset-dependent; reconstruction error alone ignores the KL/likelihood term, which can also carry useful anomaly signal (using the full -ELBO or 'reconstruction probability' from An & Cho 2015 is often better than raw MSE).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Variational Aut.real_example: Used in industrial settings (e.g. detecting defective parts on a manufacturing line by training a VAE only on images of non-defective parts) and in network security for detecting unusual traffic patterns that deviate from the learned 'normal' distribution.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Variational Aut.what_it_is: A VAE variant where both the encoder and decoder are additionally conditioned on auxiliary information y (e.g. a class label), so the model learns p(x|z,y) and q(z|x,y) — enabling controlled generation of samples belonging to a specified class.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Variational Aut.why_it_exists: Standard VAEs generate samples from the overall data distribution with no control over which 'type' of output is produced; CVAE adds controllability by letting the user specify y (e.g. 'generate a digit that is a 7') at generation time.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Variational Aut.how_it_works: Concatenate the label y (often one-hot encoded) to the input of the encoder (so q(z|x,y)) and to the latent code z fed into the decoder (so p(x|z,y)). The ELBO objective is the same as standard VAE but conditioned on y throughout. At generation, sample z~N(0,I), concatenate with the desired one-hot label y, and decode — producing a sample of the specified class.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Variational Aut.use_when: Controllable generation where you want to specify class/attribute at generation time (generate a specific digit, generate a face with specific attributes), semi-supervised learning (using labels for a subset of data).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Variational Aut.avoid_when: When no useful conditioning signal (labels/attributes) is available, or when conditioning information is continuous/high-dimensional (e.g. full text descriptions) — for the latter, cross-attention-based conditioning (as in diffusion models with CLIP text embeddings) is more expressive than simple concatenation.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Variational Aut.what_goes_wrong: Simple concatenation-based conditioning can be a weak signal that the model learns to ignore, especially if y is low-dimensional relative to x — the latent z may end up encoding the class information anyway, defeating the purpose of explicit conditioning; balancing how much information flows through y vs z requires care.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Variational Aut.real_example: Sohn, Lee & Yan 'Learning Structured Output Representation using Deep Conditional Generative Models' (NeurIPS 2015) introduced CVAE for class-conditional MNIST digit generation — a direct conceptual ancestor of class- and text-conditioned diffusion models used in Stable Diffusion and DALL-E.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.what_it_is: The half of a GAN that maps random noise vectors z (sampled from a simple distribution like N(0,I)) to synthetic data samples G(z) that resemble the training data distribution.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.why_it_exists: To learn an implicit generative model — a function that can produce new, realistic samples from a learned data distribution without ever explicitly computing a likelihood, just by transforming noise.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.how_it_works: G is a neural network (in image GANs, typically transposed convolutions / upsampling layers) that takes z ∈ R^d (e.g. d=100) and outputs a sample in data space (e.g. a 64x64x3 image). It's trained to fool the discriminator: maximise D(G(z)) (or minimise log(1-D(G(z))), depending on formulation), receiving gradients backpropagated through D. The generator never sees real data directly — it only learns from the discriminator's feedback.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.use_when: Any GAN-based generative task — image synthesis, data augmentation, style transfer, super-resolution.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.avoid_when: When you need an explicit likelihood/density estimate (GANs are implicit models — no p(x) computation); when training stability/reproducibility is critical and you have compute budget for diffusion models instead.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.what_goes_wrong: If G is too powerful relative to D (or vice versa), training becomes unbalanced — G can find a small set of outputs that reliably fool a weak D (mode collapse) without covering the true data diversity.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.real_example: In DCGAN, G is a stack of transposed-convolution layers with batch norm and ReLU (except tanh on the output) that upsamples a 100-d noise vector to a 64x64x3 image — the canonical generator architecture for early image GANs.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.what_it_is: The other half of a GAN — a binary classifier network that takes a data sample x (real or generated) and outputs the probability D(x) ∈ [0,1] that x is a real sample from the training distribution (vs. fake/generated).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.why_it_exists: Provides the training signal for the generator — instead of a hand-crafted loss function comparing G(z) to real data, the discriminator learns an adaptive, increasingly sophisticated 'critic' that the generator must fool, effectively learning the loss function itself.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.how_it_works: D is a neural network (in image GANs, typically convolutional layers with strided downsampling, LeakyReLU, ending in a sigmoid). Trained to maximise log D(x_real) + log(1-D(G(z))) — i.e. correctly classify real samples as real (output→1) and fake samples as fake (output→0). After D is updated, G is updated to maximise log D(G(z)) (fool D into outputting 1 for fakes).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.use_when: Core component of any GAN — always paired with a generator in adversarial training.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.avoid_when: If D becomes too strong too quickly (perfect at distinguishing real/fake), gradients to G vanish (D(G(z))≈0 everywhere, log(1-D(G(z)))≈0 gradient) — need to balance D and G capacity/learning rates.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.what_goes_wrong: Discriminator overpowering the generator (vanishing gradients for G) is one of the most common GAN failure modes — mitigated by techniques like label smoothing, using -log(D(G(z))) instead of log(1-D(G(z))) (non-saturating loss), or switching to Wasserstein loss which doesn't saturate.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.real_example: In DCGAN (the foundational conv-GAN architecture), the discriminator mirrors the generator: a stack of strided Conv2D layers (4x4 kernels, stride 2) with LeakyReLU(0.2) and BatchNorm, progressively downsampling a 64x64 image to a single sigmoid output — this same discriminator skeleton (conv downsampling stack + sigmoid) is the template later extended into PatchGAN discriminators (Pix2Pix, CycleGAN), which output a grid of real/fake probabilities per image patch rather than a single scalar.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.what_it_is: The game-theoretic framing of GAN training as a two-player minimax game: min_G max_D V(D,G) = E_{x~p_data}[log D(x)] + E_{z~p_z}[log(1-D(G(z)))], where D tries to maximise its ability to distinguish real from fake, and G tries to minimise D's success.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.why_it_exists: Formalises the adversarial training dynamic and provides a theoretical target: the global optimum (Nash equilibrium) is reached when p_G = p_data (the generator's distribution exactly matches the real data distribution) and D(x)=0.5 everywhere (the discriminator can't distinguish real from fake better than chance).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.how_it_works: At the theoretical optimum, V(D,G) = -log(4) (when p_G=p_data and D=0.5 everywhere), and the value function reduces to 2·JS(p_data || p_G) - log(4), where JS is the Jensen-Shannon divergence — so minimising the GAN objective is theoretically equivalent to minimising the JS divergence between the real and generated distributions. In practice, the two networks are updated alternately via gradient descent/ascent (simultaneous gradient descent), which does NOT guarantee convergence to the Nash equilibrium — unlike convex optimisation, this is a non-convex, non-cooperative game.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.use_when: Understanding this is foundational/theoretical — every GAN training procedure is implicitly trying to approach this equilibrium.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.avoid_when: Don't expect simultaneous gradient descent to reliably find the Nash equilibrium in practice — it can cycle, oscillate, or diverge; this theoretical framing explains WHY GAN training is notoriously unstable.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.what_goes_wrong: Simultaneous gradient updates on a minimax objective don't behave like gradient descent on a single loss — the dynamics can oscillate indefinitely around the equilibrium rather than converging to it, which is the root theoretical cause of GAN training instability.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.real_example: Goodfellow et al. 'Generative Adversarial Networks' (NeurIPS 2014) — the original paper proves that at the global optimum p_G=p_data, but also notes that in practice G is trained with a non-saturating heuristic loss (-log D(G(z))) rather than the theoretical minimax loss, because the latter provides poor gradients early in training.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.what_it_is: The collection of pathological training behaviors common to GANs: mode collapse (generator produces only a limited variety of outputs, ignoring large portions of the data distribution's modes) and oscillation (loss values cycle without converging, generator and discriminator chase each other indefinitely).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.why_it_exists: A direct consequence of the minimax/Nash-equilibrium framing — simultaneous gradient descent on a non-convex adversarial objective has no convergence guarantees, and the generator has no incentive to cover ALL modes of the data distribution if a single mode is enough to fool the current discriminator.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.how_it_works: Mode collapse: G discovers that mapping many different z values to one (or a few) realistic-looking x fools D well enough — since D only sees the aggregate distribution at any instant, G can 'overfit' to D's current blind spots, producing low-diversity outputs (e.g. always generating the same digit). Oscillation: as G shifts to exploit D's current weakness, D adapts, then G shifts again — a cat-and-mouse dynamic that can cycle without settling.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.use_when: N/A — this is a failure mode to diagnose and mitigate, not something to apply.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.avoid_when: Mitigations: minibatch discrimination (let D see statistics across a batch, penalising low-diversity batches), unrolled GANs, Wasserstein loss (smoother gradients, less prone to mode collapse), feature matching, experience replay of generated samples, and architectural choices (spectral normalisation).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.what_goes_wrong: Mode collapse is often silent — the generator's loss can look fine while it's secretly only producing a handful of distinct outputs; detecting it requires actually inspecting sample diversity (e.g. via metrics like Inception Score / FID, or visual inspection of generated batches).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.real_example: Early DCGAN training on datasets like CelebA would sometimes collapse to generating nearly identical faces for very different z inputs — a textbook mode collapse failure that motivated WGAN and other stabilisation techniques.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.what_it_is: Deep Convolutional GAN (Radford, Metz, Chintala 2015) — the architectural template that made GANs work reliably for image generation by replacing fully-connected layers with convolutional (discriminator) and transposed-convolutional (generator) layers, plus a set of empirically-validated design guidelines.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.why_it_exists: Early GANs with fully-connected layers were unstable and didn't scale to images; DCGAN established a recipe of architectural best practices that made convolutional GANs train reliably, becoming the baseline architecture for nearly all subsequent image GANs.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.how_it_works: Key guidelines: (1) replace pooling with strided convolutions (discriminator) and transposed/fractionally-strided convolutions (generator) for learnable up/downsampling; (2) use batch normalisation in both G and D (except output layer of G and input layer of D); (3) remove fully-connected hidden layers in favor of global average pooling/conv layers; (4) use ReLU in G (except tanh on output, since images are normalised to [-1,1]) and LeakyReLU in D (helps gradient flow for the discriminator).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.use_when: Baseline architecture for any convolutional GAN — image generation, conditional GANs, the foundation that StyleGAN, CycleGAN etc. build upon.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.avoid_when: For very high-resolution image generation (1024x1024+), plain DCGAN architecture struggles — progressive growing (ProGAN) or StyleGAN-style architectures with adaptive normalisation are needed.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.what_goes_wrong: Batch normalisation in the generator can cause artifacts when batch statistics differ between training and inference (e.g. batch size 1); without careful weight initialisation (DCGAN recommends N(0, 0.02²)), training can still be unstable.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.real_example: Radford et al. 'Unsupervised Representation Learning with Deep Convolutional GANs' (2015) — trained on LSUN bedrooms and CelebA, demonstrating both realistic image generation and that the discriminator's learned features were useful for downstream classification tasks (early evidence of GANs as representation learners).

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.what_it_is: A GAN variant (Arjovsky, Chintala, Bottou 2017) that replaces the original JS-divergence-based loss with the Wasserstein-1 (Earth Mover's) distance between real and generated distributions, using a 'critic' (not a binary classifier) that outputs an unbounded real-valued score.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.why_it_exists: The original GAN loss (JS divergence) provides poor/vanishing gradients when the real and generated distributions have little overlap (common early in training, since both are low-dimensional manifolds in high-dimensional space) — the Wasserstein distance remains meaningful and provides useful gradients even when distributions don't overlap.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.how_it_works: The critic D (renamed from 'discriminator' since it's no longer a probability classifier) is trained to approximate the Wasserstein distance: max_D E[D(x_real)] - E[D(G(z))], subject to D being 1-Lipschitz (enforced in the original WGAN via weight clipping to a small range like [-0.01, 0.01]). The generator minimises -E[D(G(z))]. Crucially, the critic's loss correlates with sample quality, providing a meaningful training-progress metric (unlike standard GAN loss).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.use_when: When training stability is a priority, or when you need a loss value that correlates with generation quality (useful for monitoring/early stopping).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.avoid_when: Weight clipping (the original Lipschitz enforcement) is crude and can hurt critic capacity — prefer WGAN-GP (gradient penalty) for better results.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.what_goes_wrong: Weight clipping can cause the critic to learn overly simple functions (capacity underuse) or cause vanishing/exploding gradients depending on the clipping range — this limitation directly motivated WGAN-GP.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.real_example: WGAN was one of the first widely-adopted fixes for GAN training instability and is the conceptual basis for the loss function used in many subsequent stable GAN variants, including StyleGAN's training recipe variants.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.what_it_is: An improvement to WGAN (Gulrajani et al. 2017) that replaces weight clipping with a gradient penalty term added to the critic's loss, enforcing the 1-Lipschitz constraint in a smoother, more theoretically-grounded way.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.why_it_exists: Weight clipping in WGAN is a crude way to enforce the Lipschitz constraint and can lead to capacity underuse or training difficulties — gradient penalty directly penalises deviations of the critic's gradient norm from 1, which is the actual mathematical condition for 1-Lipschitz functions.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.how_it_works: Loss = E[D(G(z))] - E[D(x_real)] + λ·E[(||∇_x̂ D(x̂)||₂ - 1)²], where x̂ = ε·x_real + (1-ε)·G(z) for ε~U(0,1) (random interpolation between real and fake samples), and λ is typically 10. This penalty term encourages the critic's gradient norm to be ≈1 along these interpolated points, approximately enforcing 1-Lipschitz-ness without clipping.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.use_when: The default choice for Wasserstein-style GAN training in modern implementations — more stable than weight clipping and works well across a wide range of architectures.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.avoid_when: The gradient penalty requires computing gradients of the critic's output with respect to its input (double backprop), which roughly doubles the critic's computational cost per step.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.what_goes_wrong: Computing the gradient penalty adds significant compute overhead; the interpolation-based sampling of x̂ may not cover the regions of input space that matter most for the Lipschitz constraint in very high-dimensional spaces.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.real_example: WGAN-GP became a standard component in many GAN training recipes through the late 2010s, including as an option in BigGAN ablations and various conditional image-generation GANs.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.what_it_is: A GAN architecture (Zhu et al. 2017) for image-to-image translation between two domains (e.g. horses↔zebras, photos↔paintings) WITHOUT paired training examples, using two generators (G: X→Y, F: Y→X), two discriminators, and a 'cycle consistency' loss.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.why_it_exists: Paired image translation (Pix2Pix) requires aligned (x,y) pairs, which are expensive/impossible to collect for many domains (e.g. you can't get a paired photo of the same scene as both a photo and a Monet painting) — CycleGAN learns the mapping from unpaired collections of images from each domain.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.how_it_works: Two generators G:X→Y and F:Y→X, two discriminators D_X and D_Y for adversarial losses in each domain. Cycle consistency loss enforces F(G(x))≈x and G(F(y))≈y (translating to the other domain and back should recover the original image), via L1 loss: L_cyc = E[||F(G(x))-x||₁] + E[||G(F(y))-y||₁]. Total loss = adversarial losses (both directions) + λ·cycle consistency loss.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.use_when: Unpaired image-to-image translation: style transfer (photo↔painting), domain adaptation (synthetic↔real images), season/weather transfer, species transformation.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.avoid_when: When paired training data IS available — Pix2Pix with paired data generally produces higher-fidelity, more controllable results; for translations requiring large geometric/structural changes (not just texture/style), cycle consistency can be too restrictive.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.what_goes_wrong: Cycle consistency can cause the model to 'hide' information in subtle, imperceptible high-frequency patterns to satisfy the cycle constraint without truly learning a meaningful mapping (an adversarial-steganography-like failure mode documented in follow-up research); struggles with translations involving significant shape changes (e.g. cat↔dog often fails or only changes texture/color).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.real_example: CycleGAN's original demos — horse↔zebra, summer↔winter Yosemite, photo↔Monet/Van Gogh style — became iconic examples of unpaired image translation and remain widely used for data augmentation in domains where paired data is unavailable (e.g. medical imaging modality translation).

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.what_it_is: A conditional GAN framework (Isola et al. 2017) for image-to-image translation using PAIRED training data — e.g. (sketch, photo), (semantic map, street scene), (black&white, color) — where the generator learns a direct mapping from input image to output image.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.why_it_exists: Provides a general-purpose framework for any pixel-to-pixel translation task, replacing task-specific loss functions and architectures with a single conditional-GAN-plus-L1 recipe that works across many translation problems.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.how_it_works: Generator is a U-Net (encoder-decoder with skip connections) that takes input image x and outputs translated image G(x). Discriminator is a 'PatchGAN' that classifies whether NxN patches of the output are real or fake (rather than the whole image), encouraging high-frequency detail/sharpness. Loss = conditional adversarial loss (D distinguishes real (x,y) pairs from fake (x,G(x)) pairs) + λ·L1 loss between G(x) and ground truth y (the L1 term anchors the output to be close to the target, while adversarial loss sharpens details).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.use_when: Paired image-to-image tasks: sketch-to-photo, map-to-aerial-photo, semantic-segmentation-to-photo, day-to-night, colorisation, edge-to-image.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.avoid_when: When paired (input, output) data isn't available — use CycleGAN or other unpaired methods instead.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.what_goes_wrong: PatchGAN discriminators can introduce tiling/repetitive artifacts if the patch size is poorly chosen; the L1 loss component can cause some blurriness in regions with high output uncertainty (multiple valid outputs for one input).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.real_example: Pix2Pix's interactive demos (e.g. drawing simple sketches of cats/shoes/handbags and generating photorealistic images) were widely shared and directly inspired commercial tools; the PatchGAN discriminator concept was reused in many later conditional GANs including parts of the pix2pixHD and SPADE follow-ups.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.what_it_is: A GAN architecture (Karras et al. 2019, NVIDIA) for high-resolution image synthesis that introduces a 'mapping network' to transform the input latent z into an intermediate latent w, and injects style information at each resolution level of the generator via Adaptive Instance Normalisation (AdaIN).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.why_it_exists: Standard GAN generators feed z directly into the network, entangling different visual attributes (pose, identity, lighting) in ways that are hard to control independently; StyleGAN's design enables fine-grained, disentangled control over generated image attributes at different scales (coarse features like pose vs fine details like skin texture).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.how_it_works: Mapping network (8-layer MLP) transforms z → w (an intermediate latent space, less entangled than z). At each layer of the synthesis network (which starts from a learned constant input, not z directly), w is transformed (via learned affine transforms 'A') into per-channel style parameters (scale, shift) applied via AdaIN: AdaIN(x_i) = style_scale·((x_i - μ(x_i))/σ(x_i)) + style_shift. Noise inputs are also injected at each layer for stochastic variation (e.g. hair placement). 'Style mixing' — using different w vectors for different layers — enables combining coarse features from one image with fine details from another.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.use_when: High-resolution, high-quality, controllable image generation — faces, art, any domain where fine-grained attribute control and image quality are priorities.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.avoid_when: When you need simple, fast generation without fine-grained control — the mapping network and per-layer style injection add architectural complexity; for very limited compute, simpler GANs or even VAEs might be more practical.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.what_goes_wrong: StyleGAN (v1) had characteristic 'texture sticking' artifacts where features appeared fixed to specific pixel locations regardless of pose changes — fixed in StyleGAN2 (revised normalisation, removing AdaIN's mean-subtraction issues) and StyleGAN3 (alias-free architecture for true rotation/translation equivariance).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.real_example: StyleGAN/StyleGAN2 powers thispersondoesnotexist.com (generating photorealistic non-existent human faces) and is widely used in research for studying disentangled representations and GAN inversion (finding the latent w for a given real image to enable editing).

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.what_it_is: A GAN architecture (Ledig et al. 2017) for single-image super-resolution — generating high-resolution images from low-resolution inputs, using a perceptual loss (combining content loss from a pretrained VGG network with adversarial loss) instead of pure pixel-wise MSE.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.why_it_exists: Pure MSE-based super-resolution (minimising pixel-wise squared error) produces overly smooth, blurry results because MSE rewards averaging over multiple plausible high-frequency details — SRGAN's adversarial + perceptual loss encourages photorealistic, sharp textures even if they differ slightly pixel-wise from ground truth.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.how_it_works: Generator is a deep CNN (with residual blocks) that upsamples a low-res image (e.g. via sub-pixel convolution / pixel shuffle layers) to high resolution. Discriminator distinguishes real high-res images from generator outputs. Loss = content loss (L2 distance between VGG feature maps of generated and real high-res images, i.e. 'perceptual loss', rather than raw pixel MSE) + adversarial loss (standard GAN loss encouraging photorealism).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.use_when: Perceptual image quality matters more than pixel-exact accuracy — upscaling photos for display, enhancing low-quality images/video, restoring old photos.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.avoid_when: Scientific/medical imaging where pixel-exact fidelity matters more than perceptual realism — the GAN can 'hallucinate' plausible-looking but incorrect details, which is dangerous in diagnostic contexts (use non-adversarial super-resolution with careful validation instead).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.what_goes_wrong: GAN-based super-resolution can hallucinate fine details/textures that look plausible but don't correspond to the true underlying signal — fine for photos of cats, potentially problematic for satellite imagery or medical scans where hallucinated details could be mistaken for real features.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.real_example: SRGAN's perceptual loss approach (combining VGG feature loss with adversarial loss) influenced ESRGAN (Enhanced SRGAN, 2018), which became the basis for widely-used practical upscalers like Real-ESRGAN used in image/video restoration tools.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.what_it_is: An autoencoder variant trained to reconstruct a CLEAN target from a CORRUPTED/noisy version of the input — the encoder takes x̃ (x with added noise, masking, etc.) and the decoder must output x̂ ≈ x (the original clean input).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.why_it_exists: Forces the autoencoder to learn robust features that capture the underlying structure of the data, not just an identity mapping — the network must learn what information is 'signal' (preserved across corruptions) vs 'noise' (corrupted away), preventing trivial memorisation even with high-capacity networks.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.how_it_works: Apply a stochastic corruption process to input x to get x̃ (e.g. additive Gaussian noise, randomly masking/zeroing pixels, salt-and-pepper noise). Encoder f(x̃)=z, decoder g(z)=x̂. Train to minimise ||x - x̂||² — i.e. reconstruct the ORIGINAL clean x from the CORRUPTED x̃. The network can't simply copy its input (since input ≠ target), forcing it to learn the data manifold.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.use_when: Learning robust representations for pretraining, image denoising tasks, as a regularisation technique to prevent overfitting in autoencoders.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.avoid_when: When you need a generative model with a structured/sampleable latent space — DAE doesn't constrain the latent distribution (use VAE for that); for state-of-the-art denoising, diffusion models (which are essentially iterative DAEs) often outperform single-step DAEs.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.what_goes_wrong: Choosing the right corruption type/level is task-dependent and affects what features are learned — too little corruption and the network may still partially memorise; too much and useful signal is destroyed, making reconstruction (and thus learning) too hard.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.real_example: Vincent et al. 'Extracting and Composing Robust Features with Denoising Autoencoders' (2008) — stacked DAEs were an early deep-learning pretraining technique (before ReLU/dropout/batchnorm enabled direct supervised training); the core 'predict clean from corrupted' idea is the conceptual ancestor of the noise-prediction objective in diffusion models.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.what_it_is: An autoencoder variant that adds an explicit regularisation term to the loss — the Frobenius norm of the Jacobian of the encoder's activations with respect to the input — to penalise sensitivity of the latent representation to small input perturbations.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.why_it_exists: To learn latent representations that are robust/invariant to small variations in the input (similar goal to denoising autoencoders, but achieved via an explicit analytical penalty rather than stochastic corruption), encouraging the encoder to 'contract' a neighborhood of inputs to a small neighborhood in latent space.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.how_it_works: Loss = reconstruction_loss(x, g(f(x))) + λ·||J_f(x)||²_F, where J_f(x) = ∂f(x)/∂x is the Jacobian of the encoder, and ||·||²_F is the squared Frobenius norm (sum of squared entries). This penalty directly discourages the encoder from having large gradients with respect to input — i.e. small changes in x should produce small changes in z, making the representation locally insensitive to noise/perturbations along most input directions (except those that matter for reconstruction).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.use_when: Learning robust feature representations for downstream tasks where invariance to small input perturbations is valuable; comparing/contrasting different regularisation philosophies for autoencoders (academic/research context).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.avoid_when: Computing the Jacobian penalty is computationally expensive (requires additional backprop through the encoder for the penalty term itself) — for practical robust-representation learning at scale, denoising autoencoders or modern self-supervised methods (contrastive learning) are more commonly used.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.what_goes_wrong: The Jacobian penalty computation scales with input and latent dimensionality, making it expensive for high-dimensional inputs (e.g. large images) — rarely used in modern large-scale deep learning for this reason.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.real_example: Rifai et al. 'Contractive Auto-Encoders: Explicit Invariance During Feature Extraction' (ICML 2011) — primarily of historical/conceptual interest in the lineage of regularised autoencoders (sparse, denoising, contractive, variational), illustrating different ways to prevent trivial identity-mapping solutions.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.what_it_is: A GAN variant (Mirza & Osindero 2014) where both the generator and discriminator receive additional conditioning information y (e.g. class label), enabling controlled generation: G(z,y)→x conditioned on the desired class, and D(x,y) judges realism conditioned on the claimed class.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.why_it_exists: Vanilla GANs generate samples from the overall data distribution with no control over WHICH type of sample is produced; conditional GANs add controllability, letting users specify desired attributes/classes at generation time.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.how_it_works: Generator: G(z,y) — concatenate (or otherwise combine, e.g. via conditional batch norm) the noise vector z with an embedding of label y, then generate x. Discriminator: D(x,y) — takes both the image and the (claimed) label, and must judge both whether x is realistic AND whether it's a plausible/correct sample for class y (i.e. D learns to reject both fake images and real images paired with the WRONG label). Trained with the standard adversarial loss, but now conditioned on y throughout.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.use_when: Any task requiring controlled/targeted generation — generate images of a specific class, text-to-image generation (where y is a text embedding), data augmentation for specific underrepresented classes.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.avoid_when: When no useful conditioning labels exist, or conditioning information is very high-dimensional/complex (simple concatenation-based conditioning is weak for rich conditioning like full sentences — cross-attention mechanisms, as in diffusion models, handle this better).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.what_goes_wrong: If the conditioning signal is weak (e.g. simple concatenation with a small label embedding relative to a large noise vector), the generator may partially ignore y, reducing class-fidelity; auxiliary classifier GANs (AC-GAN) address this by adding an explicit classification loss term to force the generator to produce class-recognisable outputs.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Generative Adve.real_example: Conditional GANs are the direct conceptual ancestor of modern text-to-image diffusion models — Mirza & Osindero's original cGAN paper demonstrated class-conditional MNIST digit generation, and the 'condition on auxiliary information' pattern scaled up through AC-GAN, BigGAN (class-conditional ImageNet generation at high resolution), and ultimately text-conditional diffusion models like DALL-E and Stable Diffusion.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.what_it_is: The fixed, non-learned part of a diffusion model: a Markov chain that gradually adds small amounts of Gaussian noise to a data sample x_0 over T timesteps (e.g. T=1000), producing increasingly noisy versions x_1, x_2, ..., x_T, until x_T is approximately pure Gaussian noise.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.why_it_exists: Provides a tractable way to define a generative model — by defining a simple, fixed process that destroys data into noise, the model can be trained to learn the REVERSE process (denoising), which is intractable to define directly but learnable via denoising score matching.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.how_it_works: q(x_t | x_{t-1}) = N(x_t; √(1-β_t)·x_{t-1}, β_t·I), where β_t is a small noise variance scheduled to increase over t (e.g. linearly from 0.0001 to 0.02). Due to the Gaussian chain property, there's a closed form for sampling x_t directly from x_0 without iterating: x_t = √(ᾱ_t)·x_0 + √(1-ᾱ_t)·ε, where ᾱ_t = Π_{s=1}^t (1-β_s) and ε~N(0,I) — this allows efficient training by sampling any timestep t directly.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.use_when: This is a fixed mathematical definition used during training of any diffusion model (DDPM, latent diffusion, etc.) — not something to 'choose' but a component you must understand to implement/debug diffusion training.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.avoid_when: N/A — it's a definitional component of diffusion models.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.what_goes_wrong: Choosing the noise schedule (β_t values, linear vs cosine schedule) significantly affects sample quality — too-aggressive schedules destroy information too quickly at certain timesteps, wasting model capacity; cosine schedules (Nichol & Dhariwal 2021) generally outperform the original linear schedule.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.real_example: Ho et al. 'Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models' (DDPM, 2020) used T=1000 steps with a linear β schedule from 1e-4 to 0.02 — this forward process definition is the starting point for essentially all modern diffusion models including Stable Diffusion.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.what_it_is: The score function of a probability distribution p(x) is ∇_x log p(x) — the gradient of the log-density with respect to the data, pointing in the direction of increasing probability density (i.e. toward more 'typical'/realistic data).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.why_it_exists: Provides an alternative to modeling p(x) directly (which requires a normalised density, hard for complex high-dim distributions) — instead, model the SCORE (gradient of log-density), which doesn't require normalisation (the partition function/normalising constant has zero gradient and drops out), and use it to iteratively move samples toward high-density regions (Langevin dynamics).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.how_it_works: Score-based generative models train a neural network s_θ(x,t) to estimate ∇_x log p_t(x) (the score of the noised data distribution at noise level t) via denoising score matching: train the network to predict the noise ε that was added (since ∇_x log p_t(x) ∝ -ε/σ_t for Gaussian-noised data). Generation proceeds by Langevin dynamics: starting from noise, iteratively step x ← x + η·s_θ(x,t) + noise, gradually moving samples toward the data manifold.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.use_when: Conceptual framework underlying all diffusion models — DDPM's noise-prediction objective is mathematically equivalent to score matching at each noise level.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.avoid_when: N/A — foundational theory, not an optional technique.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.what_goes_wrong: Score estimates are only accurate in regions with sufficient training data density — in low-density regions (far from the data manifold), score estimates are unreliable, which is exactly why diffusion uses MULTIPLE noise levels (noise 'spreads out' the data distribution so the score is well-estimated everywhere, then gradually denoise).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.real_example: Song & Ermon 'Generative Modeling by Estimating Gradients of the Data Distribution' (NeurIPS 2019) introduced score-based generative models with multiple noise levels (NCSN), which was later unified with DDPM into the continuous-time SDE framework (Song et al. 2021), showing DDPM and score-based models are two views of the same underlying process.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.what_it_is: The foundational diffusion model formulation (Ho, Jain, Abbeel 2020) that trains a neural network to reverse the forward noising process — predicting and removing noise step-by-step to transform pure noise x_T back into a data sample x_0.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.why_it_exists: To create a generative model that's stable to train (no adversarial min-max game like GANs), has a well-defined probabilistic objective (a variational bound on likelihood, similar to VAEs), and produces high-quality, diverse samples.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.how_it_works: Reverse process p_θ(x_{t-1}|x_t) = N(x_{t-1}; μ_θ(x_t,t), Σ_t) is learned. The simplified training objective (shown equivalent to the variational bound up to reweighting) is: L = E[||ε - ε_θ(x_t, t)||²] — train a network ε_θ to predict the noise ε that was added to produce x_t = √ᾱ_t·x_0 + √(1-ᾱ_t)·ε, given x_t and timestep t. At inference, start from x_T~N(0,I) and iteratively apply: x_{t-1} = (1/√(1-β_t))·(x_t - (β_t/√(1-ᾱ_t))·ε_θ(x_t,t)) + σ_t·z, for t=T,...,1, gradually denoising to x_0.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.use_when: High-quality, diverse generative modeling (images, audio, video) when training stability matters and you have compute budget for many-step iterative sampling.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.avoid_when: When fast/real-time generation is needed — the standard DDPM sampling requires T=1000 sequential network evaluations, making it orders of magnitude slower than GANs (single forward pass) — use DDIM or other fast samplers, or distillation methods.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.what_goes_wrong: The 1000-step sequential sampling process is extremely slow (can take many seconds to minutes per image) — this single drawback motivated nearly all subsequent diffusion research (DDIM, latent diffusion, consistency models, distillation) aimed at reducing sampling steps.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.real_example: DDPM (2020) demonstrated FID scores competitive with GANs on CIFAR-10/LSUN without adversarial training; it became the foundation for Imagen, DALL-E 2, and Stable Diffusion, all of which use the same noise-prediction training objective.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.what_it_is: The neural network architecture (a U-Net — encoder-decoder with skip connections, originally from medical image segmentation) used as ε_θ(x_t, t) in diffusion models to predict the noise present in a noisy image at a given timestep.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.why_it_exists: Noise prediction is fundamentally an image-to-image task (input: noisy image, output: predicted noise of the same spatial dimensions) — U-Net's encoder-decoder-with-skip-connections design is well-suited for tasks requiring both global context (via the bottleneck) and pixel-precise output (via skip connections preserving spatial detail).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.how_it_works: Encoder path progressively downsamples the noisy image through conv blocks (often with residual blocks and self-attention layers at lower resolutions for global coherence); decoder path progressively upsamples back to full resolution, with skip connections from corresponding encoder layers providing high-resolution detail. The timestep t is injected via a sinusoidal positional embedding (similar to Transformer position embeddings), added to feature maps throughout the network so the model knows 'how noisy' the current input is and adjusts its denoising accordingly.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.use_when: Standard backbone for diffusion models on image/spatial data; also adapted for audio (1D U-Nets) and video (3D/spatiotemporal U-Nets).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.avoid_when: For non-spatial data (e.g. tabular data, pure sequence data without spatial structure), Transformer-based or MLP-based backbones may be more appropriate (e.g. Diffusion Transformers / DiT, used in Sora and newer image models, replace U-Net with a Transformer operating on image patches).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.what_goes_wrong: U-Nets for high-resolution images require significant memory due to the self-attention layers at multiple resolutions; the timestep-conditioning mechanism must be carefully designed (e.g. via AdaGN/adaptive group norm) — getting this wrong leads to the model not properly adapting its denoising strength across noise levels.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.real_example: Stable Diffusion's noise predictor is a ~860M-parameter U-Net operating on the VAE's latent space (64x64x4 instead of 512x512x3), with cross-attention layers injecting CLIP text embeddings at multiple resolutions for text-conditioned generation.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.what_it_is: Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models (Song et al. 2020) — an alternative sampling procedure for models trained with the DDPM objective that uses a non-Markovian, DETERMINISTIC reverse process, allowing far fewer sampling steps (e.g. 50 instead of 1000) without retraining.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.why_it_exists: DDPM's 1000-step stochastic sampling is the main practical bottleneck for diffusion models — DDIM shows that the SAME trained noise-predictor network can be used with a different (deterministic, skip-step-capable) sampling formula that drastically reduces the number of steps needed for good quality.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.how_it_works: DDIM derives a family of non-Markovian forward processes that share the same training objective as DDPM but allow a deterministic reverse mapping: x_{t-1} = √ᾱ_{t-1}·(predicted x_0 from x_t) + √(1-ᾱ_{t-1})·ε_θ(x_t,t), with no added noise (σ=0, deterministic) — and crucially, you can skip timesteps (e.g. jump from t=1000 to t=980 to t=960...) using a strided subsequence of the original schedule, since the formula doesn't require consecutive steps.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.use_when: Default sampler for practical diffusion deployment — used in essentially all production diffusion systems (Stable Diffusion, etc.) to get usable generation times (seconds instead of minutes).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.avoid_when: When maximum sample diversity/stochasticity is desired — DDIM's determinism (given the same starting noise x_T, you always get the same output) reduces diversity compared to DDPM's stochastic sampling; also, DDIM with very few steps (<20) can show quality degradation vs. more advanced samplers.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.what_goes_wrong: Very aggressive step reduction (e.g. <10-20 steps) can produce visible quality degradation/artifacts; DDIM's determinism, while useful for reproducibility and image editing (e.g. inversion), means less sample diversity for a fixed model — newer samplers (DPM-Solver, etc.) often achieve better quality at similarly low step counts.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.real_example: Stable Diffusion's default web UIs (e.g. AUTOMATIC1111) offer DDIM, alongside other fast samplers like Euler, DPM++, as selectable sampling methods — going from DDPM's 1000 steps to DDIM's ~20-50 steps was the key change that made diffusion models practical for interactive use.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.what_it_is: A text-to-image diffusion model (Rombach et al. 2022, Stability AI) that performs the diffusion process in a compressed LATENT space (produced by a pretrained VAE encoder) rather than directly in pixel space, dramatically reducing computational cost.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.why_it_exists: Running diffusion directly on high-resolution pixel images (e.g. 512x512x3 = ~786K dimensions) is extremely expensive — most of that pixel-space information is perceptually redundant. By first compressing images to a much smaller latent representation (e.g. 64x64x4 = ~16K dimensions, a ~48x reduction), diffusion becomes tractable on consumer GPUs.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.how_it_works: Pipeline: (1) A pretrained VAE encoder compresses image x → latent z (e.g. 512x512x3 → 64x64x4); (2) the diffusion process (forward noising + U-Net-based reverse denoising) operates entirely on z, conditioned on text via cross-attention with CLIP/text-encoder embeddings; (3) the VAE decoder converts the final denoised latent back to a pixel-space image. The VAE is trained separately (and frozen during diffusion training) to perceptually compress images while preserving reconstruction quality.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.use_when: Text-to-image and image-to-image generation at consumer-accessible compute budgets — this latent-space approach is THE standard architecture for open and most commercial text-to-image diffusion models.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.avoid_when: When perceptual compression loses information critical to the task (e.g. fine text/typography in images is notoriously hard for latent diffusion models because the VAE compression discards fine details needed for legible text).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.what_goes_wrong: VAE compression artifacts can limit fine detail (text, small faces in crowds, fine textures); the separately-trained VAE and diffusion model can have subtle distribution mismatches; latent space isn't perceptually uniform, so noise schedules tuned for pixel space may not be optimal for latent space without adjustment.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.real_example: Stable Diffusion (1.x/2.x/XL), Midjourney (believed to use similar latent diffusion approaches), and most open-source text-to-image models use this VAE+U-Net+cross-attention latent diffusion architecture — it's the dominant paradigm that made high-quality text-to-image generation runnable on a single consumer GPU.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.what_it_is: The mechanism by which text-to-image diffusion models incorporate textual descriptions: a pretrained text encoder (typically from CLIP — Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining) converts the text prompt into embeddings, which condition the diffusion U-Net via cross-attention layers.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.why_it_exists: CLIP was trained on hundreds of millions of (image, text) pairs to produce a shared embedding space where matching image/text pairs have similar embeddings — its text encoder thus produces text embeddings that are already well-aligned with visual concepts, providing a strong, pretrained conditioning signal without needing to train a text understanding module from scratch.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.how_it_works: The text prompt is tokenized and passed through CLIP's (or a similar) text encoder to produce a sequence of token embeddings (e.g. 77 tokens x 768 dims for CLIP ViT-L/14). These embeddings are injected into the U-Net via cross-attention layers at multiple resolutions: the U-Net's intermediate feature maps serve as queries, and the text embeddings serve as keys/values — Attention(Q=image_features, K=V=text_embeddings) — allowing each spatial location in the image to 'attend to' relevant words in the prompt.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.use_when: Any text-conditioned generative model — text-to-image (Stable Diffusion, DALL-E 2), and the same cross-attention conditioning pattern extends to other modalities (text-to-video, text-to-audio).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.avoid_when: When you need precise spatial/structural control beyond what text can express — text conditioning alone can't specify exact object positions/poses; combine with additional conditioning (ControlNet for pose/depth/edge maps, image conditioning for img2img).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.what_goes_wrong: CLIP's text encoder has a limited context length (77 tokens for the original CLIP) and can struggle with complex/compositional prompts (e.g. correct binding of attributes to multiple objects — 'a red cube on a blue sphere' might get colors swapped); CLIP embeddings can also encode biases present in its training data (web-scraped image-text pairs).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.real_example: Stable Diffusion uses a frozen CLIP ViT-L/14 text encoder for cross-attention conditioning; DALL-E 2 uses CLIP embeddings even more centrally (a 'prior' network maps CLIP text embeddings to CLIP image embeddings, which then condition the diffusion decoder) — CLIP conditioning is the backbone connecting natural language to image generation across nearly all major text-to-image systems.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.what_it_is: Low-Rank Adaptation applied to diffusion models — a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique that adds small, trainable low-rank matrices to the (frozen) weights of the U-Net's (and sometimes text encoder's) attention layers, enabling customisation (new styles, characters, concepts) with a tiny fraction of the parameters of full fine-tuning.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.why_it_exists: Full fine-tuning of Stable Diffusion (~860M+ parameters) for a custom style/character requires significant compute/memory and produces a multi-GB checkpoint per customisation; LoRA enables training on consumer GPUs and produces tiny (often <100MB, sometimes just a few MB) adapter files that can be mixed/matched/shared easily.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.how_it_works: For a frozen weight matrix W (e.g. in a cross-attention projection), LoRA adds ΔW = B·A, where B is (d×r) and A is (r×k), with rank r << min(d,k) (e.g. r=4-32). Only A and B are trained; W stays frozen. The effective weight becomes W + ΔW = W + B·A. Because r is small, the number of trainable parameters is tiny (e.g. r=4 on a 768x768 matrix: 4*768*2 ≈ 6K params vs 768*768≈590K for full fine-tuning of that matrix).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.use_when: Customising a pretrained diffusion model for a specific style, character, object, or concept with limited training images (often 10-50) and limited compute (single consumer GPU); sharing/distributing custom styles (small file sizes make this practical).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.avoid_when: When the desired change is a fundamental shift in the model's overall capability/distribution (not a localised style/concept) — full fine-tuning or training from scratch may be needed; LoRA's low rank can limit how dramatically the model's behavior can change.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.what_goes_wrong: Choosing rank r and learning rate requires tuning — too high a rank approaches full fine-tuning cost/overfitting risk, too low limits expressiveness; combining multiple LoRAs (e.g. a style LoRA + a character LoRA) can produce unexpected interactions/artifacts; overtraining on small datasets causes overfitting (the model reproduces training images too literally).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.real_example: The Stable Diffusion community (Civitai, Hugging Face) hosts tens of thousands of LoRA files for specific characters, art styles, and concepts — LoRA's original technique (Hu et al. 2021, for LLM fine-tuning) was adapted to diffusion models and became the dominant method for community-driven model customisation.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.what_it_is: Two personalisation techniques for diffusion models that teach a model a new concept (a specific object, person, or style) from a handful of example images: Textual Inversion (Gal et al. 2022) learns a new token embedding representing the concept, while DreamBooth (Ruiz et al. 2022) fine-tunes the full model (or with LoRA) to associate a rare token with the subject.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.why_it_exists: Users often want to generate images of a SPECIFIC subject (their pet, themselves, a specific object) that wasn't in the original training data — these techniques enable 'few-shot' personalisation from just 3-20 images, without retraining the entire model from scratch.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.how_it_works: Textual Inversion: keeps the diffusion model entirely frozen, and optimises a NEW word embedding vector (for a placeholder token like '<my-dog>') such that the model, when prompted with this token, generates images matching the provided examples — essentially finding the point in CLIP's text-embedding space that best represents the new concept. DreamBooth: fine-tunes the diffusion model's weights (often the U-Net, optionally with LoRA for efficiency) on the provided images paired with a prompt containing a rare/unique identifier token (e.g. 'a photo of sks dog'), plus a 'prior preservation loss' (generating images of the general class, e.g. generic dogs, to prevent the model from forgetting/overfitting the whole 'dog' concept to just the new subject).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.use_when: Personalising a diffusion model to generate a specific subject/person/object/style consistently across new prompts/contexts ('my dog in a spacesuit on the moon').
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.avoid_when: Textual Inversion alone often struggles to capture fine subject-specific details (it's limited by what's expressible in the existing embedding space) — for higher fidelity, DreamBooth (or DreamBooth+LoRA) is generally preferred despite higher training cost.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.what_goes_wrong: DreamBooth without prior preservation loss can cause 'language drift'/overfitting — the model forgets how to generate the general class (e.g. all 'dog' generations start looking like the specific training dog) or overfits to the exact poses/backgrounds in training images; Textual Inversion's limited expressiveness means very distinctive subjects may not be captured well.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.real_example: DreamBooth's iconic demo images — a specific corgi generated in many different contexts (on the moon, as a painting, in a teacup) from just a few training photos — and Textual Inversion's '<concept>' placeholder tokens both became foundational techniques in the Stable Diffusion fine-tuning ecosystem, often combined with LoRA for efficiency.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.what_it_is: A technique (Ho & Salimans 2022) for strengthening the influence of conditioning information (e.g. text prompts) on diffusion model outputs, by combining the model's conditional and unconditional noise predictions — controlled by a single 'CFG scale' hyperparameter that users adjust at inference time.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.why_it_exists: Earlier conditioning approaches (classifier guidance) required training a separate classifier to guide generation toward the desired condition — classifier-free guidance achieves a similar (and often better) effect using ONLY the diffusion model itself, by training it to handle BOTH conditional and unconditional generation, then extrapolating between the two at inference.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.how_it_works: During training, the model is trained on conditional examples (ε_θ(x_t,t,c) for text/class c) AND, with some probability (e.g. 10%), the condition is replaced with a null/empty condition ∅, training ε_θ(x_t,t,∅) too — a single network learns both. At inference, compute: ε_guided = ε_θ(x_t,t,∅) + w·(ε_θ(x_t,t,c) - ε_θ(x_t,t,∅)), where w is the 'guidance scale' (CFG scale, often 7-15 for Stable Diffusion). w=1 is standard conditional sampling; w>1 extrapolates further in the direction of the condition, sharpening adherence to the prompt (at the cost of some diversity/realism if too high).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.use_when: Standard practice for all text-to-image diffusion — virtually every Stable Diffusion / DALL-E generation uses CFG with a user-tunable scale to balance prompt-adherence vs. image quality/diversity.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.avoid_when: Very high CFG scales (e.g. >15-20) often cause oversaturated colors, artifacts, and 'burned'/over-contrasted images — there's a sweet spot (commonly 7-12 for SD) beyond which quality degrades even as prompt-adherence theoretically increases.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.what_goes_wrong: Too-high CFG scale causes oversaturation, unnatural contrast, and artifacts ('CFG burn'); too-low CFG scale produces images that ignore the prompt and look more like generic samples from the unconditional distribution; the optimal scale varies by prompt and model.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.real_example: Stable Diffusion's default UI exposes 'CFG Scale' (often defaulting to 7.5) as one of the most commonly adjusted user-facing parameters — increasing it makes the output adhere more strongly to the text prompt at some cost to naturalness.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.what_it_is: Two image-editing applications of diffusion models: inpainting fills in a MASKED region of an existing image with newly-generated content consistent with the surrounding context (e.g. remove an object and fill the gap, or add a new object in a specified region), while outpainting extends an image BEYOND its original borders, generating new content that plausibly continues the scene.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.why_it_exists: Provides controllable, localised image editing capabilities using the same pretrained generative model — rather than regenerating an entire image from scratch, users can preserve most of an image while modifying/extending specific regions.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.how_it_works: Inpainting: at each denoising step, the KNOWN (unmasked) regions of the latent are replaced with the corresponding noised version of the original image's latent (re-noised to the current timestep t), while the MASKED region continues to be denoised by the model — so the model only 'generates' within the mask while the rest stays anchored to the original. Specialised inpainting models (e.g. Stable Diffusion Inpainting) are additionally fine-tuned with mask-conditioning as an extra input channel for better mask-boundary blending. Outpainting: treat the canvas as extended (new blank/masked region added beyond original image borders) and apply the same masked-inpainting procedure to the new region, conditioned on the existing image content at the boundary.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.use_when: Object removal/replacement, image extension/canvas expansion, generative photo editing (e.g. 'remove this person', 'extend this photo to landscape'), creative content creation tools.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.avoid_when: When pixel-perfect, deterministic edits are needed (e.g. precise color correction) — diffusion-based inpainting introduces generative variability; for tasks requiring exact preservation outside the mask with seamless blending, careful mask feathering and model choice (dedicated inpainting checkpoints) matter significantly.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.what_goes_wrong: Visible seams/discontinuities at mask boundaries if blending isn't handled well (mask feathering, using inpainting-specific model checkpoints helps); generated content can be contextually implausible if the mask region is large relative to available context; outpainting can produce repetitive/lower-quality content far from the original image's anchor region.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|Diffusion Model.real_example: Stable Diffusion's 'inpainting' checkpoint (additional input channels for the mask and masked image) plus tools like Adobe Photoshop's 'Generative Fill' (built on similar diffusion inpainting technology) are widely-used real-world applications of this technique.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.what_it_is: Apache Spark's distributed computing architecture: a DRIVER process coordinates the overall job and maintains the SparkContext, while WORKER nodes (executors) run tasks in parallel on partitions of data represented as RDDs (Resilient Distributed Datasets) — immutable, partitioned collections of objects distributed across the cluster.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.why_it_exists: Datasets and computations for large-scale ML (feature engineering, distributed training data prep) often exceed what fits on a single machine — Spark's architecture enables computation to be parallelised across a cluster of machines transparently, with fault tolerance built in.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.how_it_works: The driver builds a DAG (directed acyclic graph) of transformations (map, filter, join, etc. — lazy, not executed immediately) and actions (collect, count, save — trigger execution). RDDs are split into partitions, each processed by a task on a worker/executor. 'Resilient' refers to lineage-based fault tolerance: if a partition is lost (node failure), Spark recomputes it from the lineage graph (the sequence of transformations that produced it) rather than needing replication. The Cluster Manager (YARN, Kubernetes, Spark's standalone manager, or Mesos) allocates resources (executors) to the driver.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.use_when: Processing datasets too large for a single machine's memory/CPU — large-scale ETL, feature engineering for ML pipelines, distributed data preprocessing before training.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.avoid_when: Datasets that fit comfortably in memory on a single machine — Spark's distributed overhead (serialization, network shuffles, JVM startup) makes it slower than pandas/single-machine tools for small data; for purely numerical, GPU-bound deep learning training, dedicated frameworks (PyTorch DDP, Horovod) are more appropriate than Spark itself.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.what_goes_wrong: Data skew (uneven partition sizes) causes some tasks to take much longer than others, bottlenecking the whole job; excessive shuffles (operations requiring data movement across partitions, like groupBy/join on non-co-partitioned data) are expensive and a common performance pitfall; RDDs are lower-level and largely superseded by the DataFrame API for most use cases (DataFrames add a query optimiser).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.real_example: A typical large-scale ML data pipeline reads terabytes of logs from S3/HDFS across a cluster, applies Spark transformations (filter, join with lookup tables, aggregate features) distributed across hundreds of executor cores, then writes processed features to Parquet for downstream model training.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.what_it_is: SparkSession is the unified entry point (since Spark 2.0) for using Spark's DataFrame and SQL APIs — it replaces the older SQLContext/HiveContext. The DataFrame API provides a higher-level, schema-aware, SQL-like interface over distributed data, built on top of RDDs but with Catalyst query optimisation.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.why_it_exists: RDDs are flexible but low-level (no schema, no query optimisation) — DataFrames provide a tabular, named-column abstraction familiar to anyone who knows SQL or pandas, with Spark's Catalyst optimiser automatically optimising query plans (predicate pushdown, column pruning, join reordering) for much better performance than hand-written RDD operations.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.how_it_works: `spark = SparkSession.builder.appName('app').getOrCreate()` creates the entry point. DataFrames are created via `spark.read.csv/parquet/json(...)` or from RDDs/pandas. Operations are expressed via method chaining (`df.filter(df.age > 21).groupBy('category').agg(F.avg('value'))`) or Spark SQL (`spark.sql('SELECT ... FROM ...')`) — both compile to the same optimised execution plan via Catalyst, then executed lazily across the cluster when an action (`.show()`, `.collect()`, `.write()`) is called.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.use_when: The default interface for nearly all Spark workloads today — ETL, feature engineering, ML pipelines (MLlib operates on DataFrames).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.avoid_when: When you need very fine-grained control over partition-level operations not expressible via DataFrame transformations — drop down to RDDs (`df.rdd`) for those rare cases, though this loses Catalyst optimisation.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.what_goes_wrong: Using Python UDFs (user-defined functions) with DataFrames can be much slower than built-in Spark SQL functions because UDFs require serialising data between the JVM and Python process (row-by-row) — prefer built-in `pyspark.sql.functions` or vectorised pandas UDFs (Arrow-based) when custom logic is needed.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.real_example: A feature engineering pipeline: `df = spark.read.parquet('s3://bucket/events/'); features = df.groupBy('user_id').agg(F.count('*').alias('event_count'), F.avg('duration').alias('avg_duration')); features.write.parquet('s3://bucket/features/')` — this runs distributed across the cluster with Catalyst-optimised execution.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.what_it_is: Spark MLlib's Pipeline API (`pyspark.ml`) provides a structured way to chain together data transformations (feature extraction, scaling, encoding) and estimators (models) into a single fit/transform workflow — conceptually mirroring scikit-learn's `Pipeline` and `Transformer`/`Estimator` pattern, but operating on distributed DataFrames.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.why_it_exists: ML workflows require consistent, reproducible application of the SAME preprocessing steps to training and inference data — Pipelines encapsulate this sequence as a single object that can be fit once and reused, preventing train/serve skew, and providing a familiar API for teams coming from scikit-learn.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.how_it_works: Two core abstractions: Transformer (has a `.transform(df)` method, e.g. a fitted scaler or a trained model producing predictions) and Estimator (has a `.fit(df)` method that produces a Transformer, e.g. an unfitted scaler or untrained model). A `Pipeline` is itself an Estimator composed of a sequence of stages (mix of Transformers and Estimators); calling `pipeline.fit(training_df)` runs each stage in order, fitting Estimators and producing a `PipelineModel` (all Transformers) that can be applied via `.transform()` to new data — e.g. `Pipeline(stages=[tokenizer, hashingTF, lr]).fit(train_df)`.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.use_when: Any ML workflow on Spark involving multiple preprocessing steps before a model — ensures the exact same transformations (with fitted parameters, e.g. learned scaling factors) are applied consistently to train and inference data.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.avoid_when: For deep learning model training itself, MLlib's built-in algorithms (LR, trees, etc.) are limited — for DL, Spark is typically used for the data pipeline (feature engineering) feeding into a separate DL framework (PyTorch/TensorFlow), possibly via Horovod or Petastorm for distributed training.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.what_goes_wrong: Pipeline stages must all operate on DataFrame columns with compatible types — type mismatches between stages (e.g. forgetting VectorAssembler before a model that expects a 'features' vector column) are a common error; saving/loading PipelineModels requires all custom stages to be serialisable (built-in stages handle this automatically).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.real_example: A typical MLlib pipeline: `Pipeline(stages=[StringIndexer(...), OneHotEncoder(...), VectorAssembler(...), StandardScaler(...), RandomForestClassifier(...)])` — fit once on training data, the resulting PipelineModel is saved and reused for scoring new data in a production pipeline.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.what_it_is: Two commonly-used MLlib feature transformers: VectorAssembler combines multiple individual feature columns into a single vector column (the format MLlib models require as input), and StandardScaler standardises a vector column's features to zero mean and unit variance (or unit variance only, configurable).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.why_it_exists: MLlib models expect a single 'features' column of type Vector (not multiple separate scalar columns like a pandas DataFrame) — VectorAssembler bridges this gap. StandardScaler is needed because many algorithms (linear models, SVMs, anything using gradient descent or distance metrics) perform poorly or converge slowly when features have very different scales.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.how_it_works: VectorAssembler: `VectorAssembler(inputCols=['age','income','score'], outputCol='features')` — concatenates the specified columns into a single `Vector` column (dense or sparse) named 'features'. StandardScaler: `StandardScaler(inputCol='features', outputCol='scaled_features', withMean=True, withStd=True)` — an Estimator that `.fit()`s on training data to learn per-feature mean/std (producing a StandardScalerModel), then `.transform()`s any DataFrame by applying (x-μ)/σ per feature using the LEARNED statistics (critical: the same fitted scaler must be applied to test/inference data, never refit).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.use_when: VectorAssembler: always, before any MLlib model that takes multiple feature columns. StandardScaler: when using scale-sensitive algorithms (linear/logistic regression, SVM, neural nets, k-means, PCA) — typically applied AFTER VectorAssembler.
