3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.avoid_when: StandardScaler isn't needed for tree-based models (Random Forest, GBT) which are scale-invariant — including it adds unnecessary computation, though it's harmless.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.what_goes_wrong: Fitting StandardScaler separately on train and test data (rather than fitting once on train and transforming both) causes train/serve skew — always fit on training data only, save the fitted StandardScalerModel, and use it to transform test/production data; VectorAssembler will fail/error on null values in input columns, requiring imputation first.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.real_example: Standard pattern: `assembler = VectorAssembler(inputCols=numeric_cols, outputCol='raw_features'); scaler = StandardScaler(inputCol='raw_features', outputCol='features'); pipeline = Pipeline(stages=[assembler, scaler, model])` — bundling these into one Pipeline ensures consistent train/inference transformation.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.what_it_is: Spark MLlib's distributed implementations of Gradient-Boosted Trees (`GBTClassifier`/`GBTRegressor`) and Random Forests (`RandomForestClassifier`/`RandomForestRegressor`) — tree ensemble algorithms that scale to large datasets via Spark's distributed data representation.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.why_it_exists: Tree ensembles are among the most effective algorithms for tabular data, but training them on datasets too large for a single machine requires a distributed implementation — MLlib provides this, using a column-based, histogram-based approach for finding splits across distributed data partitions.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.how_it_works: Random Forest: trains many decision trees in parallel (across the cluster), each on a bootstrap sample of the data and a random subset of features at each split; predictions are averaged (regression) or majority-voted (classification) — embarrassingly parallel, scales well. GBT: trains trees SEQUENTIALLY, each correcting the residual errors of the ensemble so far — inherently more sequential/harder to parallelise than RF, but MLlib distributes the per-tree training (finding best splits) across the cluster using approximate histogram-based split-finding (similar in spirit to XGBoost's approach) rather than exact split search.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.use_when: Large-scale tabular data classification/regression where the data doesn't fit on one machine, and you want robust, relatively low-maintenance models without extensive hyperparameter tuning (Random Forest especially).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.avoid_when: If the dataset DOES fit on a single machine (even a large one with lots of RAM), single-machine implementations (XGBoost, LightGBM, scikit-learn) are typically faster and offer more features/tuning options than MLlib's GBT/RF — Spark's distributed overhead isn't worth it for data that fits locally.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.what_goes_wrong: MLlib's GBT/RF have fewer tuning knobs and generally weaker performance than XGBoost/LightGBM on the same data (less mature implementations of split-finding and regularisation); GBT in particular doesn't parallelise as cleanly as RF, so training can be slow for many boosting rounds on huge datasets.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.real_example: A common pattern for large click-through-rate or fraud-detection datasets too big for a single XGBoost run: use Spark's RandomForestClassifier or GBTClassifier within an MLlib Pipeline for an initial distributed model, sometimes followed by sampling down the data to train a more tunable XGBoost model on a single (large) machine for final production use.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.what_it_is: Approaches for training machine learning models — particularly deep learning models — across a Spark cluster, either via MLlib's native distributed algorithms, or by using Spark as a data-distribution layer for frameworks like Horovod, TensorFlow, or PyTorch (e.g. via Petastorm, TorchDistributor, or Spark's built-in `pyspark.ml.torch.distributor`).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.why_it_exists: While MLlib provides some distributed algorithms (GBT, RF, linear models), deep learning frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow) have their OWN distributed training paradigms (data/model parallelism via NCCL, etc.) that are more mature for DL — integrating these with Spark lets teams use Spark's data infrastructure (reading from data lakes, feature stores) while still using best-in-class DL training frameworks.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.how_it_works: Common approaches: (1) Native MLlib — algorithms implemented with Spark's distributed primitives (limited to MLlib's algorithm set); (2) Horovod on Spark — Horovod (Uber's distributed DL framework using ring-allreduce) can be launched from a Spark job, with each Spark task running a Horovod worker process that trains a replica of the model and synchronises gradients; (3) Petastorm — a library for loading large Parquet datasets (written by Spark) efficiently into PyTorch/TensorFlow DataLoaders for training on a GPU cluster, decoupling Spark's data prep from the DL training loop; (4) `TorchDistributor` (newer, in `pyspark.ml.torch`) — launches PyTorch distributed training processes across Spark executors directly.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.use_when: Organisations with existing Spark-based data infrastructure (data lakes, feature pipelines in Spark) who want to train DL models on that data without a separate data-movement step — Spark handles feature engineering/data prep at scale, then hands off to a DL-native distributed training mechanism.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.avoid_when: If your data infrastructure isn't Spark-based, or your DL training cluster is GPU-focused and your data fits without Spark's distributed processing — running a dedicated PyTorch DDP / Kubernetes-based training job (e.g. via Ray, SageMaker, Vertex AI) without the Spark layer is often simpler.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.what_goes_wrong: Spark (JVM-based, CPU-oriented by default) and GPU-based DL training have different resource models — getting GPU allocation correctly configured for Spark executors (e.g. via Spark 3.x's GPU scheduling) adds operational complexity; data format conversions between Spark DataFrames and DL framework tensors (via Petastorm/Arrow) can be a performance bottleneck if not tuned.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.real_example: Databricks (built on Spark) provides integrated support for Horovod and `TorchDistributor` for distributed deep learning, allowing a single notebook to do Spark-based feature engineering on a Parquet dataset and then launch multi-GPU PyTorch training on the same cluster.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.what_it_is: Spark's connectors and APIs for reading data from and writing data to cloud object storage (Amazon S3, and equivalents like GCS/Azure Blob) and relational/NoSQL databases (via JDBC, or dedicated connectors for systems like Cassandra, MongoDB, Redshift).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.why_it_exists: Production data for ML pipelines typically lives in cloud data lakes (S3 with formats like Parquet/ORC/CSV/JSON) or databases (data warehouses, operational DBs) — Spark needs first-class connectors to these systems to be useful as a data processing engine in real pipelines.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.how_it_works: S3: `spark.read.parquet('s3a://bucket/path/')` and `df.write.parquet('s3a://bucket/output/')` — uses the `s3a://` connector (Hadoop's S3A filesystem implementation), requiring AWS credentials configured (via IAM roles, environment variables, or Spark config `spark.hadoop.fs.s3a.access.key` etc.). Databases via JDBC: `spark.read.jdbc(url='jdbc:postgresql://host/db', table='mytable', properties={'user':..., 'password':...})` — Spark partitions the read by specifying `column`, `lowerBound`, `upperBound`, `numPartitions` for parallel reads; writes similarly via `df.write.jdbc(...)`.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.use_when: Any production Spark pipeline that needs to ingest raw data (from data lakes/databases) or persist processed features/results (to data lakes for downstream consumption, or back to databases for serving).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.avoid_when: For very small lookup tables, broadcasting a small DataFrame (read once, broadcast-joined) is more efficient than repeated JDBC queries per partition; JDBC reads without partition columns specified pull all data through a single connection (no parallelism) — a common performance trap.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.what_goes_wrong: Reading from JDBC without specifying partitioning columns results in a single-task (non-parallel) read, which is extremely slow for large tables and can overload the source database; S3 reads of many small files (the 'small files problem') create excessive overhead — compacting into larger files (e.g. via repartition before write) improves both write and subsequent read performance; credential management for S3/databases must follow security best practices (IAM roles preferred over hardcoded keys).
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.real_example: A typical pipeline: `raw = spark.read.option('header','true').csv('s3a://data-lake/raw/events/*.csv'); processed = raw.filter(...).groupBy(...).agg(...); processed.write.mode('overwrite').partitionBy('date').parquet('s3a://data-lake/processed/features/')` — reading raw CSVs from S3, processing, and writing partitioned Parquet for efficient downstream querying.

3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.what_it_is: Using Spark's SQL interface (`spark.sql(...)`) — standard SQL syntax executed against registered DataFrames/tables — to perform feature engineering transformations (aggregations, window functions, joins, derived columns) at scale across a distributed dataset.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.why_it_exists: SQL is a familiar, declarative, widely-understood language for data transformation — Spark SQL lets data scientists/analysts express complex feature logic (rolling aggregates, joins across tables, conditional features) without needing to learn the full DataFrame API, while still benefiting from Catalyst's distributed query optimisation.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.how_it_works: Register a DataFrame as a temporary view: `df.createOrReplaceTempView('events')`, then run `spark.sql('SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) as event_count, AVG(amount) as avg_amount, MAX(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) as rolling_max_7 FROM events GROUP BY user_id')`. Window functions (OVER/PARTITION BY/ORDER BY) are particularly important for time-series feature engineering (rolling averages, lag features, cumulative counts) — Spark distributes these computations by partitioning data appropriately (e.g. by the PARTITION BY key) across executors.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.use_when: Feature engineering for ML on large datasets where features involve aggregations, joins across multiple tables, time-windowed statistics (rolling averages, lag/lead features), or any logic naturally expressed in SQL.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.avoid_when: Highly custom, row-by-row logic that doesn't map well to SQL/relational operations — though even then, prefer Spark's built-in DataFrame functions over Python UDFs when possible for performance; for iterative numerical algorithms (not just transformations), SQL isn't the right tool.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.what_goes_wrong: Window functions with PARTITION BY on high-cardinality columns combined with large ORDER BY ranges can cause significant shuffle and memory pressure on individual partitions (data skew if some partition keys have far more rows than others); joins between large tables without proper partitioning/broadcast hints can trigger expensive shuffle joins — using broadcast joins for small 'dimension' tables is a key optimisation.
3|🟡 T2 Generative Models|PySpark for DL|.real_example: A feature store pipeline computing 'user's average transaction amount over the last 30 days' and 'count of transactions in the last 7 days' as of each event timestamp uses Spark SQL window functions with RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL clauses, distributed across the cluster partitioned by user_id, to generate point-in-time-correct features for training a fraud-detection model.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.what_it_is: A generative neural network composed of multiple stacked layers of Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs), where each layer's hidden units serve as the input ('visible units') for the next layer, trained greedily layer-by-layer before optional fine-tuning.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.why_it_exists: Before ReLU, batch normalisation, and good weight initialisation schemes made deep supervised training feasible (pre-2010), randomly-initialised deep networks suffered from vanishing gradients and poor local optima — DBNs provided a way to pretrain deep networks layer-by-layer using unsupervised RBM training, giving a good starting point for subsequent supervised fine-tuning.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.how_it_works: Train RBM 1 on raw input data (unsupervised, via contrastive divergence). Freeze RBM 1, use its hidden-layer activations as 'data' to train RBM 2 on top. Repeat for desired depth. After greedy layer-wise pretraining, stack all layers into a single feedforward network and fine-tune end-to-end with backpropagation using labeled data (supervised fine-tuning) — the pretraining provides good initial weights that backprop then refines.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.use_when: Historically: when training deep networks with limited labeled data, where unsupervised pretraining could leverage abundant unlabeled data. Today: primarily of historical/educational interest.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.avoid_when: Modern deep learning — proper initialisation (He/Xavier), normalisation (BatchNorm/LayerNorm), and architectures with skip connections (ResNet) make greedy layer-wise pretraining unnecessary; self-supervised pretraining (contrastive learning, masked modeling) has superseded DBN-style pretraining for leveraging unlabeled data.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.what_goes_wrong: Greedy layer-wise training doesn't jointly optimise all layers, so the pretrained representation may not be optimal for the final task even after fine-tuning; RBM training via contrastive divergence is itself an approximation with known biases.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.real_example: Hinton, Osindero, Teh 'A Fast Learning Algorithm for Deep Belief Nets' (2006) — this paper, demonstrating DBN pretraining enabling deep network training on MNIST, is often credited as one of the catalysts of the 2006-2012 deep learning resurgence, though the technique itself was largely superseded by 2012 (AlexNet trained a deep CNN purely with supervised backprop + good initialisation/ReLU).

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.what_it_is: A two-layer (visible + hidden), undirected, generative stochastic neural network with NO connections within a layer (only between layers — hence 'restricted'), used to learn a probability distribution over its inputs via an energy-based formulation.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.why_it_exists: Provides a building block for learning unsupervised representations of data via an energy-based probabilistic model — the restriction (no intra-layer connections) makes the otherwise-intractable inference in general Boltzmann Machines tractable (hidden units are conditionally independent given visible units, and vice versa).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.how_it_works: Defines an energy function E(v,h) = -Σv_i·a_i - Σh_j·b_j - ΣΣv_i·h_j·w_ij over visible units v and hidden units h, with joint probability p(v,h) ∝ exp(-E(v,h)). Because of the bipartite structure, p(h|v) and p(v|h) factorise into independent terms with sigmoid activations, enabling Gibbs sampling. Trained via Contrastive Divergence (CD-k): run k steps of Gibbs sampling starting from a training example to get a 'reconstruction', and update weights to increase the probability of the data and decrease the probability of the reconstruction — an approximation to maximum likelihood gradient.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.use_when: Historically: unsupervised feature learning, collaborative filtering (the famous Netflix Prize RBM-based recommender), pretraining for DBNs.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.avoid_when: Modern practice — autoencoders, VAEs, and self-supervised Transformer-based methods provide more scalable and better-performing alternatives for representation learning; RBM training via CD is slow and approximate compared to modern gradient-based methods.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.what_goes_wrong: Contrastive divergence is a biased approximation to the true maximum-likelihood gradient — can lead to suboptimal learned distributions; Gibbs sampling-based training is computationally expensive and slow to mix, especially for complex/multi-modal distributions.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.real_example: RBMs were a key component of the winning solution architecture explorations in the Netflix Prize (2006-2009) for collaborative filtering, and were the building block of Deep Belief Networks — both largely historical milestones in the lineage leading to modern deep learning.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.what_it_is: The general (unrestricted) form of a stochastic, energy-based neural network where ALL units (visible and hidden) can have symmetric connections to each other (including within the same layer), defining a joint probability distribution via an energy function, of which RBMs are a tractable restricted special case.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.why_it_exists: Provides the most general energy-based generative model framework — a fully-connected network of binary stochastic units that can represent arbitrary pairwise dependencies, motivated by analogies to statistical physics (Ising models) and theories of associative memory/cognition.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.how_it_works: Energy E(s) = -ΣΣ w_ij·s_i·s_j - Σ b_i·s_i over all unit pairs (i,j) and units i, with p(s) ∝ exp(-E(s)/T) (T=temperature). Learning requires computing expectations under the model distribution, which (without the bipartite restriction) requires expensive Markov Chain Monte Carlo (Gibbs sampling) over the FULL joint distribution — extremely slow to converge for networks of any reasonable size, since every unit depends on every other unit.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.use_when: Primarily theoretical/historical interest — understanding the lineage of energy-based models and the motivation for the RBM restriction.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.avoid_when: Practical applications — the unrestricted Boltzmann Machine is essentially intractable to train at any useful scale; RBMs (or modern alternatives) are used instead.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.what_goes_wrong: Training requires MCMC sampling from the full joint distribution at every step, which doesn't converge in practical time for networks with more than a handful of units — this intractability is precisely why RBMs (restricting connectivity to make sampling tractable) were developed.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.real_example: Introduced by Hinton & Sejnowski (1985) as a stochastic recurrent neural network capable of learning internal representations — largely a theoretical/conceptual ancestor; modern energy-based models (EBMs) revisit similar energy-function ideas but with neural-network energy functions and modern sampling/training techniques (e.g. score matching, Langevin dynamics) that scale better.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.what_it_is: A recurrent neural network model of associative memory (Hopfield 1982) consisting of fully-connected binary units with symmetric weights, where the network's dynamics converge to stable states ('attractors') that can store and retrieve patterns — given a noisy/partial pattern, the network 'completes' it to the nearest stored memory.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.why_it_exists: To model content-addressable memory — storing patterns such that presenting a corrupted or partial version of a stored pattern causes the network to converge (via its dynamics) to the complete, clean stored pattern, analogous to how associative memory is thought to work in biological brains.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.how_it_works: Units are binary (±1), with symmetric weights w_ij = w_ji and no self-connections. Patterns are stored via Hebbian learning: w_ij = Σ_patterns ξ_i^p·ξ_j^p (sum over stored patterns p of the product of unit states). At inference, units are updated asynchronously: s_i ← sign(Σ_j w_ij·s_j) — this dynamics has an associated 'energy function' E = -½ΣΣ w_ij·s_i·s_j that DECREASES with each update, guaranteeing convergence to a local minimum (a stored pattern or spurious attractor). Capacity is limited — roughly 0.14N patterns can be reliably stored for N units before interference.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.use_when: Conceptual/educational context for understanding energy-based models, associative memory, and attractor dynamics; modern 'Hopfield Networks is All You Need' (Ramsauer et al. 2020) reframes continuous/modern Hopfield networks as mathematically equivalent to the attention mechanism in Transformers, providing a theoretical lens connecting attention to associative memory.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.avoid_when: Practical pattern storage/retrieval at scale — capacity limits (~0.14N patterns) and spurious local minima make classical Hopfield networks impractical compared to modern approaches; for associative-memory-like behavior in practice, Transformer attention (or explicit key-value memory/retrieval systems) is used.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.what_goes_wrong: Limited storage capacity (~0.14N patterns for N units) before stored patterns start to interfere/overlap; the network can converge to 'spurious' attractor states that don't correspond to any stored pattern, especially as more patterns are stored near capacity.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.real_example: Ramsauer et al. 'Hopfield Networks is All You Need' (2020) showed that the update rule of MODERN (continuous-state) Hopfield networks with an exponential energy function is mathematically identical to the softmax-attention update in Transformers — reframing attention as a single-step retrieval from an exponentially-large-capacity associative memory, an influential theoretical reinterpretation of why attention works so well.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.what_it_is: A framework for recurrent neural network training (encompassing Echo State Networks and Liquid State Machines) where a large, FIXED, randomly-initialised recurrent network (the 'reservoir') projects input into a high-dimensional dynamical state space, and ONLY a simple linear readout layer on top of the reservoir's states is trained.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.why_it_exists: Training full RNN weights via BPTT is computationally expensive and prone to vanishing/exploding gradients; reservoir computing sidesteps this entirely by NOT training the recurrent weights at all — only the (cheap, convex, often closed-form) readout layer is trained, while the fixed random reservoir provides rich enough dynamics to make the input states linearly separable for the readout.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.how_it_works: The reservoir is a large RNN (hundreds to thousands of units) with randomly-initialised, FIXED weights, scaled so the 'spectral radius' of the recurrent weight matrix is around 1 (the 'edge of chaos' — enough to have rich, fading-memory dynamics without exploding). Input is fed into the reservoir, producing a high-dimensional state trajectory x(t) that nonlinearly encodes the input history. A linear (or ridge regression) readout layer y(t) = W_out·x(t) is trained on labeled (x(t), target) pairs — since only W_out is trained, this is a simple linear regression problem, trainable in closed form.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.use_when: Time-series prediction/processing tasks with limited training data/compute, edge devices, or physical/analog computing substrates (reservoir computing has been implemented in optical, photonic, and other physical systems where 'computation' happens via the physical dynamics).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.avoid_when: When maximum task-specific performance is needed and you have the compute budget to train all parameters — fully-trained RNNs/LSTMs/Transformers generally outperform reservoir computing on complex tasks since the reservoir's dynamics aren't task-optimised.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.what_goes_wrong: Performance is highly sensitive to reservoir hyperparameters (size, spectral radius, sparsity, input scaling) which must be tuned via search since the reservoir itself isn't trained; doesn't scale to the performance levels of fully-trained modern sequence models on complex tasks.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.real_example: Echo State Networks (Jaeger 2001) have been used for chaotic time-series prediction (e.g. predicting the Mackey-Glass chaotic series) and are notable for being implementable in physical/analog hardware (photonic reservoir computers), an active area of 'unconventional computing' research.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.what_it_is: Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (Chen et al. 2018) — a model class that parameterises the derivative of a hidden state with respect to a continuous variable (e.g. 'depth' or time) using a neural network: dh(t)/dt = f(h(t), t, θ), and computes the output by solving this ODE using a numerical ODE solver, rather than discrete layers.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.why_it_exists: Reframes a deep residual network's layer-stack (h_{t+1} = h_t + f(h_t)) as a discrete Euler approximation of a continuous ODE — taking this to the continuous limit gives 'infinite depth' models with adaptive computation (the ODE solver decides how many function evaluations are needed), constant memory cost for backpropagation (via the adjoint method, not storing all intermediate activations), and natural handling of irregularly-sampled time-series.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.how_it_works: Define f_θ(h,t) as a neural network. The hidden state evolves as h(T) = h(0) + ∫_0^T f_θ(h(t),t)dt, computed via a black-box ODE solver (e.g. Runge-Kutta, adaptive step-size methods) that calls f_θ as many times as needed for the desired accuracy. Gradients for backprop are computed via the 'adjoint sensitivity method' — solving a second, augmented ODE BACKWARDS in time, which requires O(1) memory regardless of the number of solver steps (unlike storing all intermediate states for standard backprop through a deep network).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.use_when: Modeling continuous-time dynamics (irregularly-sampled time series, physical systems with known dynamical structure), normalizing flows (continuous normalizing flows use Neural ODEs), settings where memory-efficient backprop through 'very deep' implicit computation is valuable.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.avoid_when: Standard supervised learning tasks (image classification, etc.) where discrete architectures (ResNets, Transformers) are simpler, faster to train, and perform comparably or better — Neural ODEs' ODE-solver calls add significant computational overhead per forward/backward pass compared to a fixed number of discrete layers.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.what_goes_wrong: ODE solver calls (especially adaptive-step solvers) can require many function evaluations, making training/inference significantly slower than an equivalent discrete network; numerical stiffness in the learned dynamics can cause the solver to take excessively small steps, further slowing computation; gradients via the adjoint method can be numerically less stable than standard backprop in some settings.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.real_example: Chen et al. 'Neural Ordinary Differential Equations' (NeurIPS 2018, best paper) demonstrated continuous normalizing flows and continuous-time latent variable models for time-series with irregular sampling (e.g. medical records with irregular visit times) — an elegant theoretical framework, though adoption in mainstream production deep learning has remained niche compared to discrete architectures.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.what_it_is: A neural network architecture (Sabour, Frosst, Hinton 2017) that replaces scalar-valued neurons with 'capsules' — groups of neurons whose output is a VECTOR encoding both the probability that an entity (e.g. an object part) exists AND its instantiation parameters (pose, size, orientation), with a 'dynamic routing' mechanism connecting capsules across layers based on agreement.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.why_it_exists: CNNs with pooling discard precise spatial/pose information (max pooling keeps 'whether a feature is present' but loses 'exactly where/how it's oriented') — CapsNets aim to preserve hierarchical part-whole relationships and viewpoint-equivariant pose information, so the network understands that a face is a face regardless of rotation/viewpoint, by explicitly representing and routing pose information between 'part' capsules and 'whole' capsules.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.how_it_works: Each capsule outputs a vector whose LENGTH represents the probability of the entity's presence (normalised via a 'squashing' nonlinearity to [0,1)) and whose DIRECTION encodes pose/instantiation parameters. 'Dynamic routing by agreement': lower-level capsules (e.g. 'eye', 'nose') send their output to higher-level capsules (e.g. 'face') weighted by routing coefficients that are iteratively updated based on AGREEMENT (dot-product similarity) between the lower capsule's prediction and the higher capsule's current output — capsules that 'agree' get routed more strongly to that parent, implementing a soft form of part-whole assignment.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.use_when: Research/educational context for understanding alternatives to pooling-based spatial invariance and exploring part-whole hierarchical representations; tasks where viewpoint robustness and explicit pose representation are valuable (e.g. some 3D/pose-related applications, though adoption is limited).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.avoid_when: Production computer vision at scale — CapsNets' dynamic routing is computationally expensive (iterative routing between all capsule pairs) and hasn't demonstrated consistent advantages over CNNs/Transformers/ViTs on large-scale benchmarks (ImageNet etc.); the architecture hasn't seen wide industrial adoption.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.what_goes_wrong: Dynamic routing is iterative and computationally expensive, making CapsNets slow to train/run compared to standard CNNs; scaling to large images/datasets has proven difficult, and subsequent research hasn't shown CapsNets outperforming well-tuned CNNs/ViTs on standard large-scale benchmarks despite the appealing theoretical motivation.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.real_example: Sabour, Frosst, Hinton 'Dynamic Routing Between Capsules' (NeurIPS 2017) demonstrated strong results on MNIST (including the 'MultiMNIST' overlapping-digit task, showcasing part-whole disentanglement) but the architecture has remained largely a research direction rather than a production-deployed technique, with Vision Transformers becoming the dominant CNN alternative instead.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.what_it_is: A neural network architecture (Liu et al. 2024) inspired by the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem, which replaces the fixed, scalar activation functions on NODES (as in standard MLPs) with LEARNABLE univariate functions (parameterised as splines) on the EDGES/weights of the network — there are no traditional 'linear weight matrices' at all.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.why_it_exists: The Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem states that any multivariate continuous function can be represented as a composition of univariate functions and sums — KANs operationalise this as a neural architecture, with the hope of achieving better accuracy/parameter-efficiency and INTERPRETABILITY (since each edge's learned univariate function can be visualised and potentially simplified to a symbolic expression).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.how_it_works: Standard MLP: x_{l+1} = σ(W_l·x_l + b_l) — fixed activation σ, learnable LINEAR weights W. KAN: each connection (i,j) between layers has its own learnable univariate function φ_{i,j}(x) (typically parameterised as a B-spline plus a base function like SiLU), and the output of node j is x_j = Σ_i φ_{i,j}(x_i) — i.e. learnable nonlinear functions on edges, summed at nodes (no separate linear weight + fixed nonlinearity). This makes the network's learned functions directly visualisable per-edge, and the authors showed it can sometimes match larger MLPs with far fewer parameters on certain scientific/symbolic-regression tasks.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.use_when: Small-scale scientific computing / symbolic regression tasks where interpretability (extracting human-readable formulas from a trained network) is valuable, and the underlying function has compositional structure that splines can capture efficiently.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.avoid_when: Large-scale deep learning (vision, language) — as of 2024-2025, KANs have shown training instability and computational inefficiency (spline evaluation is much slower than matrix multiplication, which GPUs are extremely optimised for) at scale, and have not demonstrated competitive results on standard large benchmarks vs. MLPs/Transformers.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.what_goes_wrong: Spline-based computations don't map efficiently onto GPU matrix-multiplication hardware, making KANs significantly slower to train than equivalently-sized MLPs; scaling KANs to high dimensions/large datasets has proven challenging, with several follow-up papers reporting that simple MLPs with comparable parameter counts often match or beat KANs on non-scientific-computing tasks.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.real_example: Liu et al. 'KAN: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks' (2024) demonstrated KANs rediscovering known physical laws/formulas from data in small symbolic-regression and PDE-solving tasks with far fewer parameters than MLPs — generated significant research interest in 2024 as a potential MLP alternative, though follow-up work has tempered expectations for general-purpose deep learning use.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.what_it_is: Mamba (Gu & Dao, 2023) is a sequence modeling architecture based on Structured State Space Models (S4/SSMs) with input-dependent ('selective') parameters, achieving Transformer-competitive quality with LINEAR (not quadratic) time complexity in sequence length and fast autoregressive inference via a recurrent formulation.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.why_it_exists: Transformers' self-attention has O(n²) compute/memory in sequence length n, making very long sequences (documents, genomics, audio) expensive; classical SSMs (S4) achieve linear complexity but with FIXED (input-independent) parameters, limiting their ability to selectively focus on relevant context — Mamba's key innovation is making SSM parameters input-DEPENDENT ('selective'), giving content-aware processing similar in spirit to attention while keeping linear complexity.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.how_it_works: A continuous-time SSM is defined by h'(t)=A·h(t)+B·x(t), y(t)=C·h(t) — discretised into a recurrence h_t = Ā·h_{t-1} + B̄·x_t. Mamba makes B, C, and the discretisation step size Δ FUNCTIONS OF THE INPUT x_t (selective SSM) — allowing the model to selectively 'remember' or 'forget' information based on content, addressing a key limitation of fixed-parameter SSMs (which struggled with tasks requiring content-based reasoning, e.g. selective copying). For training, a parallel-scan algorithm computes the recurrence efficiently on GPUs (avoiding the apparent sequential bottleneck); for inference, the recurrent form gives O(1) per-token state update (vs. Transformers' growing KV-cache).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.use_when: Very long sequence modeling (long documents, genomics/DNA sequences, audio, high-resolution video) where Transformer's O(n²) attention becomes prohibitive, and where fast, constant-memory autoregressive inference is valuable.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.avoid_when: Tasks requiring precise, exact retrieval/copying of specific tokens from far in the context (some studies show SSMs can lag attention on tasks needing exact long-range token retrieval, e.g. needle-in-a-haystack-style tasks) — hybrid architectures (mixing attention and SSM layers) are increasingly used to get both benefits.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.what_goes_wrong: While linear in compute, the fixed-size recurrent STATE means information must be compressed into a bounded-size representation — for tasks needing exact recall of arbitrary earlier tokens, this compression can lose information that an attention mechanism (with its full KV cache) would retain exactly; implementation requires custom CUDA kernels for the selective-scan operation to be efficient.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.real_example: Mamba (2023) matched or exceeded Transformer performance on language modeling up to 2.8B parameters while offering 5x higher inference throughput; subsequent hybrid models (e.g. Jamba by AI21, combining Mamba and Transformer/MoE layers) and Mamba-2 (2024, reformulating the selective SSM as a form of structured attention) extended this line of research significantly.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.what_it_is: An architectural pattern where the standard feedforward (FFN) sublayer of a Transformer block is replaced with multiple parallel FFN 'experts', and a learned ROUTER selects a small subset (e.g. top-1 or top-2) of experts to process each token — increasing total model PARAMETERS dramatically while keeping per-token COMPUTE roughly constant.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.why_it_exists: Scaling dense Transformers (where every parameter is used for every token) requires proportional increases in compute for proportional increases in capacity — MoE decouples these: total parameter count can grow much larger (more 'knowledge capacity') while the ACTIVE compute per token stays small (only the selected experts run), enabling much larger models within the same compute/inference-latency budget.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.how_it_works: Each MoE layer has N experts (each a standard FFN) and a router (a small learned linear layer + softmax over experts, given the token's representation). For each token, the router selects the top-k experts (commonly k=1 or k=2) by router score; the token is processed by only those experts, and their outputs are combined (weighted by router scores). Auxiliary 'load balancing' losses are added during training to encourage roughly even utilisation across experts (preventing the router from collapsing to always picking the same 1-2 experts).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.use_when: Scaling model capacity beyond what a dense model's compute budget would allow — used in large frontier LLMs to get more 'knowledge' per unit of inference compute.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.avoid_when: Small models, or settings where inference infrastructure can't easily support the all-to-all communication/routing overhead (expert parallelism requires distributing different experts across devices and routing tokens between them, adding system complexity); when training data/compute is limited, the additional router and load-balancing complexity may not pay off vs. a well-tuned dense model.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.what_goes_wrong: Load imbalance — without careful auxiliary losses, the router can collapse to favoring a small subset of experts, wasting the capacity of underused experts and creating compute bottlenecks (overloaded experts become a serial bottleneck in distributed training); MoE models have higher TOTAL parameter/memory footprint (all experts must be stored, even if not all are active per token) despite lower active-compute, complicating deployment.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Neur.real_example: Mixtral 8x7B (Mistral AI, 2023) used 8 experts with top-2 routing per token, achieving performance competitive with much larger dense models at lower inference cost; GPT-4 and other frontier models are widely believed to use MoE architectures; DeepSeek-V2/V3 pushed MoE further with many small, fine-grained experts plus shared experts for common knowledge.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.what_it_is: A training strategy that presents training examples to the model in a meaningful ORDER — typically easy-to-hard — rather than the random shuffling used in standard training, inspired by how humans/curricula teach progressively harder concepts.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.why_it_exists: Optimisation of non-convex neural network losses can benefit from a 'warm start' on easier examples that establishes good initial representations/parameters, before tackling harder examples that would otherwise produce noisy/unhelpful gradients early in training when the model isn't ready for them.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.how_it_works: Define a difficulty measure for training examples (e.g. sentence length for language tasks, noise level, label ambiguity, a pretrained model's loss on each example). Order or weight the training data so easier examples are seen more/earlier in training, gradually introducing harder examples as training progresses (e.g. via a difficulty threshold that increases over epochs, or sampling probabilities that shift over time).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.use_when: Tasks with a natural notion of difficulty (sequence length, noise level, compositional complexity), training from scratch on complex tasks where random-order training converges slowly or to poor optima, reinforcement learning (progressively harder environments/tasks).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.avoid_when: When difficulty is hard to define/measure reliably for the task — a poorly-chosen difficulty metric can hurt rather than help; for well-behaved tasks/datasets where standard training already converges well, the added complexity of curriculum design may not pay off.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.what_goes_wrong: Defining 'difficulty' is often heuristic and dataset-specific — a bad difficulty proxy can bias training toward unhelpful orderings; transitioning too abruptly between difficulty stages can cause training instability (sudden distribution shift in the training data).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.real_example: Bengio et al. 'Curriculum Learning' (ICML 2009) showed faster convergence and better generalisation on shape-recognition and language modeling tasks when training examples were ordered from simple to complex; modern large-scale LLM pretraining sometimes uses curriculum-like data mixture schedules (e.g. starting with cleaner/shorter data, introducing longer-context or noisier data later).

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.what_it_is: A variant of curriculum learning where, instead of a human-designed difficulty ordering, the MODEL ITSELF determines which examples are 'easy' (based on its current loss on each example) and prioritises training on those, with the set of 'easy' examples expanding as training progresses.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.why_it_exists: Curriculum learning requires a difficulty measure defined in advance — self-paced learning automates this by letting the model's own current performance define difficulty dynamically, adapting the curriculum to the model's learning trajectory rather than a fixed external ordering.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.how_it_works: Add a binary (or soft) weight v_i for each training example to the objective: min_{w,v} Σ_i v_i·L(x_i,y_i;w) + g(v,λ), where g is a regulariser controlling how many examples are 'active' (v_i=1) based on a threshold λ. Alternates between: (1) fixing v, optimise model weights w on the currently-weighted examples; (2) fixing w, update v — examples with loss below threshold λ get v_i=1 (included), others v_i=0 (excluded). λ is gradually increased over training, progressively including harder (higher-loss) examples.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.use_when: Noisy or weakly-labeled datasets where some examples may be mislabeled/very hard, and you want the model to focus on 'learnable' examples first and gradually expand to harder ones; semi-supervised or weakly-supervised settings.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.avoid_when: Clean, well-curated datasets where all examples are similarly informative — the extra complexity of self-paced weighting may not provide benefit; can interact poorly with class imbalance (the model might initially 'pace' itself to ignore minority-class hard examples).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.what_goes_wrong: The model's own loss-based difficulty signal can be unreliable early in training (before the model has learned anything meaningful, ALL examples may have high loss); risk of the model permanently avoiding genuinely important but hard examples if the pacing schedule doesn't eventually include them.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.real_example: Kumar, Packer, Koller 'Self-Paced Learning for Latent Variable Models' (NeurIPS 2010) introduced the alternating-optimisation framework described above for latent-variable models (e.g. structured prediction); the core idea — using current model loss as a proxy for example difficulty to control training order — has influenced later work on noisy-label learning and data selection for LLM fine-tuning.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.what_it_is: A technique for simulating a larger batch size than fits in GPU memory by accumulating (summing) gradients over multiple smaller 'micro-batches' before performing a single optimizer weight-update step.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.why_it_exists: Memory constraints (GPU VRAM) limit the maximum batch size that fits during training, but many training recipes are tuned/work best with large effective batch sizes (for stable gradient estimates, BatchNorm statistics, or to match published hyperparameters) — gradient accumulation decouples the EFFECTIVE batch size (for the optimizer update) from the PER-STEP memory-bound micro-batch size.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.how_it_works: For N accumulation steps with micro-batch size B: run forward+backward on micro-batch 1, accumulate (sum, don't reset) gradients into `.grad` buffers; repeat for micro-batches 2..N WITHOUT calling `optimizer.step()` or `zero_grad()` between them; after N micro-batches, call `optimizer.step()` (with gradients scaled by 1/N if using mean reduction, to match the loss of a true batch of size N*B) then `zero_grad()`. The effective batch size is N*B, but peak memory usage is bounded by B (one micro-batch's activations at a time).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.use_when: Training large models/large batch sizes that don't fit in GPU memory at the desired effective batch size; reproducing published training recipes that specify a large batch size on hardware with less memory.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.avoid_when: When the desired batch size already fits in memory — gradient accumulation adds training-loop complexity and slightly increases wall-clock time (N forward/backward passes per optimizer step) for no benefit; operations whose behavior depends on the ACTUAL per-step batch (e.g. BatchNorm statistics are computed per micro-batch, not over the accumulated effective batch) won't behave identically to true large-batch training.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.what_goes_wrong: BatchNorm layers compute statistics over the micro-batch, NOT the accumulated effective batch — so gradient accumulation with BatchNorm doesn't perfectly replicate true large-batch training (LayerNorm-based models, e.g. Transformers, don't have this issue); forgetting to scale the loss by 1/N (when using sum-reduction) or forgetting to zero gradients at the right point are common implementation bugs.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.real_example: Training large language models with an effective batch size of millions of tokens on hardware where a single forward/backward pass only fits a much smaller micro-batch — gradient accumulation (often combined with data/model parallelism across many GPUs) is how frameworks like Megatron-LM and DeepSpeed achieve the target effective batch size.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.what_it_is: A memory-saving technique (also called 'gradient checkpointing') that trades compute for memory by NOT storing all intermediate activations during the forward pass — instead, only a subset ('checkpoints') are saved, and the rest are RECOMPUTED on-the-fly during the backward pass when needed for gradient computation.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.why_it_exists: Standard backpropagation requires storing every layer's activations from the forward pass (needed to compute gradients during the backward pass) — for very deep networks or long sequences, this activation memory can exceed available GPU memory even when the model's weights would fit; activation checkpointing reduces activation memory from O(depth) to O(√depth) (or other sub-linear amounts) at the cost of extra forward computation.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.how_it_works: Divide the network into segments. During the forward pass, only save the INPUT activation to each segment (the 'checkpoint'), discarding intermediate activations within the segment. During the backward pass, when gradients for a segment are needed, RE-RUN the forward pass for just that segment (using the saved checkpoint input) to regenerate the intermediate activations, then compute gradients normally. This roughly doubles the forward-pass compute (each checkpointed segment is computed twice: once during the original forward, once during backward) but can reduce activation memory dramatically.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.use_when: Training very deep networks or very long sequences (e.g. long-context Transformers) where activation memory is the binding constraint, allowing larger batch sizes or longer sequences than would otherwise fit.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.avoid_when: When activation memory isn't the bottleneck (e.g. small models, short sequences, or weight/optimizer-state memory dominates) — the extra recomputation adds ~20-30% wall-clock training time overhead, which is wasted if memory wasn't actually constraining you.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.what_goes_wrong: Choosing WHICH layers to checkpoint involves a memory/compute tradeoff that requires some tuning (checkpoint every layer = maximum memory savings but maximum recompute overhead; checkpoint every Nth layer = a tunable middle ground); operations with side effects or non-determinism (e.g. dropout) need careful handling to ensure the recomputed forward pass matches the original (frameworks handle this by saving/restoring RNG state for checkpointed segments).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.real_example: PyTorch's `torch.utils.checkpoint` and Hugging Face Transformers' `gradient_checkpointing=True` flag are standard tools for training large Transformer models on memory-constrained GPUs — commonly used when fine-tuning large LLMs on a single GPU, trading ~20-30% slower training for the ability to fit a model/batch size that would otherwise OOM.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.what_it_is: A model-parallelism technique that splits individual WEIGHT MATRICES (and their corresponding computations) of a neural network layer ACROSS multiple devices/GPUs, so that a single layer's forward/backward pass is computed cooperatively by multiple devices, each holding only a SLICE of the layer's parameters.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.why_it_exists: When a single layer's weight matrices are too large to fit on one GPU (common for the attention and FFN layers of very large Transformers), tensor parallelism allows that layer to be computed using multiple GPUs' combined memory and compute, by partitioning the matrix multiplications themselves.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.how_it_works: For an FFN layer Y = GeLU(X·A)·B with A (d_model × d_ff) and B (d_ff × d_model): split A COLUMN-wise across GPUs (A = [A1, A2]), each GPU computes GeLU(X·A_i) producing a slice of the intermediate activation; split B ROW-wise correspondingly (B = [B1; B2]), each GPU computes (GeLU(X·A_i))·B_i, and the partial results are summed via an ALL-REDUCE across GPUs to get the final Y. For attention layers, different attention HEADS are typically assigned to different GPUs (each GPU computes a subset of heads independently, with an all-reduce at the end). Requires fast interconnect (NVLink/InfiniBand) since all-reduces happen on every layer's forward AND backward pass.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.use_when: Models with individual layers too large to fit on a single GPU (very wide Transformers — large d_model/d_ff/number of attention heads); typically combined with pipeline and data parallelism (3D parallelism) for training the largest models.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.avoid_when: Models that fit comfortably on a single GPU — tensor parallelism's frequent all-reduce communication (every layer, every forward/backward) requires very high-bandwidth interconnects, and is wasted overhead if not needed; across slow interconnects (e.g. between different machines/nodes), tensor parallelism's communication overhead can dominate and should be limited to within a single node.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.what_goes_wrong: Communication overhead (all-reduces on every layer) can become the bottleneck if interconnect bandwidth is insufficient — tensor parallelism is typically restricted to GPUs within a single node (connected via NVLink) for this reason, with pipeline/data parallelism used ACROSS nodes; degree of tensor parallelism must evenly divide the relevant dimensions (number of attention heads, hidden dimension) of the model.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.real_example: Megatron-LM (NVIDIA) pioneered practical tensor parallelism for Transformer training, splitting attention heads and FFN matrices across GPUs within a node with all-reduce synchronisation — this technique, combined with pipeline parallelism and data parallelism, is how models like GPT-3/Megatron-Turing NLG (530B parameters) were trained across thousands of GPUs.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.what_it_is: A model-parallelism technique that splits a neural network's LAYERS (sequentially, by depth) across multiple devices — e.g. layers 1-10 on GPU 1, layers 11-20 on GPU 2 — so that different devices hold and compute different STAGES of the model, with activations passed between devices as data flows through the pipeline.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.why_it_exists: For models too deep/large to fit on a single device even after other optimisations, pipeline parallelism distributes the model's LAYERS across devices (unlike tensor parallelism, which splits WITHIN layers) — enabling training of models whose total parameter count vastly exceeds any single device's memory.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.how_it_works: Partition the model into K sequential stages, each assigned to a different device. Naively, processing one micro-batch sequentially through all stages leaves most devices idle most of the time ('pipeline bubble'). To improve utilisation, split the batch into multiple MICRO-BATCHES and pipeline them — while device 2 processes micro-batch 1's forward pass, device 1 starts micro-batch 2's forward pass, etc. Schedules like 'GPipe' (all forward passes, then all backward passes) or '1F1B' (one-forward-one-backward, interleaving forward and backward micro-batches to reduce memory and bubble time) determine the exact ordering. 'Bubble' (idle time) is proportional to (K-1)/M where K=number of stages and M=number of micro-batches — more micro-batches reduce bubble overhead but increase activation memory.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.use_when: Models too large (in total parameters/layers) to fit on a single device or even within tensor-parallel-sized groups — used for the largest models, typically as one dimension of '3D parallelism' (data + tensor + pipeline).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.avoid_when: Smaller models that fit within data/tensor parallelism alone — pipeline parallelism adds scheduling complexity and inherent 'bubble' overhead (idle device time) that's pure waste if not needed.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.what_goes_wrong: Pipeline bubbles (idle time while the pipeline 'fills' and 'drains') waste compute — minimising this requires many micro-batches, which increases activation memory (more in-flight micro-batches need their activations stored for the backward pass); load balancing across stages (each stage should take roughly equal compute time) requires careful layer-assignment, especially for heterogeneous architectures (e.g. MoE layers vs. dense layers).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.real_example: GPipe (Google, 2018) introduced micro-batch pipelining for training giant models across TPU pods; the '1F1B' (one-forward-one-backward) schedule from PipeDream/Megatron-LM reduces memory usage vs. GPipe's 'all-forward-then-all-backward' by interleaving forward and backward micro-batches — both are standard components of modern large-model training stacks (DeepSpeed, Megatron-LM).

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.what_it_is: Learning rate schedules that start training with a SMALL learning rate and gradually INCREASE it to the target/peak value over an initial number of steps/epochs ('warmup period'), before transitioning to the main decay schedule (cosine, linear, step, etc.).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.why_it_exists: At the very start of training, model weights are randomly initialised and gradient estimates (especially with adaptive optimizers like Adam, whose second-moment estimates are initialised to zero and need time to 'warm up') can be very noisy/large — using the full target learning rate immediately can cause large, destabilising updates early on; warmup lets the model take small, safe steps initially while gradient statistics stabilise.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.how_it_works: Common forms: linear warmup — LR increases linearly from 0 (or a small value) to the peak LR over W warmup steps: lr(t) = peak_lr · (t/W) for t≤W, then the main schedule (e.g. cosine decay) takes over for t>W. Warmup duration is typically a small fraction of total training (e.g. a few hundred to a few thousand steps, or 1-10% of total steps) — longer warmup is often needed for larger batch sizes and larger models.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.use_when: Almost universally used for training Transformers (especially with Adam/AdamW) and for large-batch training of any architecture — warmup is considered standard practice for modern deep learning training recipes.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.avoid_when: Very short training runs where the warmup period would consume a disproportionate fraction of total steps; some optimizer variants (e.g. RAdam — 'Rectified Adam') were designed to be more robust to the early-training variance issue without requiring explicit warmup, though warmup + AdamW remains far more common in practice.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.what_goes_wrong: Too-short warmup can still allow early instability/divergence, especially for large models or large batch/learning rates; too-long warmup wastes training steps at suboptimal (low) learning rates; the interaction between warmup length and PEAK learning rate is an important hyperparameter pairing — larger peak LRs generally need longer warmup.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.real_example: The original Transformer paper ('Attention is All You Need', 2017) used a specific warmup schedule (LR increasing linearly for the first 4000 steps, then decaying proportionally to step^-0.5) — and essentially every subsequent large Transformer/LLM training recipe (BERT, GPT, etc.) includes some form of linear warmup followed by cosine or linear decay.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.what_it_is: A diagnostic technique (Smith 2015, popularised by the `fastai` library) for empirically finding a good learning rate range BEFORE full training, by running a short trial where the learning rate is increased exponentially across mini-batches while tracking the loss, then plotting loss vs. LR to identify the optimal range.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.why_it_exists: Choosing the learning rate is one of the most important and hardest-to-guess hyperparameters — manually trying many full training runs at different LRs is expensive; the LR finder gets useful signal about good LR ranges from a SINGLE short run (a few hundred to a thousand mini-batches) rather than multiple full training runs.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.how_it_works: Starting from a very small LR (e.g. 1e-7), run training for a short number of steps/mini-batches, EXPONENTIALLY increasing the LR after each step (e.g. multiply by a constant factor each step) up to a large value (e.g. 1 or 10). Record the loss at each step. Plot loss vs. LR (log scale) — the loss typically decreases initially (LR too small to matter, then 'finding' an effective LR), reaches a minimum/plateau, then increases sharply (LR too large, training diverging). Choose a learning rate from the steepest-descent region of this curve, typically somewhat below the point where loss starts increasing (e.g. one order of magnitude below the divergence point).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.use_when: At the start of a new training run/new architecture/new dataset, to quickly narrow down the learning rate search space before committing to a full training run; especially useful when fine-tuning, where the optimal LR can differ significantly from pretraining.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.avoid_when: When you already have a well-validated LR from a similar setup (e.g. reproducing a published recipe) — running the LR finder is an extra step that may not change your choice; the LR finder's result is only a STARTING POINT — it doesn't account for how the optimal LR might change with a full LR schedule (warmup/decay) over the entire training run.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.what_goes_wrong: The result is sensitive to the batch size and other hyperparameters used during the LR-finder run (should roughly match the actual training setup); the 'steepest descent' heuristic for picking the final LR from the plot is somewhat subjective and requires visual inspection (though some automated heuristics exist, e.g. picking the LR with steepest negative gradient of the loss curve).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.real_example: The `fastai` library's `lr_find()` method is a widely-used implementation of this technique, commonly run before fine-tuning a pretrained model on a new dataset to quickly identify an appropriate learning rate range without expensive grid search.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.what_it_is: A 'wrapper' optimisation algorithm (Zhang et al. 2019) that maintains TWO sets of weights — 'fast weights' updated by a standard inner optimizer (e.g. SGD or Adam) for k steps, and 'slow weights' that are periodically updated by interpolating toward the fast weights — improving stability and reducing variance of the underlying optimizer.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.why_it_exists: Standard optimizers can have high-variance update trajectories (especially with adaptive methods or in sharp loss landscape regions), occasionally taking the parameters into poor regions; Lookahead reduces this variance by 'looking ahead' k steps with a fast optimizer, then taking a more conservative step toward that lookahead point from the slow weights — combining the fast exploration of the inner optimizer with the stability of a slower, averaged trajectory.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.how_it_works: Maintain slow weights φ and fast weights θ (initialised θ=φ). For k inner steps, update θ using the base optimizer (e.g. Adam) as normal. After k steps, update the slow weights: φ ← φ + α·(θ_k - φ) (linear interpolation toward the fast weights' position, with α typically 0.5), then reset θ ← φ for the next k-step cycle. The slow weights φ are what's eventually used/saved.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.use_when: As a drop-in wrapper around an existing optimizer (SGD, Adam) to potentially improve stability/final performance with minimal code changes — the authors showed benefits across vision (CIFAR, ImageNet) and language tasks with various base optimizers.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.avoid_when: When the base optimizer is already well-tuned and stable for the task — Lookahead adds two extra hyperparameters (k, α) to tune, and gains are often modest; not as widely adopted/battle-tested as AdamW for large-scale LLM training.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.what_goes_wrong: Adds memory overhead (storing both fast and slow weight copies); choosing k (lookahead steps, e.g. 5-10) and α (interpolation factor, e.g. 0.5) requires some tuning, and improvements over a well-tuned base optimizer alone are often modest in practice.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.real_example: Zhang, Lucas, Hinton, Ba 'Lookahead Optimizer: k steps forward, 1 step back' (NeurIPS 2019) showed improved stability and sometimes faster convergence when wrapping SGD/Adam on CIFAR and ImageNet — used occasionally in Kaggle competition solutions and some training recipes, but hasn't become as standard as AdamW for foundation model training.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.what_it_is: An optimisation procedure (Foret et al. 2020) that explicitly seeks parameters lying in NEIGHBORHOODS of uniformly low loss (flat minima), rather than just low loss at a single point — by computing gradients at a perturbed point (the 'worst-case' direction within a small neighborhood) rather than the current point.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.why_it_exists: Flat minima (where the loss is low across a wide neighborhood of parameter space) tend to generalise better than sharp minima (where loss is low only at a single point but rises quickly nearby) — SAM directly optimises for flatness by minimising the WORST-CASE loss in a neighborhood around the current parameters, rather than just the loss AT the current parameters.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.how_it_works: SAM's objective: min_w max_{||ε||≤ρ} L(w+ε) — find w such that even the WORST perturbation ε (within an L2 ball of radius ρ) doesn't increase the loss much. Approximated in two steps per training iteration: (1) compute the 'adversarial' perturbation ε̂ = ρ·∇L(w)/||∇L(w)|| (an approximation of the worst-case direction, via a single gradient ascent step); (2) compute the actual parameter update using the gradient AT THE PERTURBED POINT: w ← w - η·∇L(w+ε̂). This requires TWO forward-backward passes per step (one to find ε̂, one to compute the update gradient) — roughly doubling per-step compute.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.use_when: When generalisation gap (train vs. test performance) is a concern and you have the compute budget for ~2x the forward/backward passes per step — has shown particular benefits for vision models (ImageNet) and some Transformer training.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.avoid_when: Compute-constrained settings where the ~2x per-step overhead isn't worth the (often modest) generalisation improvements; very large-scale LLM pretraining where the 2x compute cost at massive scale is prohibitively expensive relative to the benefit.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.what_goes_wrong: Doubles the compute cost per training step (two forward-backward passes), which is a significant overhead at scale; the perturbation radius ρ is an additional hyperparameter that needs tuning and can affect results significantly.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.real_example: Foret et al. 'Sharpness-Aware Minimization for Efficiently Improving Generalization' (ICLR 2021) showed SAM improving ImageNet accuracy for various architectures (ResNet, ViT) and achieving SOTA results when combined with strong augmentation — Vision Transformer training recipes (e.g. some ViT variants) have used SAM to close the generalisation gap vs. CNNs on smaller datasets.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.what_it_is: A technique that maintains a separate copy of model weights — the 'EMA weights' — updated as an exponentially-weighted moving average of the training weights at each step: θ_EMA ← decay·θ_EMA + (1-decay)·θ_train, with decay typically very close to 1 (e.g. 0.999 or 0.9999).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.why_it_exists: The training weights at any single step can be 'noisy' (especially late in training with non-decaying or cyclic LR schedules, or in adversarial training like GANs where weights oscillate) — the EMA weights represent a temporally-SMOOTHED trajectory through parameter space, which often generalises better and is used as the FINAL/deployed model instead of the raw training weights.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.how_it_works: After each training step (or every N steps), update: θ_EMA ← decay·θ_EMA + (1-decay)·θ_train (initialised θ_EMA = θ_train at step 0, often with a warmup/bias-correction in early steps since θ_EMA starts heavily weighted toward initialisation). At evaluation/deployment time, use θ_EMA instead of θ_train. The decay rate controls the 'averaging window' — decay=0.999 averages over roughly the last ~1000 steps, decay=0.9999 over ~10000 steps.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.use_when: GAN training (EMA of the generator's weights is standard — e.g. StyleGAN uses EMA generator weights for sample generation, since the raw generator oscillates due to adversarial dynamics); diffusion model training (EMA weights are standard for the denoiser, e.g. used in Stable Diffusion checkpoints); generally useful whenever training has high step-to-step variance.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.avoid_when: Very short training runs where the EMA hasn't had time to 'converge' to a meaningfully different/better state than the raw weights; if memory is extremely constrained (EMA requires storing a full second copy of all model weights).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.what_goes_wrong: Doubles the memory footprint for model weights (storing both training and EMA copies); choosing the decay rate matters — too high (slow-moving EMA) means the EMA lags far behind the actual training trajectory and may underperform if training hasn't converged; too low provides little smoothing benefit.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Trai.real_example: StyleGAN and virtually all subsequent GAN papers report results using the EMA of the generator's weights (not the raw training weights) for sample generation/evaluation — similarly, diffusion model checkpoints (e.g. Stable Diffusion) are typically released as EMA weights, which empirically produce smoother, higher-quality samples than the raw training weights.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.what_it_is: A class of generative models (Normalizing Flows) that learn an EXACT, INVERTIBLE transformation f between a simple base distribution (e.g. Gaussian) and the complex data distribution — enabling exact likelihood computation (unlike VAEs' approximate ELBO) AND exact sampling AND exact inversion (data → latent).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.why_it_exists: VAEs only provide a LOWER BOUND on likelihood (ELBO) and GANs provide no likelihood at all — for applications needing exact density estimation (e.g. anomaly detection via exact likelihood, or scientific applications requiring probability values), flows provide a generative model with TRACTABLE EXACT likelihood via the change-of-variables formula.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.how_it_works: Construct f as a composition of simple, INVERTIBLE transformations f = f_K∘...∘f_1, each designed so both f_i and f_i^{-1} are easy to compute AND the Jacobian determinant |det(∂f_i/∂x)| is easy to compute (e.g. triangular Jacobian via 'coupling layers' that transform only part of the input conditioned on the rest). The change-of-variables formula gives the exact log-likelihood: log p_X(x) = log p_Z(f(x)) + log|det(∂f/∂x)|, where p_Z is the simple base distribution. Training maximises this exact log-likelihood directly via gradient ascent. Sampling: z~p_Z, x=f^{-1}(z).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.use_when: Applications requiring EXACT likelihood/density values (anomaly detection, scientific modeling, density estimation for downstream probabilistic reasoning); as the underlying mechanism for continuous normalizing flows (Neural ODE-based flows).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.avoid_when: Pure sample-quality-focused generation (image/audio synthesis) where GANs/diffusion models generally achieve better perceptual quality; the invertibility constraint restricts architecture choices (every layer must be invertible with tractable Jacobian), limiting expressiveness compared to unconstrained architectures.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.what_goes_wrong: The invertibility + tractable-Jacobian constraints significantly limit architectural flexibility compared to standard (non-invertible) networks — designing expressive-yet-invertible layers (coupling layers, autoregressive flows, invertible 1x1 convolutions) is itself a research area; flows for high-dimensional data (large images) require many layers and can be memory/compute intensive.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.real_example: RealNVP (2016) and Glow (2018, OpenAI) demonstrated flow-based image generation with exact likelihood and latent-space manipulation (e.g. smooth interpolation between faces via the invertible latent space); flows are also used as the 'normalizing flow' component in some VAE posteriors (to make q(z|x) more flexible than a simple Gaussian).

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.what_it_is: A general class of generative models that define an unnormalised 'energy function' E_θ(x) (typically a neural network) over the data space, with the implied probability distribution p_θ(x) ∝ exp(-E_θ(x)) — LOWER energy corresponds to HIGHER probability, with no requirement that the energy function be analytically integrable/normalisable.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.why_it_exists: EBMs provide maximum architectural flexibility for defining a 'compatibility'/'plausibility' score over data (E_θ(x) can be ANY neural network, with no invertibility or normalisation constraints, unlike flows or VAEs) — useful for both generative modeling and as a flexible scoring function for tasks like anomaly detection, denoising, or as components of other models (e.g. the discriminator-as-energy-function view of GANs).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.how_it_works: Training maximises log-likelihood, whose gradient is: ∇_θ log p_θ(x) = -∇_θE_θ(x) + E_{x'~p_θ}[∇_θE_θ(x')] — the first term pushes down energy at training data points, the second term (an expectation over the MODEL's distribution, requiring MCMC/Langevin dynamics sampling since p_θ is unnormalised) pushes UP energy everywhere else. This 'contrastive' training (lower energy at data, higher energy at model samples) is the unifying principle behind RBMs, score-based models, and modern EBMs. Sampling from p_θ requires iterative MCMC (e.g. Langevin dynamics: x ← x - η·∇_xE_θ(x) + noise), which is the main practical bottleneck.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.use_when: Research/flexible modeling contexts requiring an unconstrained scoring function over data; as a unifying theoretical framework connecting diffusion models (score-based models are EBMs where the score ∇_x log p(x) = -∇_xE_θ(x) is modeled directly), GANs (discriminator can be viewed as an energy function), and classical models (RBMs, Hopfield networks).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.avoid_when: Production generation tasks where MCMC-based sampling is too slow — diffusion models (which can be viewed as EBMs trained via score matching with a tractable, simulation-free training objective and a practical iterative sampler) are the practical descendant that sidesteps EBM's sampling bottleneck.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.what_goes_wrong: MCMC sampling (needed both for training's negative-phase expectation and for generation) is slow to converge ('mixing') especially for multi-modal distributions — this is the central practical challenge that has limited EBM adoption compared to GANs/diffusion/VAEs, which have more tractable training/sampling.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.real_example: Du & Mordatch 'Implicit Generation and Modeling with Energy-Based Models' (2019) demonstrated image generation via EBMs with Langevin dynamics sampling; the broader EBM framework is foreshadowed in the energy functions of Boltzmann Machines/Hopfield networks and is theoretically unified with diffusion models via the score-based generative modeling framework (Song & Ermon 2019, Song et al. 2021).

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.what_it_is: A training objective for estimating the SCORE FUNCTION (∇_x log p(x)) of a data distribution directly, WITHOUT needing to know/compute the normalising constant of p(x) — the foundational training principle behind score-based generative models and diffusion models.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.why_it_exists: Maximum likelihood training of energy-based/unnormalised models requires the intractable normalising constant Z=∫exp(-E(x))dx; score matching sidesteps this entirely by training a network to match the GRADIENT of log-density (the score), since ∇_x log p(x) = ∇_x log(p̃(x)/Z) = ∇_x log p̃(x) (the normalising constant Z, being constant w.r.t. x, has zero gradient and drops out).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.how_it_works: Original score matching (Hyvärinen 2005) minimises E_{p_data}[||∇_x log p_θ(x) - ∇_x log p_data(x)||²] — but this requires knowing the TRUE score of the data, which is unknown. Hyvärinen's trick: this objective is equivalent (up to a constant) to E_{p_data}[tr(∇_x²log p_θ(x)) + ½||∇_x log p_θ(x)||²], which doesn't require the true score — but involves the Hessian trace (expensive).
