DENOISING score matching (Vincent 2011) avoids the Hessian: add noise to data x̃=x+σε, and train the network to predict ∇_x̃ log p(x̃|x) = -ε/σ² — i.e. train a network s_θ(x̃,σ) to predict (a rescaling of) the ADDED NOISE, given the noisy input. This is exactly the training objective used in DDPM diffusion models.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.use_when: The foundational training objective for ALL diffusion models (DDPM's noise-prediction loss IS denoising score matching) and explicit score-based generative models (NCSN).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.avoid_when: N/A — this is foundational theory underlying diffusion training, understood rather than 'applied' as a separate choice.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.what_goes_wrong: Original (non-denoising) score matching's Hessian-trace term is computationally expensive for high-dimensional data, making it impractical at scale — this is precisely why DENOISING score matching (which avoids the Hessian via the noise-corruption trick) became the practical standard, directly enabling diffusion models.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.real_example: Song & Ermon (2019, NeurIPS) used denoising score matching at MULTIPLE noise levels to train score-based generative models (NCSN), directly establishing the mathematical framework that DDPM (Ho et al. 2020) and all subsequent diffusion models build on — the 'predict the noise' training objective ubiquitous in Stable Diffusion etc. IS a (rescaled) denoising score matching objective.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.what_it_is: Autoregressive generative models for images (van den Oord et al. 2016) that model the joint distribution of pixels as a product of conditional distributions p(x) = Π_i p(x_i | x_1,...,x_{i-1}) — each pixel generated sequentially, conditioned on all previously-generated pixels (in raster-scan order), using CNNs (PixelCNN, with masked convolutions) or RNNs (PixelRNN, with LSTMs over rows/diagonals).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.why_it_exists: Provides a generative model with EXACT, TRACTABLE likelihood (unlike VAEs/GANs) by exploiting the chain rule of probability — each conditional p(x_i|x_{<i}) is modeled by a neural network, and the full joint likelihood is just the product (sum of logs) of these tractable conditionals, directly optimisable via maximum likelihood.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.how_it_works: PixelRNN: process the image pixel-by-pixel (or row-by-row) using LSTMs, where each pixel's distribution (e.g. a categorical distribution over 256 intensity values, or a mixture for color channels) is conditioned on the LSTM's hidden state summarising all previous pixels. PixelCNN: uses MASKED CONVOLUTIONS — convolutional filters where weights corresponding to 'future' pixels (in raster-scan order) are masked to zero, ensuring the receptive field for predicting pixel i only includes pixels <i — this allows parallel TRAINING (compute all conditionals' losses in one forward pass, like teacher forcing) even though GENERATION must still proceed pixel-by-pixel sequentially.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.use_when: Applications needing exact likelihood (density estimation, lossless compression — these models directly give bits-per-pixel); as a component/decoder in other models (e.g. PixelCNN decoder in VQ-VAE for modeling the discrete latent code distribution).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.avoid_when: High-resolution image generation where sample speed matters — generating pixel-by-pixel (potentially millions of sequential steps for a large image) is extremely slow compared to GANs (single forward pass) or even diffusion models (tens of steps); for perceptual quality at scale, GANs/diffusion generally produce better results faster.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.what_goes_wrong: Sequential pixel-by-pixel generation is extremely slow (a single high-resolution image can take a very long time to generate) — this sampling-speed bottleneck is the primary reason autoregressive pixel models were largely superseded by GANs and later diffusion models for image generation, though the autoregressive paradigm (just at a coarser/compressed granularity) returned via VQ-VAE+Transformer approaches and modern autoregressive image models.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.real_example: PixelCNN's masked-convolution idea (causal/autoregressive masking) directly influenced WaveNet's (2016) causal convolutions for audio generation, and the discrete-codebook + autoregressive-prior pattern (PixelCNN modeling a VQ-VAE's discrete latent codes) is the conceptual basis for VQ-VAE-2 and later Transformer-based autoregressive image generators (e.g. early versions of DALL-E used a Transformer in place of PixelCNN over VQ-VAE codes).

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.what_it_is: A VAE variant (van den Oord et al. 2017) where the latent space is DISCRETE rather than continuous — the encoder output is mapped (via nearest-neighbor lookup) to one of a finite set of learned 'codebook' vectors, producing a discrete latent representation that can be modeled by powerful autoregressive priors (e.g. PixelCNN, Transformers).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.why_it_exists: Continuous VAE latents are hard for autoregressive models to model well (continuous distributions need careful mixture-density output layers); many real-world signals (e.g. phonemes in speech, discrete 'tokens' of meaning in images) have a naturally discrete/categorical structure — VQ-VAE provides a way to learn a discrete 'vocabulary' of latent codes that can then be modeled with the same kind of autoregressive/Transformer machinery used for discrete text tokens.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.how_it_works: Encoder produces a continuous latent z_e(x). A learned CODEBOOK of K embedding vectors {e_1,...,e_K} is maintained; z_e(x) is replaced ('quantised') by its NEAREST codebook vector: z_q(x) = e_k where k=argmin_j||z_e(x)-e_j||. The decoder reconstructs from z_q(x). Loss = reconstruction loss + 'codebook loss' (||sg[z_e(x)] - e_k||² — moves codebook vectors toward encoder outputs) + 'commitment loss' (||z_e(x) - sg[e_k]||² — encourages encoder outputs to stay close to codebook vectors), where sg=stop-gradient. The argmin (nearest-neighbor) operation is non-differentiable, so gradients are passed straight-through from decoder input to encoder output (straight-through estimator). After training, a separate autoregressive prior (PixelCNN, Transformer) is trained over the SEQUENCE of discrete codebook indices to enable generation.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.use_when: Building discrete latent representations of images/audio for subsequent autoregressive/Transformer-based generative modeling; tokenising continuous signals (images, audio, video) into discrete 'tokens' for multi-modal Transformer models.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.avoid_when: When a continuous latent space is sufficient/preferable (standard VAE use cases); when codebook collapse (only a small fraction of codebook vectors get used) becomes an issue — requires techniques like codebook resets or exponential-moving-average updates to mitigate.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.what_goes_wrong: 'Codebook collapse' — many codebook vectors go unused (the encoder only ever maps to a small subset), wasting representational capacity — mitigated with EMA-based codebook updates or periodically resetting unused codes; the straight-through gradient estimator is a biased approximation that can cause training instability if not tuned carefully.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.real_example: VQ-VAE-2 (2019) demonstrated high-fidelity image generation by combining hierarchical VQ-VAE discrete latents with PixelCNN priors; VQ-VAE's discrete-tokenisation approach is the direct conceptual ancestor of how modern multimodal models (e.g. tokenising images for input to Transformer-based LLMs) and the latent representations used in some video generation models work.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.what_it_is: A model (Esser, Rombach, Ommer 2021) that combines VQ-VAE's discrete codebook/tokenisation approach with an ADVERSARIAL (GAN) loss and PERCEPTUAL loss for the reconstruction objective, producing much higher-fidelity discrete image tokenisations than VQ-VAE's pixel-wise reconstruction loss alone, paired with a Transformer for autoregressive generation over the resulting tokens.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.why_it_exists: VQ-VAE's pixel-wise (L2/L1) reconstruction loss produces somewhat blurry reconstructions, limiting the quality of the discrete tokens it learns; VQ-GAN replaces/augments this with adversarial + perceptual losses (similar to how SRGAN improved on MSE-based super-resolution), producing sharper, more perceptually-faithful discrete image tokens — and the resulting compact token sequences can be modeled by a Transformer for high-quality, controllable generation.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.how_it_works: Same encoder-quantise-decoder structure as VQ-VAE, but the training loss adds: a PatchGAN-style discriminator (adversarial loss, distinguishing real images from VQ-GAN reconstructions) and a perceptual loss (e.g. LPIPS, comparing deep-feature representations of original vs. reconstructed images) — alongside the VQ-VAE codebook/commitment losses. After training the tokeniser (encoder+codebook+decoder) this way, a Transformer is trained autoregressively over the sequence of discrete token indices (e.g. a 16x16 grid of codebook indices for a 256x256 image), enabling high-resolution image generation by sampling tokens then decoding.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.use_when: High-resolution image (and video) generation via discrete-token + Transformer pipelines; as the tokeniser/detokeniser component in multimodal Transformer systems that need to represent images as discrete token sequences alongside text tokens.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.avoid_when: When latent diffusion (continuous latent + U-Net diffusion, as in Stable Diffusion) is more appropriate — VQ-GAN+Transformer autoregressive generation is generally SLOWER (sequential token generation) than diffusion's parallel denoising, though VQ-GAN's discrete tokeniser itself is ALSO used as a component within some latent diffusion-adjacent pipelines.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.what_goes_wrong: Autoregressive generation over the token sequence is sequential and can be slow for high-resolution images (many tokens); the adversarial training of the tokeniser introduces the usual GAN training instabilities (though typically more stable than full image-GAN training since the discriminator only needs to judge reconstruction quality, not generate from noise).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.real_example: VQ-GAN + Transformer (the 'Taming Transformers for High-Resolution Image Synthesis' paper, 2021) showed strong high-resolution generation results; this approach influenced subsequent multimodal models, and VQ-GAN-style discrete tokenisers (with adversarial+perceptual losses) remain a common building block for image tokenisation in vision-language and video generation research.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.what_it_is: An open-source library/family of models from Meta AI (2023) for generative audio — including MusicGen (text-to-music generation), AudioGen (text-to-sound-effect generation), and EnCodec (a neural audio codec) — combining discrete audio tokenisation (via EnCodec, conceptually similar to VQ-VAE/VQ-GAN for audio) with autoregressive Transformer-based generation conditioned on text.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.why_it_exists: Provides an accessible, open framework for text-conditioned audio generation (music and sound effects), addressing the need for high-quality, controllable audio synthesis analogous to what diffusion models achieved for images — built on a discrete-tokenisation + Transformer paradigm (similar to VQ-GAN's approach for images, but for audio waveforms).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.how_it_works: EnCodec (the audio tokeniser) is a neural codec — an autoencoder with a quantisation bottleneck (residual vector quantisation, RVQ — multiple codebooks applied in sequence to progressively reduce quantisation error) — trained with reconstruction + adversarial + perceptual losses (similar spirit to VQ-GAN) to compress raw audio waveforms into discrete token sequences at a much lower 'frame rate' than the original audio sample rate. MusicGen/AudioGen then train a Transformer LANGUAGE MODEL over these discrete audio tokens, conditioned on text embeddings (from a text encoder like T5), to autoregressively generate new audio token sequences from a text prompt — EnCodec's decoder then converts generated tokens back to a waveform. MusicGen uses a 'delay pattern' to handle the multiple RVQ codebook streams efficiently within a single Transformer.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.use_when: Text-to-music or text-to-sound-effect generation tasks; research/applications needing an open, modifiable audio generation stack (e.g. for fine-tuning on specific music styles).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.avoid_when: Tasks needing precise control over musical structure/composition beyond what text prompts can express (text-to-music models generally don't offer fine-grained note-level control); real-time/streaming generation where the autoregressive token-by-token generation introduces latency.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.what_goes_wrong: Like other autoregressive token-sequence generation, can be slower than parallel (diffusion-based) alternatives; the quality of generated audio is bounded by the EnCodec tokeniser's reconstruction fidelity (lossy compression artifacts can propagate); text-to-music models can struggle with precise temporal alignment to text descriptions involving specific timing/structure requests.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.real_example: MusicGen (part of AudioCraft, 2023) demonstrated generating coherent, stylistically-appropriate music clips from text prompts (e.g. 'upbeat electronic dance track with a strong bassline') and was released as open-source, enabling community fine-tuning for specific genres/styles — an example of the discrete-audio-token + Transformer paradigm applied to a new modality.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.what_it_is: A text-to-video generation model (announced by OpenAI, 2024) that generates high-resolution, temporally-coherent video clips (up to ~1 minute) from text prompts, built on a DIFFUSION TRANSFORMER (DiT) architecture operating on 'spacetime patches' — extending the latent-diffusion + Transformer paradigm from images to video.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.why_it_exists: Extending text-to-image diffusion success (Stable Diffusion, DALL-E) to VIDEO requires handling the additional temporal dimension — maintaining consistency of objects/scenes across frames, handling variable video lengths/resolutions/aspect ratios, and scaling compute for the much higher dimensionality of video data — Sora represents a significant scaling/architecture effort to address these challenges.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.how_it_works: Based on publicly-described details: videos (and images) are compressed into a lower-dimensional LATENT SPACE (via a video compression network, conceptually extending the VAE-based latent compression of Stable Diffusion to the temporal dimension), then represented as a sequence of 'spacetime patches' (analogous to image patches in ViT, but spanning both spatial and temporal extents). A DIFFUSION TRANSFORMER (DiT — replacing the U-Net backbone with a Transformer operating on these patch tokens) is trained to denoise these spacetime patches, conditioned on text (via cross-attention with text embeddings, similar to other text-to-image/video diffusion models). The patch-based representation natively supports variable video durations, resolutions, and aspect ratios (unlike fixed-resolution U-Net approaches) — patches just form a longer/shorter/differently-shaped sequence.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.use_when: Conceptual reference for understanding state-of-the-art (as of 2024) text-to-video generation architecture trends — specifically the shift from U-Net-based diffusion to TRANSFORMER-based diffusion (DiT) for scaling to higher-dimensional modalities like video.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.avoid_when: As of the 2024-2025 period, Sora itself was not broadly publicly available for general use (limited access) — for hands-on text-to-video work, open alternatives (e.g. various open-source video diffusion models) were the practical options; understanding Sora is primarily for grasping ARCHITECTURAL TRENDS (DiT for video) rather than as a tool to use directly.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.what_goes_wrong: Video generation models (including Sora, per OpenAI's own published limitations) can struggle with physical plausibility over longer durations (objects appearing/disappearing inconsistently, violations of physical dynamics like objects passing through each other), and the enormous compute cost of training/running video diffusion models at scale remains a major barrier.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Gene.real_example: Sora's 'spacetime patches' + DiT approach reflects the broader 2023-2025 trend (also seen in Stable Diffusion 3's MM-DiT) of replacing U-Net backbones with Transformer backbones in diffusion models — leveraging Transformers' proven scaling properties (more compute/data → predictably better performance) for generative modeling of increasingly high-dimensional data (video, after images).

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_it_is: A regularisation technique for classification that replaces 'hard' one-hot target labels (1 for the correct class, 0 for others) with 'soft' targets — e.g. (1-ε) for the correct class and ε/(K-1) for each of the other K-1 classes, where ε is a small constant (e.g. 0.1).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.why_it_exists: Training with hard 0/1 targets and softmax+cross-entropy pushes the model toward producing extremely confident (near 0/1) predictions, requiring logits to diverge toward ±∞ — this can lead to overfitting and overconfident/poorly-calibrated predictions; label smoothing caps the achievable 'confidence' and acts as a regulariser.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.how_it_works: Cross-entropy loss L = -Σ_k y_k·log(p_k) where y_k is the target. With label smoothing, y_correct = 1-ε and y_other = ε/(K-1) (instead of 1 and 0). The model is now penalised for being TOO confident even on correct predictions (since the target for the correct class is <1), preventing logits from growing unboundedly and keeping the model's output distribution less peaked/more calibrated.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.use_when: Training classifiers (image classification, etc.) where calibration and slight regularisation are beneficial — widely used in training recipes for ImageNet classifiers (Inception, EfficientNet) and sequence models (machine translation in the original Transformer paper).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.avoid_when: Tasks where extremely confident/sharp predictions are explicitly desired and well-justified by abundant clean data; knowledge distillation pipelines where the 'soft' teacher signal already serves a similar regularising role (combining both may need careful tuning).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_goes_wrong: Too-high ε (e.g. >0.2-0.3) can hurt accuracy by making the targets too uniform/uninformative; label smoothing slightly changes the interpretation of output probabilities (they're systematically less extreme), which can affect downstream uses of the raw probabilities (e.g. confidence thresholding) if not accounted for.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.real_example: The original Transformer paper ('Attention is All You Need', 2017) used label smoothing with ε=0.1 for machine translation, reporting it 'hurts perplexity... but improves accuracy and BLEU score' — a frequently-cited example of a regulariser that trades off one metric for better generalisation on another.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_it_is: A regularisation technique for deep residual networks that, during training, RANDOMLY SKIPS entire residual blocks/layers (with some probability, replacing the block's output with just the identity/skip-connection pass-through) — at inference, all blocks are used (often with a rescaling).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.why_it_exists: Very deep residual networks (hundreds of layers) can suffer from diminishing returns/overfitting/vanishing gradients despite skip connections — stochastic depth acts like 'dropout at the layer level', creating an implicit ensemble of networks with varying effective depths during training, improving gradient flow to early layers (shorter effective paths during training) and regularising the model.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.how_it_works: For a residual block computing y = x + f(x), with 'survival probability' p_l (often varying linearly with depth — later layers have lower survival probability), during training: with probability p_l, y = x + f(x) (block active); with probability 1-p_l, y = x (block skipped entirely, f(x) not computed, identity pass-through). At inference, all blocks are active, with f(x) sometimes rescaled by the expected survival probability p_l to match the expected value seen during training (similar to dropout's train/inference scaling).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.use_when: Training very deep networks (ResNets with 100+ layers, Vision Transformers with many blocks) where overfitting or training difficulty at extreme depth is a concern.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.avoid_when: Shallow/moderate-depth networks where the regularisation benefit is minimal and the added training complexity/hyperparameters (per-layer survival probabilities) aren't worth it.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_goes_wrong: Choosing the survival probability schedule (constant vs. linearly decaying with depth) is an additional hyperparameter; if applied too aggressively (very low survival probabilities), can slow convergence by effectively creating very shallow networks early in training too often.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.real_example: Huang et al. 'Deep Networks with Stochastic Depth' (2016) enabled training of 1200+ layer ResNets that would otherwise be impractical to train; 'DropPath' (the same technique, renamed) is a standard component of modern Vision Transformer and ConvNeXt training recipes (e.g. timm library's training configs for ViT/ConvNeXt use DropPath rates that increase with network depth).

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_it_is: A data augmentation technique (Zhang et al. 2017) that creates new training examples by taking CONVEX COMBINATIONS (weighted linear interpolations) of pairs of training images AND their labels: x_mix = λ·x_i + (1-λ)·x_j, y_mix = λ·y_i + (1-λ)·y_j, where λ~Beta(α,α).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.why_it_exists: Standard training only sees 'hard' examples at the vertices of the data manifold's convex hull (the original images and their one-hot labels) — mixup encourages the model to behave LINEARLY between training examples, smoothing decision boundaries, improving generalisation, robustness to adversarial examples, and calibration.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.how_it_works: For each training step, sample a mixing coefficient λ from a Beta(α,α) distribution (α is a hyperparameter, e.g. 0.2-1.0 — controls how 'mixed' examples typically are; α→0 means λ is usually close to 0 or 1, i.e. mostly original images; α=1 gives a uniform distribution over λ). Pick two random training examples (x_i,y_i) and (x_j,y_j), form x_mix=λx_i+(1-λ)x_j (pixel-wise interpolation) and y_mix=λy_i+(1-λ)y_j (soft label interpolation, requiring one-hot/soft labels and cross-entropy with the SOFT target). Train on (x_mix, y_mix) instead of (or in addition to) original examples.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.use_when: Image classification tasks (and beyond — mixup has been applied to tabular, speech, NLP data) where additional regularisation, robustness, and calibration improvements are desired, especially with limited data.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.avoid_when: Tasks where pixel-wise linear interpolation between images doesn't produce semantically meaningful inputs in a way that helps (e.g. some structured prediction tasks); when combined with other strong augmentations (CutMix, RandAugment), the combination needs tuning to avoid over-regularising.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_goes_wrong: Mixed images can look unnatural/blurry (a ghostly blend of two images) — some argue this creates an unrealistic training distribution; the α hyperparameter requires tuning, and mixup's benefits are less pronounced for some architectures/tasks than others.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.real_example: Mixup is a standard component of strong image classification training recipes (e.g. used in training EfficientNet, and the 'bag of tricks' recipes for ResNet that pushed ImageNet accuracy higher); also adapted for tasks like speech recognition and tabular data classification.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_it_is: A data augmentation technique (Yun et al. 2019) that, like Mixup, combines two training images and their labels — but instead of pixel-wise blending, CUTS a rectangular PATCH from one image and PASTES it onto another, with the label mixed proportionally to the AREA of the patch.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.why_it_exists: Mixup's pixel-blended images can look unnatural (ghosting artifacts) and may not match real-world image statistics well; CutMix produces more 'natural-looking' composite images (a patch of one image embedded in another, like a collage) while still providing the regularisation/robustness benefits of mixed-label training — and additionally encourages the model to attend to multiple/localised regions (since the patch could contain a different object than the rest of the image).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.how_it_works: Sample a mixing ratio λ~Beta(α,α), determine a rectangular region with area proportional to (1-λ) of the total image area, randomly positioned. Cut that region from image x_j and paste it into the corresponding region of image x_i, producing x_mix. The label is mixed proportionally to the patch area: y_mix = λ·y_i + (1-λ)·y_j (where λ is the fraction of the image area NOT replaced, i.e. still from x_i).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.use_when: Image classification (and object detection, with adapted bounding-box handling) where you want regularisation benefits with more 'realistic' augmented images than Mixup's blending; particularly effective alongside label smoothing and other regularisers in strong training recipes.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.avoid_when: Tasks where pasting a rectangular patch from one image onto another could create misleading spatial/contextual cues that conflict with the task (e.g. some segmentation tasks where exact pixel-level labels matter and the patch boundary creates label ambiguity at the cut edges).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_goes_wrong: The patch boundary creates a 'hard edge' that's not present in natural images — though this is generally less problematic than Mixup's full-image blending; like Mixup, requires soft/mixed-label-compatible loss functions (cross-entropy with non-one-hot targets).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.real_example: CutMix was shown to improve ImageNet classification accuracy and, notably, OBJECT DETECTION AND WEAKLY-SUPERVISED LOCALISATION performance (since the model learns to find relevant features even when objects are partially occluded by the pasted patch) — it's part of many modern 'training recipe' papers (e.g. ResNet strikes back, ConvNeXt training recipes) combined with Mixup, RandAugment, and label smoothing.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_it_is: A data augmentation technique (Hendrycks et al. 2020) that generates augmented images by applying CHAINS of randomly-sampled augmentation operations (from a set like AutoAugment's operation pool) in PARALLEL, then mixing the results together via convex combination, and additionally enforces consistency between the original and augmented images' predictions via a Jensen-Shannon Divergence consistency loss.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.why_it_exists: Many augmentation strategies improve in-distribution accuracy but can hurt robustness to DISTRIBUTION SHIFT (e.g. images corrupted by noise, blur, weather effects not seen in training) — AugMix is designed to improve both standard accuracy AND robustness to such corruptions/distribution shift, without training on the actual corruption types being evaluated.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.how_it_works: Generate k (e.g. 3) different 'augmentation chains', each a composition of several randomly-sampled augmentation operations (rotate, translate, color jitter, etc., each with random severity) applied to the original image. Combine these k augmented versions via a random convex combination (weights from a Dirichlet distribution) to produce the final augmented image — this 'mixing' of multiple augmentation chains produces more diverse, less extreme augmented images than any single chain alone. Additionally, the training loss includes a Jensen-Shannon Divergence term encouraging the model's predictions on the original image and its augmented version(s) to be CONSISTENT (similar to consistency regularisation in semi-supervised learning).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.use_when: When robustness to distributional shift/corruptions (not just in-distribution test accuracy) is an important evaluation criterion — safety-critical vision applications, deployment scenarios with variable image quality/conditions.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.avoid_when: When only standard in-distribution accuracy matters and computational simplicity is preferred — AugMix's multiple augmentation chains + JSD consistency loss adds training complexity/compute compared to simpler augmentation schemes (RandAugment, Mixup).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_goes_wrong: Adds computational overhead (generating multiple augmentation chains and computing predictions for consistency loss); the benefit is most pronounced on ROBUSTNESS benchmarks (e.g. ImageNet-C, a corrupted version of ImageNet) — gains on standard clean-accuracy benchmarks may be more modest.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.real_example: AugMix significantly improved performance on ImageNet-C (a benchmark of ImageNet images with 15 types of synthetic corruptions like noise, blur, fog, at 5 severity levels) without training on any corrupted images — demonstrating that the AUGMENTATION DIVERSITY + CONSISTENCY REGULARISATION combination generalises to unseen corruption types, an important result for robustness research.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_it_is: An automated data augmentation policy (Cubuk et al. 2019) that randomly samples a sequence of N augmentation operations (from a fixed set of ~14 operations like rotation, shear, color jitter, contrast, etc.) with a SINGLE global magnitude parameter M controlling the strength of all operations — a much simpler search space than its predecessor AutoAugment.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.why_it_exists: AutoAugment (the predecessor) searches for optimal augmentation POLICIES (which operations, in what order, at what magnitudes, with what probabilities) using reinforcement learning over a huge search space — extremely expensive (thousands of GPU-hours). RandAugment showed that a much SIMPLER scheme — randomly sample N operations each time, with a SHARED magnitude M — achieves comparable or better results, with only 2 hyperparameters (N, M) to tune via a small grid search instead of a massive policy search.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.how_it_works: Define a set of K=~14 augmentation operations (rotate, translate-x/y, shear-x/y, color, contrast, brightness, sharpness, posterize, solarize, equalize, autocontrast, cutout, etc.), each parameterised by a magnitude in [0, M_max]. For each training image, randomly sample N operations (uniformly, with replacement) from this set, and apply them in sequence, each at magnitude M (the SAME M for all operations and all images — a single global hyperparameter, found via grid search, often N=2, M~9-10 out of a max scale of ~30).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.use_when: Image classification training where strong augmentation improves generalisation, and you want an automated augmentation scheme without the cost of AutoAugment's policy search — RandAugment is a standard component of many 'training recipe' papers.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.avoid_when: Very small datasets where strong augmentation might destroy too much signal relative to the limited data; tasks where the predefined operation set isn't appropriate (e.g. operations like rotation/shear may not make sense for certain non-natural-image data).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_goes_wrong: The global magnitude M is a single number applied uniformly — some images/operations may be more sensitive to high magnitude than others (no per-operation tuning), though this simplicity is also RandAugment's main advantage; combining RandAugment with other strong augmentations (Mixup, CutMix) without re-tuning N/M can over-regularise.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.real_example: RandAugment is part of the training recipes for EfficientNet (the 'EfficientNet-B7 + RandAugment' results), Vision Transformers, and many subsequent 'recipe' papers — it's available as a standard transform in `torchvision.transforms.RandAugment` and TensorFlow's augmentation libraries.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_it_is: An inference-time technique that generates MULTIPLE augmented versions of a single test input (e.g. original, horizontally-flipped, multiple crops/scales), runs the model on each, and AVERAGES (or otherwise aggregates) the predictions to produce the final output.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.why_it_exists: A model's prediction can vary depending on small input variations (crop position, flip, scale) — averaging predictions across several such variations reduces prediction variance, often improving accuracy/robustness at the cost of additional INFERENCE compute (multiple forward passes per test example).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.how_it_works: For a test image x, generate a set of augmented versions {x_1=x, x_2=flip(x), x_3=crop_1(x), ...} (often using the SAME types of augmentations used during training, but without randomness — a fixed, deterministic set of transforms). Run the model on each x_i to get predictions p_i (e.g. softmax probability vectors). Aggregate: p_final = average(p_1,...,p_n) (or other aggregation like geometric mean). Use p_final for the final classification/prediction.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.use_when: When inference-time compute budget allows multiple forward passes per example and accuracy matters more than latency — common in competitions (Kaggle) and offline batch-prediction scenarios; particularly useful for ensembling predictions across multiple scales/crops in image classification or segmentation.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.avoid_when: Real-time/low-latency inference scenarios — TTA multiplies inference cost by the number of augmented views (e.g. 5-10x), which is often unacceptable for production serving with tight latency requirements.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_goes_wrong: Increases inference latency/cost proportionally to the number of augmented views, which can be a deal-breaker for production serving; gains from TTA are often modest (a fraction of a percent to a couple percent accuracy) and must be weighed against the compute cost.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.real_example: Kaggle competition winning solutions frequently use TTA (e.g. horizontal flip + multiple crop scales, averaged) as a 'free' accuracy boost when leaderboard score matters more than inference cost; some production image classification systems use a LIMITED form of TTA (e.g. just horizontal flip averaging) when the latency cost is acceptable.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_it_is: A model compression technique (Hinton, Vinyals, Dean 2015) where a smaller 'student' model is trained to mimic the output distribution of a larger, pretrained 'teacher' model — using the teacher's SOFT predictions (probability distributions, not just hard labels) as additional training signal.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.why_it_exists: Large models often generalise better but are too expensive for deployment (latency, memory, cost); knowledge distillation transfers some of the large model's learned 'knowledge' — encoded in the RELATIVE probabilities it assigns to incorrect classes (e.g. a teacher might say an image of a '7' is 90% '7' but also 5% '1' and 3% '9', reflecting visual similarity) — to a smaller, deployable student model, often achieving better accuracy than training the student from scratch on hard labels alone.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.how_it_works: Train (or use a pretrained) large teacher model T. For each training example, compute the teacher's SOFTENED output distribution (using a 'temperature' τ>1 in the softmax: p_i = exp(z_i/τ)/Σexp(z_j/τ), which makes the distribution less peaked, revealing more information about relative class similarities). Train the student S to minimise a combination of: (1) standard cross-entropy with the true hard labels, and (2) a 'distillation loss' — typically KL-divergence or cross-entropy between the student's softened output and the teacher's softened output (also at temperature τ). The combined loss is often weighted: L = α·L_hard + (1-α)·τ²·L_soft (the τ² factor compensates for the gradient-scaling effect of the temperature).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.use_when: Deploying a smaller/faster model while retaining as much accuracy as possible from a larger model — model compression for edge/mobile deployment, reducing inference cost in production, or transferring knowledge from an ensemble to a single model.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.avoid_when: When the student architecture is fundamentally too small/different to represent the teacher's learned function well (distillation can't make a tiny model learn what a vastly larger model 'knows' if the capacity gap is too large); when training compute for running BOTH teacher and student (teacher inference needed during student training, unless precomputed) isn't available.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_goes_wrong: Choosing the temperature τ and the α weighting between hard and soft losses requires tuning; if the teacher is poorly calibrated or makes systematic errors, the student inherits those biases; very large capacity gaps between teacher and student can limit how much distillation helps (sometimes an intermediate-sized 'teaching assistant' model helps bridge large gaps).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.real_example: DistilBERT (2019) used knowledge distillation to compress BERT into a model with ~40% fewer parameters while retaining ~97% of BERT's performance on language understanding benchmarks — a widely-cited example of distillation enabling practical deployment of large pretrained language models; distillation is also used to compress large vision models for mobile deployment (e.g. distilling a ResNet teacher into a MobileNet student).

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.what_it_is: The CNN architecture (Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Hinton 2012) that won the ImageNet ILSVRC 2012 competition by a massive margin (top-5 error 15.3% vs. 26.2% for the runner-up), often credited as the catalyst for the deep learning revolution in computer vision.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.why_it_exists: To demonstrate that a sufficiently large, deep CNN trained on a sufficiently large dataset (ImageNet, 1.2M images) with sufficient compute (GPUs) could dramatically outperform hand-engineered feature + classifier pipelines (SIFT/HOG + SVM) that dominated computer vision before 2012.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.how_it_works: 8 learned layers: 5 convolutional layers (with large filters in early layers, e.g. 11x11 stride 4 in layer 1) followed by 3 fully-connected layers, ending in a 1000-way softmax. Key innovations for its time: ReLU activations (instead of tanh/sigmoid — much faster training), training on TWO GPUs (splitting the network across them due to memory limits — 3GB GPUs at the time), local response normalisation (largely abandoned later in favor of batch norm), overlapping max pooling, and dropout (0.5) in the fully-connected layers plus data augmentation (crops, flips, PCA color jitter) to combat overfitting given the then-large 60M parameter count.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.use_when: Educational/historical context — understanding the architecture that proved deep CNNs + GPUs + big data could work; rarely used directly today.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.avoid_when: Any modern application — AlexNet is significantly outperformed by virtually every architecture developed since (VGG, ResNet, EfficientNet, ViT) on accuracy, and its large fully-connected layers (most of its 60M parameters) are inefficient by modern standards.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.what_goes_wrong: By modern standards: too many parameters concentrated in FC layers (inefficient), no batch normalisation (wasn't invented yet — relied on careful initialisation and local response norm), the dual-GPU split architecture is an artifact of 2012 hardware constraints not a design choice worth replicating.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.real_example: AlexNet's ImageNet 2012 win (15.3% vs 26.2% top-5 error) is the canonical 'before and after' moment cited in nearly every deep learning history/course — within a few years, the entire computer vision field shifted from hand-engineered features to learned CNN features as a direct consequence.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.what_it_is: A family of CNN architectures (Simonyan & Zisserman 2014, Visual Geometry Group at Oxford) — most famously VGG-16 and VGG-19 — characterised by extreme architectural UNIFORMITY: stacks of small 3x3 convolutions (with ReLU) and 2x2 max pooling, repeated to build very deep (16-19 weight layers) networks.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.why_it_exists: To systematically study the effect of network DEPTH on performance, while keeping the architecture as simple/uniform as possible (only 3x3 convs and 2x2 max pools) — demonstrating that depth alone (with small, uniform filters) was a key driver of accuracy improvements over AlexNet's larger, more varied filter sizes.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.how_it_works: Stacks of 3x3 conv layers (stride 1, padding 1 — preserves spatial dimensions) with ReLU, periodically followed by 2x2 max pooling (stride 2 — halves spatial dimensions), with the number of channels doubling after each pooling stage (64→128→256→512→512). Two stacked 3x3 convs have the same RECEPTIVE FIELD as one 5x5 conv but with fewer parameters and an extra nonlinearity (more expressive) — this 'small filters, more layers' principle became foundational. Ends with 3 large fully-connected layers (4096, 4096, 1000) — these FC layers contain the vast majority (~90%) of VGG's ~138M parameters.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.use_when: As a FEATURE EXTRACTOR for transfer learning in some applications (VGG features are still used in some perceptual loss functions, e.g. VGG-based perceptual loss in SRGAN/style transfer, due to their well-studied, smooth feature representations); educational context for understanding the 'depth + small filters' design principle.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.avoid_when: Training from scratch for new tasks — VGG's huge parameter count (138M, mostly in FC layers) and computational cost are inefficient compared to ResNet/EfficientNet/ConvNeXt which achieve much better accuracy with far fewer parameters/FLOPs.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.what_goes_wrong: The massive FC layers (mostly redundant parameters) make VGG slow and memory-hungry; without residual connections, VGG-19 is near the practical depth limit trainable without architectural tricks — going deeper with this design (without skip connections) leads to the vanishing gradient/degradation problem that ResNet later solved.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.real_example: VGG-16's features (particularly intermediate conv layer activations) remain widely used as the 'perceptual loss' network in style transfer (Gatys et al. neural style transfer) and super-resolution (SRGAN) — even though VGG itself is rarely used as a primary classifier today, its learned features are valued for capturing perceptually-meaningful image statistics.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.what_it_is: A CNN architecture (Szegedy et al. 2014, Google) that won ImageNet 2014, introducing the 'Inception module' — a building block that applies MULTIPLE filter sizes (1x1, 3x3, 5x5) and pooling IN PARALLEL within the same layer, concatenating their outputs, allowing the network to capture features at multiple scales simultaneously.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.why_it_exists: Different objects/features in images appear at different scales — rather than committing to a single filter size per layer (as VGG does), Inception modules let the network learn to combine information from multiple receptive field sizes at each stage, while 1x1 convolutions ('bottleneck' layers) reduce channel dimensionality before expensive 3x3/5x5 convolutions, keeping computational cost manageable despite the multi-branch design.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.how_it_works: Each Inception module has parallel branches: a 1x1 conv, a 1x1 conv followed by 3x3 conv, a 1x1 conv followed by 5x5 conv, and a pooling branch — outputs concatenated along the channel dimension. The 1x1 convs BEFORE the 3x3/5x5 branches act as dimensionality-reduction 'bottlenecks' (e.g. reducing 256 channels to 64 before a 5x5 conv reduces that conv's compute by ~16x compared to operating on 256 channels directly). GoogLeNet (22 layers) also used AUXILIARY CLASSIFIERS — extra softmax outputs attached to intermediate layers during training, providing additional gradient signal to combat vanishing gradients in this deep network (auxiliary classifiers are discarded at inference).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.use_when: Educational context for understanding multi-scale feature extraction and the 1x1-conv-as-bottleneck pattern — both ideas (multi-branch modules, 1x1 bottlenecks) heavily influenced later architectures (ResNet's bottleneck blocks, EfficientNet's inverted bottlenecks).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.avoid_when: Modern production use — Inception's complex multi-branch design is harder to implement/optimise efficiently on modern hardware than simpler, more uniform architectures (ResNet, EfficientNet); later Inception versions (v2/v3/v4) added batch norm and further refinements but the architecture family has largely been superseded.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.what_goes_wrong: The multi-branch design with many different operations per module makes the architecture harder to tune and less hardware-friendly (modern accelerators favor simple, repeated, uniform operations that can be heavily optimised) compared to ResNet's simple repeated blocks.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.real_example: The 1x1-convolution-as-channel-bottleneck idea from Inception directly inspired ResNet's 'bottleneck block' design (1x1 reduce → 3x3 → 1x1 expand) used in ResNet-50/101/152, and the broader 'depthwise separable convolution' efficiency techniques in MobileNet trace conceptual lineage to Inception's factorisation ideas (Inception v3 explicitly used factorised/separable convolutions).

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.what_it_is: Residual Network (He et al. 2015, Microsoft Research) — the architecture that introduced 'skip connections' (residual connections) allowing layers to learn a RESIDUAL function f(x) relative to the identity, via y = f(x) + x, enabling training of networks with 50, 101, even 1000+ layers that were previously untrainable due to vanishing gradients/degradation.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.why_it_exists: Before ResNet, simply stacking more layers (even with batch norm) caused TRAINING accuracy to get WORSE beyond a certain depth (the 'degradation problem') — counterintuitively, deeper plain networks were harder to optimise, not just more prone to overfitting. ResNet's insight: if the identity mapping is a good solution for extra layers, it should be EASY for the network to learn — but plain (non-residual) layers struggle to learn an identity mapping via stacked nonlinear transformations; explicitly providing the identity as a 'shortcut' makes learning small modifications to it trivial (just push the residual branch's weights toward zero).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.how_it_works: Each residual block computes y = F(x, {W_i}) + x — the input x is added directly to the block's transformed output (a skip/shortcut connection, using a 1x1 conv if dimensions need to change for the addition). This means gradients can flow directly through the identity shortcut during backprop (∂y/∂x includes a direct +1 term, regardless of how small F's gradients become), largely solving vanishing gradients for very deep networks. ResNet-50/101/152 use 'bottleneck blocks' (1x1 conv to reduce channels → 3x3 conv → 1x1 conv to restore channels — reducing compute, inspired by Inception's bottleneck idea) instead of the simple 'basic blocks' (two 3x3 convs) used in ResNet-18/34.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.use_when: THE default backbone choice for a huge range of computer vision tasks (classification, detection, segmentation) for years — still a strong, well-understood baseline; the residual connection PRINCIPLE (not necessarily the exact ResNet architecture) is used in essentially every modern deep architecture, including Transformers (residual connections around attention/FFN sublayers).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.avoid_when: When state-of-the-art accuracy/efficiency is the priority — EfficientNet, ConvNeXt, and Vision Transformers generally outperform ResNet at equivalent compute budgets on ImageNet and other benchmarks (though ResNet remains a respectable, well-tooled baseline).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.what_goes_wrong: Plain (non-residual) very deep networks suffer the degradation problem ResNet solves — without skip connections, training accuracy DECREASES with added depth beyond ~20-30 layers, an at-first-surprising empirical finding that motivated ResNet's design.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.real_example: ResNet won ImageNet 2015 and its core idea — additive skip connections enabling gradient flow through arbitrarily deep stacks — is THE single architectural innovation most directly reused across the entire deep learning field, including being a core component of every Transformer block (`x = x + Attention(LayerNorm(x))` and `x = x + FFN(LayerNorm(x))` are residual connections).

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.what_it_is: Densely Connected Convolutional Network (Huang et al. 2017) — an architecture where each layer within a 'dense block' receives as input the CONCATENATION of the feature maps from ALL preceding layers in that block (not just the immediately preceding layer), and passes its own output forward to all subsequent layers.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.why_it_exists: ResNet's additive skip connections (y=F(x)+x) sum information, potentially losing some distinctiveness between feature maps from different depths; DenseNet's CONCATENATION-based connections preserve all feature maps explicitly, encouraging feature reuse across the network, improving gradient flow (every layer has a direct path to the loss via shorter connections to all subsequent layers), and often achieving comparable accuracy with FEWER parameters than ResNet (since each layer can be narrower — it has access to all previous features via concatenation, not just its immediate predecessor's transformed output).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.how_it_works: Within a 'dense block', layer L's input is the concatenation of ALL feature maps from layers 0,1,...,L-1 (where layer 0 is the block's input). Each layer produces a small number of new feature maps ('growth rate' k, e.g. k=32), which get concatenated onto the growing 'collective knowledge' passed to subsequent layers. Between dense blocks, 'transition layers' (1x1 conv + pooling) reduce the channel count and spatial dimensions (since concatenation otherwise causes channel counts to grow linearly with depth within a block — transitions periodically reset/reduce this).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.use_when: Tasks where parameter efficiency matters (DenseNet often matches ResNet accuracy with significantly fewer parameters) and where feature reuse across scales is valuable (e.g. some medical imaging applications where DenseNet variants remain popular).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.avoid_when: Very memory-constrained training — the concatenation operations mean DenseNet's MEMORY usage during training can be higher than its parameter count would suggest (all the concatenated feature maps must be kept for backprop), a notable practical drawback despite parameter efficiency.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.what_goes_wrong: Memory consumption during training can be surprisingly high due to the concatenation-heavy design (many feature maps must be retained), even though the PARAMETER count is low — this memory/parameter mismatch is a common point of confusion and a practical deployment consideration.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.real_example: DenseNet-121/169/201 remain popular backbones in medical imaging (e.g. chest X-ray classification, as in the CheXNet model for pneumonia detection) where the parameter efficiency and strong gradient flow for relatively smaller training datasets is valued.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.what_it_is: A family of CNN architectures (Howard et al. 2017, Google; MobileNetV2 2018, MobileNetV3 2019) designed specifically for MOBILE/EDGE deployment, built around DEPTHWISE SEPARABLE CONVOLUTIONS — factorising a standard convolution into a depthwise (per-channel spatial) convolution followed by a pointwise (1x1, cross-channel) convolution, dramatically reducing parameters and computation.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.why_it_exists: Standard convolutions (which mix spatial AND cross-channel information simultaneously in one operation) are computationally expensive; mobile/embedded devices have tight constraints on model size, FLOPs, and latency/power consumption — MobileNet's depthwise-separable factorisation provides a ~8-9x reduction in computation/parameters vs. standard convolutions with similar receptive fields, at a modest accuracy cost.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.how_it_works: A standard conv with kernel k×k, C_in input channels, C_out output channels costs k²·C_in·C_out per output pixel. Depthwise separable factorises this into: (1) DEPTHWISE conv — apply a k×k filter to EACH input channel SEPARATELY (no cross-channel mixing), cost k²·C_in; (2) POINTWISE conv — a 1x1 conv mixing channels, cost C_in·C_out. Total cost k²·C_in + C_in·C_out vs. k²·C_in·C_out for standard conv — for k=3, C_out=256, this is roughly an 8-9x reduction. MobileNetV2 added 'inverted residuals' (expand channels with 1x1 conv → depthwise 3x3 → project back down with 1x1, with a residual connection around the whole block — 'inverted' because the residual connects the NARROW representations, while expansion happens in between) and linear bottlenecks (no nonlinearity on the final projection, to avoid destroying information in the low-dimensional space). MobileNetV3 used neural architecture search (NAS) plus the 'squeeze-and-excitation' attention mechanism and h-swish activation.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.use_when: On-device/edge inference — mobile apps, embedded vision systems, any deployment where model size, FLOPs, and power consumption are primary constraints alongside accuracy.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.avoid_when: Server-side/cloud inference where compute is abundant and maximum accuracy matters more than efficiency — larger architectures (ResNet, EfficientNet, ConvNeXt) typically achieve higher accuracy when efficiency isn't the binding constraint.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.what_goes_wrong: Depthwise separable convolutions, while FLOP-efficient, don't always translate to proportional WALL-CLOCK speedups on all hardware (memory access patterns/kernel launch overhead for depthwise convs can be less GPU-friendly than dense convs on some accelerators) — efficiency gains are most pronounced on mobile CPUs/specialised mobile accelerators that MobileNet was designed for.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.real_example: MobileNet (all versions) powers on-device computer vision in countless Android/iOS apps (e.g. Google's MLKit, real-time object detection/segmentation in camera apps) where running a ResNet-sized model would be infeasible on phone hardware/battery constraints.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.what_it_is: A family of CNN architectures (Tan & Le 2019, Google) derived via 'compound scaling' — a principled method for jointly scaling network DEPTH, WIDTH, and input RESOLUTION together (using a single compound coefficient φ) rather than scaling just one dimension, applied to a NAS-discovered baseline architecture (EfficientNet-B0).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.why_it_exists: Prior scaling practice typically scaled ONE dimension at a time (deeper OR wider OR higher resolution) somewhat arbitrarily — EfficientNet's authors observed that depth, width, and resolution are INTERDEPENDENT (e.g. higher resolution images benefit from more layers/channels to capture the additional detail) and derived a balanced scaling rule (depth∝α^φ, width∝β^φ, resolution∝γ^φ, with α·β²·γ²≈2, found via small grid search) that achieves much better accuracy-per-FLOP than single-dimension scaling.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.how_it_works: Start with EfficientNet-B0, a baseline architecture found via neural architecture search (using MobileNetV2's inverted-residual/MBConv blocks as the search space, plus squeeze-and-excitation attention). Apply compound scaling with coefficient φ (B0→φ=0, B1→φ=1, ..., B7→φ=7) to scale depth/width/resolution together according to the found α,β,γ — producing EfficientNet-B0 through B7, spanning a wide range of accuracy/compute tradeoffs from a SINGLE base architecture and scaling rule, rather than separately-designed architectures for each size.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.use_when: When you need a model at a SPECIFIC accuracy/compute operating point and want a principled way to choose the right 'size' — EfficientNet's B0-B7 family provides a smooth Pareto frontier of accuracy vs. FLOPs that was state-of-the-art for CNN efficiency for several years.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.avoid_when: When training infrastructure/hardware isn't well-suited to the MBConv block's depthwise convolutions and squeeze-excitation operations (similar hardware-utilisation caveats as MobileNet); ConvNeXt and Vision Transformers have since matched/exceeded EfficientNet's accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs on modern accelerators with simpler, more hardware-friendly designs.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.what_goes_wrong: Like MobileNet, the depthwise-conv-heavy MBConv blocks can have less favorable actual GPU utilisation/throughput than their FLOP-count would suggest, especially on hardware optimised for dense matrix multiplications (this observation partly motivated ConvNeXt's return to simpler, larger, dense convolutions).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.real_example: EfficientNet-B7 achieved then-SOTA ImageNet accuracy (84.4% top-1) with significantly fewer parameters/FLOPs than prior SOTA models (e.g. ~8.4x fewer parameters than the previous best GPipe-trained AmoebaNet) — EfficientNet's compound scaling methodology also influenced later work like EfficientDet (object detection) and the scaling-law-driven design philosophy seen in later LLM scaling research.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.what_it_is: A 'modernised' pure-convolutional architecture (Liu et al. 2022, Meta/FAIR) that takes a standard ResNet and incrementally applies a series of design choices BORROWED FROM Vision Transformers (large kernel sizes, fewer activation functions, LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm, GELU instead of ReLU, inverted bottleneck/depthwise convs, separate downsampling layers) — showing that a pure-ConvNet can MATCH or EXCEED Vision Transformer (Swin) performance, challenging the narrative that Transformers are inherently superior to CNNs for vision.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.why_it_exists: Vision Transformers (ViT, Swin) had begun outperforming CNNs on ImageNet and downstream tasks around 2020-2021, leading to a narrative that attention-based architectures were fundamentally better for vision — ConvNeXt's authors systematically tested whether the GAP was due to the attention MECHANISM itself, or due to many smaller TRAINING/ARCHITECTURE design choices that had accumulated in the Transformer literature — finding it was largely the latter.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.how_it_works: Starting from ResNet-50, apply a sequence of changes one at a time, measuring the impact of each: (1) change stage compute ratio to match Swin (1:1:3:1); (2) replace the stem with a 'patchify' layer (4x4 non-overlapping conv, like ViT's patch embedding); (3) adopt ResNeXt-style grouped/depthwise convolutions; (4) use an INVERTED bottleneck (wide→narrow→wide, like MobileNetV2/Transformer FFN, rather than ResNet's narrow→wide→narrow); (5) increase kernel size to 7x7 (large kernels, like attention's large receptive field); (6) replace ReLU with GELU, BatchNorm with LayerNorm, and reduce the NUMBER of activation/normalisation layers (Transformers use far fewer nonlinearities per block than CNNs traditionally did); (7) use separate downsampling layers between stages. Each change is ADDITIVE and the paper shows the accumulated improvements close the gap with Swin Transformer entirely — ending with a pure-convolutional architecture matching Swin's accuracy.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.use_when: Modern computer vision tasks where you want a strong, simple, hardware-friendly (pure convolution, no attention) backbone with accuracy competitive with Vision Transformers — ConvNeXt is a strong default choice for many vision tasks as of 2022+.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.avoid_when: Tasks specifically benefiting from attention's global receptive field/dynamic routing properties from the first layer (though ConvNeXt's 7x7 kernels provide fairly large receptive fields too); multimodal settings where a shared Transformer architecture across modalities (vision + text) is architecturally convenient.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.what_goes_wrong: N/A as a 'failure mode' — ConvNeXt's main 'lesson' is more about methodology: it demonstrates that comparing 'CNN vs Transformer' often conflates ARCHITECTURE differences with TRAINING RECIPE differences (data augmentation, optimizer, schedule, regularisation) — much of Transformers' apparent advantage came from modern training recipes that are equally applicable to CNNs.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.real_example: ConvNeXt matched Swin Transformer's accuracy on ImageNet classification, COCO object detection, and ADE20K segmentation while being a pure ConvNet — frequently cited as a key data point in the ongoing 'CNN vs Transformer for vision' discussion, showing the gap is much smaller than headline numbers from 2020-2021 suggested once training recipes are equalised.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.what_it_is: A family of CNN architectures (Radosavovic et al. 2020, Facebook AI) discovered via 'design space design' — instead of searching for a single best architecture (standard NAS) or hand-designing one, RegNet's authors define and analyse POPULATIONS of architectures via simple parameterised design spaces, identifying simple QUANTIZED LINEAR rules (e.g. how width/depth should scale across stages) that consistently produce good networks across a wide range of compute budgets.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.why_it_exists: Standard NAS produces a single architecture optimised for a single compute target — RegNet's goal was to find general DESIGN PRINCIPLES (simple functional forms relating network width, depth, group width across stages) that generalise across many compute budgets, providing both efficient architectures AND interpretable insight into WHY certain design choices work (unlike black-box NAS-discovered architectures).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.how_it_works: Define a design space of CNNs parameterised by per-stage width and depth (following ResNet-style stage structure). Sample many configurations from this space, train them (briefly) on a proxy task, and analyse the distribution of error rates — progressively refining the design space by ADDING CONSTRAINTS that empirically correlate with good performance (e.g. constraining stage widths to follow a simple linear/quantized function of stage index, rather than allowing arbitrary widths). The end result (RegNetY) is characterised by simple rules: width increases roughly linearly across stages (quantized to multiples of a 'group width'), and includes squeeze-and-excitation blocks (RegNetY vs RegNetX without SE).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.use_when: When you need a strong, EFFICIENT CNN backbone across a range of compute budgets with a principled (not black-box) basis for the architecture — RegNet models are used in some production vision systems (e.g. as backbones in Detectron2/object detection pipelines) and were used as the backbone family for some of Meta's self-supervised learning research (e.g. SEER).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.avoid_when: When a single specific accuracy target is the only goal and other well-established architectures (EfficientNet, ConvNeXt) already meet it — RegNet's main VALUE is the design-space-analysis methodology and the resulting family's efficiency across budgets, not necessarily best-in-class accuracy at any single point.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.what_goes_wrong: Like other 'discovered design' approaches, the simple scaling rules were found on specific proxy tasks/datasets (ImageNet) and may not transfer perfectly to very different domains without re-validation.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|CNN.real_example: RegNetY architectures were used as backbones in Facebook's SEER project (self-supervised learning on billions of uncurated images) due to their efficiency and strong scaling properties, and remain available as standard backbone options in detection frameworks like Detectron2.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_it_is: A sequence model architecture (Gu & Dao, Dec 2023) based on Structured State Space Models (SSMs) with a SELECTIVE (input-dependent) mechanism — SSM parameters (Δ, B, C) are computed as functions of the input at each timestep, allowing the model to selectively 'remember' or 'forget' information, unlike prior time-invariant SSMs (S4).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.why_it_exists: Transformers' attention has O(n²) compute/memory in sequence length and a KV-cache that grows linearly with context — Mamba aims for LINEAR-time sequence modeling (like RNNs/SSMs) with CONSTANT-size recurrent state at inference, while matching or exceeding Transformer quality on language modeling, something earlier linear-time SSMs (S4, H3) couldn't quite achieve due to their lack of input-dependent (content-aware) selectivity.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.how_it_works: The continuous-time SSM x'(t)=Ax(t)+Bu(t), y(t)=Cx(t) is discretised with a timestep Δ. In Mamba, Δ, B, and C are made functions of the INPUT u_t (via learned linear projections) — this 'selection mechanism' lets the model decide, per-token, how much to update its hidden state vs. retain it (analogous to gating in LSTMs but derived from first-principles continuous-time systems theory). Because the resulting recurrence is no longer time-invariant, the efficient FFT-based convolution trick used by S4 doesn't directly apply — Mamba instead uses a custom HARDWARE-AWARE PARALLEL SCAN algorithm (implemented with custom CUDA kernels) that computes the selective-SSM recurrence efficiently on GPUs, keeping the larger intermediate states in fast SRAM rather than materialising them in HBM.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.use_when: Long-context sequence modeling where linear scaling and constant-memory inference (no growing KV cache) are valuable — Mamba models (130M-2.8B+ params) showed competitive perplexity with Transformers of similar size on language modeling, with much faster inference at long sequence lengths.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.avoid_when: Tasks heavily reliant on precise, content-based RETRIEVAL over very long contexts (e.g. needle-in-a-haystack style exact copying) where pure SSM-based models historically lag attention — hence the rise of HYBRID architectures (Mamba + occasional attention layers, e.g. Jamba, Zamba) for production use.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_goes_wrong: Pure SSM models (including Mamba) can underperform Transformers on tasks requiring exact copying/retrieval of specific tokens from far back in context — the fixed-size recurrent state is a genuine information bottleneck compared to attention's ability to directly 'look up' any past token; this motivated the hybrid Mamba+attention designs that followed.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.real_example: Mamba's selective SSM and hardware-aware scan directly inspired the 'hybrid' LLM architectures of 2024 — AI21's Jamba (52B MoE, mixing Mamba and Transformer/attention layers) and Zyphra's Zamba use Mamba blocks for most layers with occasional attention layers to recover long-range retrieval ability, achieving Transformer-competitive quality with much smaller KV-cache memory footprints.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_it_is: The successor to Mamba (Dao & Gu, 2024) that reformulates the selective SSM as a 'Structured State Space Duality' (SSD) — showing that selective SSMs are mathematically equivalent to a form of structured (masked) linear attention, unifying the SSM and attention literatures and enabling a much faster, simpler, matrix-multiplication-based implementation.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.why_it_exists: Mamba's custom parallel-scan CUDA kernel, while effective, was complex and not as hardware-efficient as it could be (scans don't map as cleanly to GPU tensor cores as matmuls do) — Mamba-2's SSD framing recasts the SSM recurrence as block-wise matrix multiplications, allowing it to leverage highly-optimised GPU matmul kernels (similar to how FlashAttention optimises attention), yielding 2-8x speedups over Mamba-1 while ALSO simplifying the architecture (larger, more Transformer-like 'heads' for the SSM state).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.how_it_works: SSD shows the selective SSM's output can be computed as y = (L ∘ (CB^T)) x where L is a particular lower-triangular structured matrix (determined by the Δ/decay terms) — this is structurally analogous to attention's softmax(QK^T) ∘ mask, but with a structured decay mask instead of softmax. This duality means SSM computation can be expressed via 'chunked' matmul-based algorithms (split sequence into chunks, compute intra-chunk via quadratic attention-like matmul, inter-chunk via the recurrent/linear SSM form) — getting the best of both: matmul efficiency for short-range, linear recurrence for long-range. Mamba-2 also increases the state dimension per 'head' substantially compared to Mamba-1, improving expressivity.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.use_when: When building/training large SSM-based or hybrid language models where training throughput matters — Mamba-2's matmul-friendly formulation trains significantly faster than Mamba-1 at scale on modern GPUs (especially with tensor cores).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.avoid_when: Same fundamental retrieval limitations as Mamba-1 apply (pure SSD layers still have a finite-size state) — Mamba-2 is an efficiency/implementation improvement over Mamba-1, not a fix for the retrieval gap relative to full attention.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_goes_wrong: The SSD reformulation reveals an important THEORETICAL connection (SSMs ⊂ a family of structured/linear attention variants) — practitioners sometimes conflate this with 'SSMs and attention are interchangeable', but the structured decay/mask in SSD is much more constrained than general softmax attention, which is precisely why hybrids retain some full-attention layers.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.real_example: The SSD duality paper explicitly connects Mamba-2 to linear attention variants like GLA (Gated Linear Attention) and DeltaNet, providing a unifying theoretical lens — this framing has influenced subsequent 'linear-attention vs SSM' architecture comparisons in 2024-2025 research (e.g. analyses comparing RWKV, RetNet, Mamba-2, and GLA as points in the same structured-matrix design space).

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_it_is: Adaptations of the Mamba SSM architecture to visual data: Vision Mamba (Vim, 2024) applies bidirectional Mamba blocks to image patch sequences (analogous to how ViT applies Transformer blocks to patches), and VideoMamba extends this to video, exploiting Mamba's linear-time scaling to handle the much longer token sequences that video produces.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.why_it_exists: Vision Transformers' O(n²) attention becomes especially costly for high-resolution images or video (where the number of patch/frame tokens is very large) — Mamba's linear-time sequence modeling is attractive for these long visual sequences, and these works test whether SSM-based architectures (originally designed for causal 1D language) can match ViT-style performance on 2D/3D, non-causal visual data.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.how_it_works: Vision Mamba flattens an image into a sequence of patches (like ViT) but, since vision is fundamentally non-causal (a pixel's meaning doesn't only depend on 'past' pixels in raster order), uses BIDIRECTIONAL Mamba blocks — processing the patch sequence both forward and backward and combining the results, to give each patch access to context from all directions. VideoMamba extends this with spatiotemporal scanning strategies to handle the additional temporal dimension, leveraging linear scaling to process many more frames than a comparable ViT could afford.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.use_when: Research into efficient architectures for high-resolution images, long videos, or other long visual sequences where attention's quadratic cost is a bottleneck and linear-time alternatives are being explored.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.avoid_when: Production vision systems as of 2024-2025 — ViT/Swin/ConvNeXt-family models remain the dominant, better-tooled choices; Vision Mamba variants are still primarily a research direction demonstrating FEASIBILITY rather than a clear win in deployed accuracy/efficiency tradeoffs.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_goes_wrong: The causal, 1D-sequential inductive bias that makes Mamba natural for language doesn't map cleanly onto 2D/3D visual data — bidirectional scanning is a workaround but adds computational overhead (effectively 2x the scans) and the optimal way to 'serialise' 2D/3D structure into 1D sequences for SSMs remains an open research question (various scan orderings — raster, zigzag, hierarchical — have been proposed with different tradeoffs).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.real_example: Vision Mamba (Vim) and VideoMamba reported competitive accuracy with DeiT/ViT-style models at lower memory for high-resolution inputs and long video clips, and are frequently cited in 2024-2025 papers exploring whether SSM-based 'linear vision backbones' can become a viable alternative to attention-based ones, paralleling the language-model Mamba-vs-Transformer debate in the vision domain.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_it_is: 'Receptance Weighted Key Value' — an RNN-based language model architecture (Peng et al., ongoing since 2021, with major versions RWKV-4 through RWKV-7) designed to combine Transformer-level training PARALLELISM with RNN-level CONSTANT-memory, linear-time INFERENCE, via a linear-attention-like recurrence with learned per-channel decay.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.why_it_exists: Transformers train efficiently (parallel over sequence positions) but have a KV-cache that grows with context at inference; traditional RNNs (LSTM/GRU) have constant memory but train slowly (sequential, can't parallelise over time). RWKV's design seeks the best of both — a recurrence formulated so that, like linear attention, the TRAINING-time computation can be expressed as a parallelisable operation (similar to a 'WKV' weighted sum that can be computed via cumulative sums), while INFERENCE proceeds as a simple constant-size-state RNN update, giving O(1) memory per generated token regardless of context length.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.how_it_works: RWKV replaces self-attention with a 'WKV' (weighted key-value) operator: each channel has a learned, time-decaying weighting (a per-channel decay rate, somewhat analogous to a per-channel 'forget gate' but with a fixed/learned exponential decay shape rather than a dynamically-computed gate) that combines past key-value pairs into a running weighted sum — the 'receptance' (R) gate (sigmoid-activated) then determines how much of this accumulated WKV output is used for the current token, similar in spirit to an LSTM output gate. Because the decay is structured (not arbitrary, data-dependent), the WKV computation over a full sequence can be computed efficiently via a parallel/chunked formulation during training, while at inference it reduces to updating a small fixed-size running state per layer per channel — true O(1) memory generation, unlike Transformers' growing KV cache.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.use_when: Resource-constrained inference scenarios (edge devices, very long-context generation) where avoiding a growing KV cache is the primary concern, and where the community-driven, fully open RWKV models (trained on multilingual data) fit licensing/deployment needs.
