3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.avoid_when: Tasks demanding the strongest possible long-range exact-retrieval (similar caveat to Mamba/SSMs — fixed per-channel decay states are less flexible than full attention's direct token-to-token lookups) or where the broader tooling/ecosystem support for mainstream Transformer LLMs is required.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_goes_wrong: Like other linear-recurrence architectures, RWKV's fixed-size state per layer is an information bottleneck for tasks needing precise recall of arbitrary earlier tokens; successive RWKV versions (5, 6 'Finch', 7 'Goose') have progressively added more expressive, more data-dependent decay/gating mechanisms (moving closer to Mamba's input-dependent selectivity) specifically to address this.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.real_example: RWKV models (up to ~14B parameters) are fully open-source and have been used in community/edge deployments (e.g. running on consumer hardware, browser-based inference via RWKV.cpp) specifically because of the constant-memory generation property — RWKV is frequently cited alongside Mamba and RetNet as one of the leading 'linear-time successor to Transformers' candidates in the 2023-2025 efficient-architecture research wave.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_it_is: Retentive Network (Sun et al. 2023, Microsoft Research) — an architecture proposing a 'retention' mechanism as a replacement for self-attention, explicitly designed to support THREE equivalent computation paradigms: parallel (for training, like attention), recurrent (for O(1)-memory inference, like RNNs), and chunkwise-recurrent (a hybrid for efficient long-sequence training).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.why_it_exists: RetNet's authors frame the Transformer-vs-RNN tradeoff explicitly as 'impossible triangle': you can't simultaneously have training parallelism, low-cost (constant memory) inference, AND strong performance with standard architectures (Transformers sacrifice inference cost, RNNs sacrifice training parallelism). RetNet's retention mechanism is designed via a mathematical formulation (a linear recurrence with a complex-valued, rotation-based decay term, related to rotary position embeddings) that provably admits ALL THREE computational forms as equivalent reformulations of the same underlying operation.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.how_it_works: Retention replaces softmax(QK^T)V attention with QK^T ∘ D applied to V, where D is a decay matrix D_{nm} = γ^(n-m) for n≥m (and 0 otherwise) — an exponentially-decaying, position-difference-dependent mask (no softmax). Because this decay has a simple exponential form, the SAME computation can be written as: (1) the PARALLEL form above (a matmul, efficient for training, similar to linear attention); (2) a RECURRENT form state_n = γ·state_{n-1} + k_n^T v_n, output_n = q_n · state_n (O(1) memory per step, for efficient autoregressive generation); or (3) a CHUNKWISE form that processes the sequence in chunks, using the recurrent form across chunks and the parallel form within each chunk (balancing memory and parallelism for very long sequences during training).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.use_when: Research/production settings prioritising a single architecture that's efficient for BOTH training (parallel form) and long-context autoregressive inference (recurrent form, constant memory) — RetNet reported matching Transformer perplexity at various scales while offering 8.4x lower GPU memory and substantially higher throughput at inference for long sequences.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.avoid_when: When the broader ecosystem (pretrained checkpoints, fine-tuning tools, inference servers) for standard Transformers (or for the more widely-adopted Mamba family) is needed — RetNet has less ecosystem traction than Mamba despite the elegant theoretical framing.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_goes_wrong: Like other linear/exponential-decay recurrence models, the fixed per-channel decay rate γ limits how 'selectively' the model can retain specific past information compared to fully data-dependent gating (Mamba's selection mechanism) — RetNet's elegance comes partly from this simplicity, but it's also the main expressivity tradeoff versus more complex selective architectures.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.real_example: RetNet is frequently grouped with Mamba, RWKV, and GLA (Gated Linear Attention) in 2024-2025 'efficient architecture' survey papers and benchmarks comparing linear-time alternatives to Transformer attention — its three-equivalent-forms framing (the 'impossible triangle' resolution) is widely cited as a clean conceptual articulation of WHY these architectures matter for production LLM serving costs.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_it_is: Hyena (Poli et al. 2023) is a sequence model that replaces attention with implicitly-parameterised LONG CONVOLUTIONS combined with data-dependent gating; StripedHyena (Together AI, 2023) is a hybrid architecture interleaving ('striping') Hyena convolution layers with a smaller number of attention layers.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.why_it_exists: Attention's O(n²) cost comes from computing pairwise token interactions; Hyena's premise is that LONG CONVOLUTIONS (filters spanning the entire sequence length) can be computed in O(n log n) via FFT, and — when combined with input-dependent gating (multiplying by projections of the input, similar in spirit to Mamba's selectivity) — can approximate the expressivity of attention for many tasks at much lower asymptotic cost for long sequences. StripedHyena's hybrid design acknowledges that pure convolution-based models alone may still lag attention on certain tasks (e.g. in-context retrieval), so it mixes in occasional attention layers.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.how_it_works: A Hyena operator applies a sequence of operations: data-dependent linear projections (gating, similar to how SSMs/RWKV use input-dependent terms) interleaved with long implicit convolutions — the convolution FILTERS themselves are parameterised by a small neural network (an 'implicit' parameterisation, e.g. via positional embeddings fed through an MLP, similar to how implicit neural representations like NeRF parameterise continuous functions) rather than stored as explicit weight tensors, enabling filters as long as the sequence while keeping parameter count manageable. The FFT-based convolution gives O(n log n) scaling vs attention's O(n²). StripedHyena interleaves these Hyena blocks with standard grouped-query-attention blocks at a fixed ratio (e.g. mostly Hyena layers, periodic attention layers).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.use_when: Long-sequence modeling (e.g. genomics — Hyena was notably applied to DNA sequence modeling with context lengths in the hundreds of thousands of base pairs, far beyond typical Transformer context windows) where sub-quadratic scaling is essential.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.avoid_when: Short-sequence tasks where attention's quadratic cost isn't a bottleneck and its stronger in-context retrieval properties are more valuable; pure-Hyena (non-hybrid) models for tasks requiring precise token-level retrieval.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_goes_wrong: Pure long-convolution models, like other sub-quadratic architectures, can underperform attention on tasks needing exact associative recall — StripedHyena's hybrid design is a direct response to this, similar to how Jamba hybridises Mamba with attention.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.real_example: HyenaDNA used Hyena operators to model genomic sequences up to 1 million tokens long — context lengths that would be computationally infeasible for standard Transformer attention — demonstrating a concrete domain (genomics) where sub-quadratic long-convolution architectures provide a capability (very-long-context modeling) that quadratic attention simply cannot offer at any reasonable cost.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_it_is: A class of continuous-time recurrent neural networks (Hasani et al., MIT, ~2020-2021, commercialised via Liquid AI from 2023) based on Liquid Time-Constant (LTC) networks — RNNs where the 'time constant' governing how quickly each neuron's state decays/responds is itself a learned, input-dependent function, drawing inspiration from the dynamics of biological neurons (e.g. C. elegans).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.why_it_exists: Standard RNNs (and Neural ODEs with fixed dynamics) have state-update dynamics that don't adapt their TIMESCALE based on input — Liquid Networks aim to model systems where the relevant timescale of change varies (e.g. some inputs should cause rapid state changes, others slow ones), motivated by biological neural circuits where synaptic time constants are themselves dynamic, potentially giving better generalisation/robustness on time-series with varying dynamics from small networks.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.how_it_works: LTC neurons are governed by an ODE dx/dt = -x/τ(I(t),θ) + f(x,I(t),θ), where the time constant τ is itself a function of the input I(t) (via a learned neural network) — meaning the neuron's 'speed of forgetting/updating' adapts dynamically per input, unlike a standard Neural ODE or RNN with fixed decay. This is implemented/solved similarly to Neural ODEs (numerical ODE solvers or closed-form approximations for tractability — 'Closed-form Continuous-depth' (CfC) networks are a follow-up that avoid expensive ODE solvers).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.use_when: Resource-constrained, robustness-critical time-series/control tasks (robotics, autonomous drones/vehicles) where Liquid AI and academic work have shown small (thousands of parameters) Liquid Networks matching larger conventional RNNs on tasks like drone navigation, with claimed better out-of-distribution robustness.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.avoid_when: Large-scale language/vision modeling — Liquid Networks (as originally proposed) target small-scale, dynamical-systems-style time-series tasks; Liquid AI's later commercial 'LFM' (Liquid Foundation Models, 2024) extend the underlying ideas to larger-scale models but this is a distinct, less-established research direction compared to Transformer/Mamba-family LLMs.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_goes_wrong: ODE-based formulations can be computationally expensive (numerical solvers) — a key follow-up contribution (CfC, closed-form continuous-depth networks) specifically addresses this by deriving closed-form approximations to the LTC dynamics, trading some theoretical elegance for practical trainability/speed.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.real_example: Liquid AI (founded by the LTC/CfC authors) released Liquid Foundation Models (LFM) in 2024, claiming competitive language-modeling quality with smaller memory footprints than comparable Transformers, applying the 'adaptive/input-dependent dynamics' philosophy from the original small-scale Liquid Network research to larger foundation-model scales — part of the broader 2024 trend of exploring non-Transformer architectures for efficient LLMs.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_it_is: A neural network architecture (Liu et al., MIT, April 2024) based on the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem, which replaces the standard MLP design (fixed activation functions on nodes, learnable weights on edges) with LEARNABLE ACTIVATION FUNCTIONS on the EDGES (parameterised as splines), and FIXED summation at nodes.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.why_it_exists: Standard MLPs (per the universal approximation theorem) approximate functions using fixed nonlinearities (ReLU, GELU, etc.) and linear weight matrices; the Kolmogorov-Arnold theorem states that any multivariate continuous function can be represented as a finite composition of CONTINUOUS UNIVARIATE functions and addition — KAN's authors propose directly parameterising these univariate functions as learnable splines on each edge, hypothesising this could give better accuracy/parameter-efficiency and INTERPRETABILITY (each edge's learned spline can be visualised/inspected as a 1D function) for certain scientific/symbolic-regression tasks compared to MLPs.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.how_it_works: A KAN layer replaces each weight w_ij (a single learnable scalar in an MLP) with a learnable 1D function φ_ij(x) — typically parameterised as a B-spline (a piecewise polynomial curve with learnable control points) plus a base function (e.g. SiLU). The layer's output is the SUM over incoming edges of these spline-transformed inputs: y_j = Σ_i φ_ij(x_i) — so 'activation' happens on edges (each edge applies its own learned nonlinear transform) and nodes simply sum, the reverse of MLPs (fixed nonlinearity at nodes, linear weights on edges). The authors demonstrate KANs can achieve favorable accuracy-vs-parameter scaling on certain function-fitting and PDE-solving tasks, and that the learned spline shapes can sometimes be interpreted/simplified into closed-form symbolic expressions.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.use_when: Scientific computing / symbolic regression tasks where interpretability of learned functions matters (e.g. discovering closed-form physical laws from data) and where the input dimensionality is modest — the original paper's strongest results are on small-scale function-fitting and PDE problems, not large-scale perception/language tasks.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.avoid_when: Large-scale tasks (image classification, language modeling) — subsequent independent evaluations found KANs generally do NOT outperform well-tuned MLPs at scale, and the per-edge spline computations are significantly more expensive (in compute and memory) than simple matrix multiplications, making KANs much slower to train than equivalently-sized MLPs.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_goes_wrong: The computational cost of evaluating learnable splines on every edge (vs. a single matmul + elementwise activation in an MLP) is substantially higher — KANs as originally proposed don't parallelise as efficiently on GPUs as MLPs, and several follow-up analyses (mid-2024) found that, for a fixed parameter/compute budget, MLPs often matched or beat KANs on tasks beyond the narrow symbolic-regression/PDE settings of the original paper, tempering initial hype.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.real_example: KAN generated significant research community discussion immediately after its April 2024 release (one of the most-discussed ML papers of that period on social media/arXiv), but by mid-to-late 2024, multiple replication studies (e.g. comparisons on vision/tabular benchmarks) found limited advantages outside the scientific/symbolic-regression niche — illustrating how a theoretically elegant idea's practical impact depends heavily on whether it translates to favorable compute-efficiency at the scales that matter for the target application.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_it_is: Diffusion Transformer (Peebles & Xie, late 2022, became hugely influential through 2023-2024) — a diffusion model architecture that replaces the U-Net backbone (used in DDPM, Stable Diffusion 1/2) with a TRANSFORMER operating on latent image patches (tokens), applying the diffusion denoising objective within this Transformer-based design.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.why_it_exists: U-Net backbones, while effective, are CNN-based and don't benefit from the SCALING LAWS and architectural uniformity that Transformers enjoy in language modeling — DiT's authors hypothesised that diffusion models could benefit from the same 'scale the Transformer' recipe that drove LLM progress, and empirically showed DiT's performance scales smoothly and favorably with model size/compute (FLOPs), eventually surpassing U-Net-based diffusion models on ImageNet generation benchmarks.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.how_it_works: An input latent (e.g. from a VAE encoder, as in Latent Diffusion) is divided into patches and embedded as tokens (like ViT's patchify), with positional embeddings added. The diffusion timestep t and any conditioning (e.g. class label) are injected via 'adaptive layer norm' (adaLN) — modulating the Transformer block's layer norm scale/shift parameters based on t and conditioning, rather than concatenating them as extra tokens (adaLN-Zero, which initialises the modulation to produce zero output at the start, was found to work best). The Transformer processes these tokens through standard self-attention + MLP blocks, and the output is 'unpatchified' back into the latent space to predict the noise (or velocity, in flow-matching formulations).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.use_when: Building/scaling large image (and video) generation models where Transformer scaling laws and infrastructure (highly optimised attention kernels, established scaling recipes) are advantageous — DiT became the foundation for Stable Diffusion 3 and Sora's architecture.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.avoid_when: Small-scale or resource-constrained image generation where a well-tuned U-Net (e.g. the original Stable Diffusion 1.5 architecture) remains competitive and has a more mature ecosystem of fine-tuning tools/LoRAs/ControlNets built around the U-Net structure.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_goes_wrong: DiT's quadratic attention cost over image patch tokens becomes significant at high resolutions (many patches) — this motivated subsequent efficiency work (e.g. using fewer, larger patches, or hierarchical/windowed attention variants) when scaling DiT to high-resolution image and especially VIDEO generation, where the token count multiplies further with the temporal dimension.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.real_example: Stable Diffusion 3 (Stability AI, 2024) replaced its predecessors' U-Net with a DiT-based architecture (specifically MM-DiT, see below); OpenAI's Sora (2024) described its architecture as a DiT operating on spacetime patches of video latents — DiT is now the dominant architectural paradigm for state-of-the-art image and video diffusion models as of 2024-2025.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_it_is: Multimodal Diffusion Transformer — the architecture used in Stable Diffusion 3 (Stability AI, 2024), extending DiT to process TWO separate token streams (image/video latent patches AND text/caption embeddings) through SEPARATE weight sets per modality within each Transformer block, with JOINT attention allowing the streams to interact.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.why_it_exists: Earlier text-to-image diffusion models (Stable Diffusion 1/2) injected text conditioning via cross-attention from a frozen CLIP/T5 text encoder into a U-Net — this gives the text representation a 'fixed' role that doesn't get refined jointly with the image representation during generation. MM-DiT's separate-but-jointly-attending streams let BOTH the image and text representations be updated/refined together through the network's depth, allowing richer text-image interaction and improving prompt adherence/text rendering in generated images.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.how_it_works: Each MM-DiT block maintains two sets of weights — one for image-latent tokens, one for text-embedding tokens — each stream has its own layer norm, QKV projections, and adaLN modulation (conditioned on the diffusion timestep). The QUERY/KEY/VALUE from BOTH streams are concatenated for a JOINT self-attention operation (so image tokens can attend to text tokens and vice versa, and to themselves), after which the attention output is split back and each stream proceeds through its own (separate-weight) MLP. SD3 also uses multiple text encoders (CLIP + T5-XXL) concatenated to provide richer text representations, and employs FLOW MATCHING (a rectified-flow formulation) rather than the traditional DDPM noise-prediction objective for the diffusion process itself.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.use_when: State-of-the-art text-to-image/video generation where strong prompt adherence (including rendering legible text within images — a notorious weakness of earlier diffusion models) is important.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.avoid_when: Simpler conditioning scenarios (e.g. class-conditional generation, as in the original DiT/ImageNet setting) where a single conditioning signal via adaLN (without a full joint-attention multimodal stream) suffices and is cheaper.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_goes_wrong: Maintaining separate weight sets per modality roughly doubles certain parameter counts compared to a single shared-weight stream — a design tradeoff explicitly made to preserve each modality's distinct statistical characteristics while still enabling joint attention; ablations in the SD3 paper found this separate-but-joint design outperformed fully-shared-weight alternatives.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.real_example: Stable Diffusion 3's MM-DiT architecture, combined with flow matching and improved text encoders, substantially improved text rendering and prompt-following compared to SD1.5/SDXL's U-Net + cross-attention design — MM-DiT-style joint multimodal attention has since influenced other multimodal generative architectures combining diffusion with text/video/audio streams.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_it_is: The core mechanism of sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Transformer layers: a 'router' (a small learned linear layer + softmax) computes a score for each of N 'expert' sub-networks (typically FFN/MLP blocks) per token, and only the TOP-k experts (commonly k=1 or k=2) are activated for that token — combined with 'expert parallelism', the distributed-training/serving strategy of placing different experts on different devices/GPUs.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.why_it_exists: Dense Transformers activate ALL parameters for every token — MoE decouples a model's TOTAL parameter count from its PER-TOKEN compute cost: an MoE model can have, say, 8x more total parameters (8 experts) while each token only computes through 1-2 of them, giving much higher parameter-count (and thus potentially capability) per unit of inference compute. Expert parallelism is the systems counterpart needed to actually TRAIN/SERVE such models efficiently across many GPUs, since routing different tokens to different experts means different GPUs handle different tokens at the FFN layer.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.how_it_works: ROUTING: for each token's hidden state h, the router computes logits = h·W_router (shape [N_experts]), takes softmax, and selects the top-k experts by score; the token's FFN output is the weighted sum (by router probability) of the selected experts' outputs. A common challenge is LOAD BALANCING — without intervention, the router may collapse to using only a few 'popular' experts; an auxiliary LOAD-BALANCING LOSS (encouraging roughly equal token counts per expert across a batch) is added to the training objective to prevent this. EXPERT PARALLELISM: experts are sharded across GPUs (e.g. 8 experts across 8 GPUs, one each); tokens are routed (via an all-to-all communication operation) to the GPU holding their selected expert(s), processed, and routed back — this all-to-all communication is the key systems cost of MoE training/serving, distinct from the tensor/pipeline/data parallelism used for dense layers.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.use_when: Scaling model CAPACITY (total parameters, and thus knowledge/capability) without proportionally scaling per-token INFERENCE compute — MoE is the dominant architecture for the largest 2024-2025 open and closed LLMs (Mixtral, DeepSeek-V2/V3, GPT-4 rumored, Grok).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.avoid_when: Smaller-scale models or settings where the engineering complexity of expert parallelism (all-to-all communication, load balancing, routing instability) isn't justified by the capacity benefit — dense models remain simpler to train/serve and are preferred below a certain scale.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_goes_wrong: Router 'collapse' (a few experts get most tokens, others are undertrained) is the classic MoE failure mode, addressed via load-balancing auxiliary losses; the all-to-all communication for expert parallelism can become a bottleneck at scale, especially with poor network topology; MoE models also have notoriously HIGHER MEMORY requirements for serving (must hold ALL experts' weights even though only a few are used per token) despite lower per-token FLOPs — a memory-vs-compute tradeoff that complicates deployment.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.real_example: Mixtral 8x7B (Mistral AI, late 2023) uses top-2 routing across 8 experts per layer — ~47B total parameters but only ~13B active per token — matching or exceeding dense 70B-parameter model quality at roughly 1/5 the inference FLOPs, a concrete demonstration of MoE's capacity-vs-compute decoupling.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_it_is: An MoE design refinement (DeepSeek-AI, 2024, used in DeepSeek-V2 and V3) consisting of two key changes from 'standard' MoE (e.g. Mixtral-style): (1) FINE-GRAINED EXPERT SEGMENTATION — splitting each expert FFN into many smaller experts (e.g. instead of 8 large experts, use 64+ smaller ones) and routing to more of them (higher k) for finer-grained specialisation; (2) SHARED EXPERTS — a small number of experts that are ALWAYS activated for every token (not subject to routing), intended to capture common/general knowledge so the routed experts can specialise more on token-specific patterns.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.why_it_exists: Standard top-k MoE with a small number of large experts forces each expert to be a 'generalist' for whatever subset of tokens it receives, potentially causing REDUNDANCY across experts (each independently re-learning common patterns) and limiting how specialised any one expert can become. DeepSeek's fine-grained segmentation increases the COMBINATORIAL diversity of expert COMBINATIONS available per token (choosing k from many small experts gives vastly more possible combinations than k from few large experts, for the same total/active parameter count), while shared experts explicitly factor out common knowledge, freeing routed experts to specialise further — together improving parameter efficiency and reducing knowledge redundancy.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.how_it_works: Given a total FFN parameter budget, instead of N experts each of size F, create mN experts each of size F/m (fine-grained segmentation, m>1) and route to mk of them (preserving total active compute) — this exponentially increases the number of possible expert subsets a token could be routed to, enabling much finer specialisation patterns to emerge during training. Additionally, designate a small fixed number of experts (e.g. 1-2) as 'shared' — every token passes through these regardless of routing, in addition to its routed fine-grained experts; the shared experts' outputs and the routed experts' (weighted) outputs are summed. DeepSeek-V2/V3 combine this with their 'Multi-head Latent Attention' (MLA, a KV-cache compression technique) and auxiliary-loss-free load balancing strategies (using a bias term adjusted via a separate update rule rather than an auxiliary loss term, reducing interference with the main training objective).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.use_when: Training very large MoE LLMs where maximising the 'effective specialisation' per active-parameter is a priority — DeepSeek-V2 (236B total/21B active) and V3 (671B total/37B active) used this design to achieve strong benchmarks at relatively low active-parameter (and thus inference-cost) counts.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.avoid_when: Smaller MoE models where the added routing complexity (many more, smaller experts to manage, route to, and parallelise across devices) isn't justified — fine-grained MoE adds engineering complexity to expert-parallelism implementations (more, smaller all-to-all transfers).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_goes_wrong: More, smaller experts means more, smaller communication operations for expert parallelism — without careful batching/scheduling this can hurt hardware utilisation (small matmuls are less efficient); DeepSeek's reported training efficiency gains depend on co-designed systems work (e.g. their custom communication kernels) alongside the architectural change.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.real_example: DeepSeek-V3 (Dec 2024) — 671B total parameters, only 37B activated per token via fine-grained + shared expert MoE, plus MLA for KV-cache compression — was trained for a famously low reported cost (~$5.5M for the final training run) and achieved benchmark results competitive with GPT-4-class closed models, becoming a widely-discussed example of architectural efficiency innovations enabling frontier-level capability at a fraction of the presumed compute of competitors.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_it_is: Successive versions of FlashAttention (Dao et al.) — an IO-aware exact attention algorithm that computes standard softmax attention without materialising the full N×N attention matrix in GPU HBM (high-bandwidth memory), instead using tiling/blocking and online softmax recomputation to keep intermediate values in fast on-chip SRAM. FlashAttention-2 (2023) improved GPU utilisation via better work partitioning/parallelism; FlashAttention-3 (2024) targets Hopper-generation GPUs (H100), exploiting new hardware features (warp specialisation, FP8 support, asynchrony between tensor cores and memory).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.why_it_exists: Standard attention implementations are MEMORY-BANDWIDTH bound (not compute bound) — they spend most of their time reading/writing the large N×N attention matrix to/from slow HBM, even though the FLOPs themselves could be done much faster. FlashAttention reformulates the computation to avoid ever fully materialising this matrix, making attention FASTER (often 2-4x) and enabling much LONGER context lengths (memory usage becomes linear, not quadratic, in sequence length) — without any approximation (it computes the EXACT same attention output, just via a more memory-efficient algorithm).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.how_it_works: The Q, K, V matrices are processed in BLOCKS/TILES that fit in SRAM. For each query block, the algorithm iterates over key/value blocks, computing partial attention scores and incrementally updating the output using the 'online softmax' trick (maintaining running max and sum statistics that allow the softmax normalisation to be computed incrementally without seeing all scores at once — avoiding numerical issues from naive incremental softmax). FlashAttention-2 improved on v1 by reducing non-matmul FLOPs, better parallelising across thread blocks (parallelising over the sequence length dimension too, not just batch/heads), and improving work partitioning between warps. FlashAttention-3 further exploits H100-specific features: WARP SPECIALISATION (different warps handle data movement vs. computation asynchronously, overlapping them), and low-precision (FP8) computation paths with careful error compensation, achieving up to ~75% of H100's theoretical FP16 peak FLOPs for attention (vs. ~35% for FlashAttention-2).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.use_when: Essentially ALWAYS for Transformer training/inference on modern GPUs — FlashAttention (in some version) is the default attention implementation in virtually all major frameworks (PyTorch's scaled_dot_product_attention, HuggingFace, vLLM, etc.) given it's a free, exact speedup with no accuracy tradeoff.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.avoid_when: Extremely short sequences where the memory-bandwidth bottleneck FlashAttention addresses isn't significant (the overhead of the tiling logic may not pay off for tiny matrices) — though even here it's rarely worse, just less impactful.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_goes_wrong: FlashAttention-3's biggest gains are HARDWARE-SPECIFIC (H100/Hopper features) — on older GPUs (A100 and earlier), FlashAttention-2 remains the relevant version, and the FP8 paths in FA3 require careful handling to maintain numerical accuracy (FA3 includes specific techniques like incoherent processing to mitigate FP8 quantisation error in the attention computation).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.real_example: FlashAttention's IO-awareness directly enabled the jump from ~2K-4K context windows (common pre-2023) to the 100K-1M+ token context windows seen in 2024-2025 models (Claude, Gemini 1.5, GPT-4-Turbo) — without it, the memory cost of even storing the attention matrix for such sequences would be prohibitive (a 1M-token sequence would need a 1M x 1M attention matrix per head, infeasible in HBM, but FlashAttention never materialises it).

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_it_is: A distributed attention algorithm (Liu, Zaharia, Abbeel 2023, UC Berkeley) that enables computing exact self-attention over EXTREMELY long sequences by distributing the sequence across MANY devices arranged in a ring topology, overlapping the communication of key/value blocks between devices with the attention computation itself — achieving near-infinite context length limited only by total cluster memory, not single-device memory.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.why_it_exists: Even with FlashAttention's memory-efficient algorithm, a single device still needs to hold (or stream through) the full sequence's K/V — for sequences of millions of tokens, this exceeds any single GPU's memory. Ring Attention's goal is to make context length scale with the NUMBER OF DEVICES (linearly), by having each device hold only a SHARD of the sequence and exchanging the shards needed for attention computation via a ring communication pattern, with communication HIDDEN behind (overlapped with) compute.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.how_it_works: The sequence is split into blocks, one (or more) per device, arranged in a logical ring. Each device computes attention for its local query block against its local key/value block (using FlashAttention-style block-wise computation), while SIMULTANEOUSLY sending its key/value block to the next device in the ring and receiving the previous device's block — after all devices have rotated through all blocks (D steps for D devices), every query block has attended to every key/value block, i.e., full (unmasked or causally-masked) attention has been computed, but no single device ever held the full sequence. Because the communication (sending/receiving KV blocks) happens CONCURRENTLY with the local attention computation (compute-communication overlap), the communication cost is largely hidden, and total context length scales linearly with the number of devices in the ring.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.use_when: Training/inference with extremely long context windows (hundreds of thousands to millions of tokens) that exceed single-device memory even with FlashAttention — Ring Attention is a key building block for million-token-context model training.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.avoid_when: Context lengths that fit comfortably within single-device memory using FlashAttention alone — Ring Attention adds distributed-systems complexity (network topology considerations, the ring communication pattern) that's unnecessary at moderate context lengths.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_goes_wrong: Ring Attention's efficiency depends on communication-compute overlap being achievable in practice — this requires sufficiently fast interconnects (e.g. NVLink/InfiniBand) relative to the per-block compute time; on slower networks, communication can become the bottleneck despite the overlapping design. Causal masking (for autoregressive models) also introduces load imbalance (later blocks in the ring have fewer valid KV pairs to attend to than would be naively expected), requiring careful scheduling.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.real_example: Ring Attention (and related 'context parallelism' techniques) underpin training of million-token-context models — Google's Gemini 1.5 (context windows up to 1M-2M tokens) and various open research efforts (e.g. LWM - Large World Model, from the Ring Attention authors) explicitly cite ring-attention-style context parallelism as the mechanism enabling such long contexts during training.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.what_it_is: FSDP2 (`torch.distributed._composable.fsdp.fully_shard`, stabilising in PyTorch 2.4+) is a rewrite of PyTorch's Fully Sharded Data Parallel API using `DTensor` (distributed tensor) as its core abstraction, replacing FSDP1's `FlatParameter`-based design with per-parameter sharding represented as DTensors.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.why_it_exists: FSDP1 (the original `FSDP` wrapper class, ~2021) flattens and concatenates all parameters in a module into one big 1D `FlatParameter` which is then sharded — this made certain operations (parameter-specific optimizer states, mixing frozen/trainable params, partial checkpointing, composing with tensor parallelism) awkward because individual parameter identity was lost inside the flat buffer. FSDP2 shards each parameter INDIVIDUALLY as a DTensor, preserving per-parameter structure, making it composable with other DTensor-based parallelism strategies (tensor parallelism via DTensor) and simplifying state-dict handling.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.how_it_works: `fully_shard(module)` is applied to submodules (typically transformer blocks) — each parameter is sharded along dim 0 across the data-parallel process group and represented as a `DTensor` with a `Shard(0)` placement. During forward/backward, FSDP2 performs an `all-gather` to reconstruct the full parameter just-in-time before use, then frees it after, and a `reduce-scatter` for gradients (same communication pattern as FSDP1, but the underlying representation is DTensor-based rather than flat-buffer-based). Because parameters remain individually addressable DTensors, FSDP2 composes cleanly with tensor-parallel DTensor sharding (2D parallelism: shard across both TP and FSDP dimensions) and supports per-parameter mixed precision / frozen-parameter handling more naturally than FSDP1.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.use_when: New PyTorch training code on 2.4+ targeting large-model data-parallel sharding, especially when COMBINING with tensor parallelism (2D/3D parallelism) — FSDP2 is the forward-looking, actively-developed API that the PyTorch team recommends for new projects.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.avoid_when: Existing codebases already stable on FSDP1 with no need for DTensor composability — migration has some API differences (e.g. checkpoint format changes) that may not be worth the churn if FSDP1 already meets the project's needs; also relevant on PyTorch versions before 2.4 where FSDP2 isn't yet stable.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.what_goes_wrong: Migrating checkpoints between FSDP1 (FlatParameter-based state dicts) and FSDP2 (DTensor-based state dicts) requires conversion — the on-disk formats differ, and mixing the two APIs within one training run isn't supported; teams need to plan a clean migration point rather than incrementally mixing.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.real_example: PyTorch's official 'torchtitan' reference implementation for large language model pretraining uses FSDP2 (`fully_shard`) combined with DTensor-based tensor parallelism to demonstrate 3D parallelism (data + tensor + pipeline) on Llama-style models, serving as the canonical example of FSDP2's composability advantages over FSDP1.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.what_it_is: A comparison of the two underlying sharding representations across PyTorch's FSDP generations: FSDP1's `FlatParameter` (all of a module's parameters flattened and concatenated into one 1D tensor, then chunked across ranks) vs. FSDP2's per-parameter `DTensor` (each parameter individually represented as a sharded tensor with explicit placement metadata).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.why_it_exists: This comparison matters because the representation choice has cascading effects on what operations are easy/hard: FlatParameter was simple and memory-efficient (one big contiguous buffer, efficient all-gather) but opaque (individual parameters can't be easily inspected, sharded differently from each other, or composed with other sharding schemes mid-flight). DTensor's per-parameter representation trades a small amount of efficiency (more, smaller communication ops in principle, though FSDP2 batches these) for COMPOSABILITY and TRANSPARENCY — each parameter's shape, sharding, and placement remain queryable/manipulable as normal tensor-like objects.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.how_it_works: FlatParameter: at wrap time, FSDP1 takes all parameters in a wrapped module, flattens each to 1D, concatenates them into one big tensor, then shards this single tensor evenly across the data-parallel group (rank i holds a contiguous 1/N slice of the concatenated buffer) — at compute time, the full FlatParameter is all-gathered, then 'unflattened' (views are created back into the individual original parameter shapes) for the forward/backward computation, then freed. DTensor: each parameter P is wrapped as a `DTensor` with a `DeviceMesh` and `Placement` (e.g. `Shard(0)` for FSDP-style sharding, `Replicate()`, or combinations for 2D/3D parallelism) — operations on DTensors automatically dispatch the correct collective communication (all-gather, reduce-scatter, all-reduce) based on the placement, and DTensors compose: a parameter can be `Shard(0)` along the FSDP mesh dimension AND `Shard(1)` along a tensor-parallel mesh dimension simultaneously, representing 2D sharding naturally.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.use_when: Understanding this distinction matters when debugging checkpoint compatibility issues, when deciding whether to adopt FSDP2 for a project needing combined FSDP+TP parallelism, or when reading PyTorch distributed training internals/source code.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.avoid_when: N/A — this is conceptual/comparative knowledge rather than something to 'use' directly; relevant whenever choosing or migrating between FSDP versions.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.what_goes_wrong: A common pitfall: code that inspects/manipulates `model.parameters()` assuming FlatParameter semantics (e.g. expecting one giant tensor per wrapped module) breaks when the model uses FSDP2's per-parameter DTensors (now `len(list(model.parameters()))` matches the unwrapped model's parameter count, not 1-per-wrapped-module) — debugging/introspection code written for FSDP1 often needs updating for FSDP2.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.real_example: The PyTorch FSDP2 design documents and migration guides explicitly walk through this FlatParameter→DTensor transition as the central architectural change, and note that state_dict checkpoints produced by FSDP1 (flat, rank-sharded buffers) require a conversion utility to load into an FSDP2 (per-parameter DTensor) model, a common practical issue for teams migrating long-running pretraining codebases.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.what_it_is: ZeRO (Zero Redundancy Optimizer, Microsoft DeepSpeed) is a family of memory-optimization stages for data-parallel training that progressively shard different components of training state across data-parallel ranks: ZeRO-1 shards OPTIMIZER STATES, ZeRO-2 additionally shards GRADIENTS, and ZeRO-3 additionally shards MODEL PARAMETERS themselves (conceptually equivalent to what FSDP does).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.why_it_exists: Standard data-parallel training REPLICATES the full model parameters, gradients, AND optimizer states (e.g. Adam's momentum + variance, which for FP32 Adam can be 2x the parameter memory) on EVERY GPU — for large models this redundancy is the dominant memory cost, often far exceeding the memory needed for activations. ZeRO's insight: since each data-parallel rank only NEEDS its own shard of optimizer states/gradients/parameters at the moment it's updating that shard, these can be PARTITIONED across ranks (each rank owns 1/N of each) and reconstructed via communication only when needed — eliminating the redundancy with no loss of mathematical equivalence to standard data parallelism.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.how_it_works: ZeRO-1: optimizer states (e.g. Adam moments) are partitioned across ranks — each rank updates only its 1/N shard of parameters using its shard of optimizer state, then the updated parameter shards are broadcast/all-gathered so all ranks have full updated parameters for the next forward pass. ZeRO-2: additionally, GRADIENTS are partitioned during the backward pass — instead of all-reducing full gradients (sum across ranks, every rank gets the full sum), a reduce-scatter is used so each rank ends up with only its shard of the (summed) gradient, matching its optimizer-state shard. ZeRO-3: additionally, PARAMETERS themselves are partitioned at rest — each rank holds only 1/N of each parameter, and full parameters are all-gathered just-in-time for each layer's forward/backward (then freed) — this is the stage that achieves the largest memory savings (linear reduction in per-GPU memory with number of GPUs) but incurs the most communication (additional all-gathers for parameters, beyond ZeRO-2's gradient reduce-scatter).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.use_when: Training models too large to fit on a single GPU with standard data parallelism — ZeRO-1/2 are 'cheaper' (less communication overhead) options when parameter memory alone (without optimizer state/gradient redundancy) fits; ZeRO-3 is needed when even the parameters don't fit replicated, at the cost of more communication.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.avoid_when: Small models where standard DDP (full replication) fits comfortably in memory — ZeRO's partitioning adds communication overhead that's pure cost if memory isn't the binding constraint; also, ZeRO-3's frequent all-gathers can become a bottleneck on slower interconnects for very large models, where combining with tensor/pipeline parallelism (reducing the data-parallel degree) may be preferable.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.what_goes_wrong: ZeRO-3's parameter all-gather/free cycle adds communication and can interact poorly with `torch.compile`/graph-capture-based optimizations if not configured carefully (the dynamic gather/free pattern can break static graph assumptions); ZeRO-Offload (moving optimizer states/parameters to CPU memory or NVMe) extends memory savings further but at a significant throughput cost from CPU-GPU transfer — a common tuning question is finding the right ZeRO stage + offload combination for a given hardware/model size.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.real_example: DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 was used to train models like BLOOM (176B parameters) across hundreds of GPUs, partitioning parameters/gradients/optimizer states such that no single GPU needed to hold the full 176B-parameter model's training state — ZeRO's conceptual approach (shard everything, gather on demand) is also the direct conceptual ancestor of PyTorch's FSDP.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.what_it_is: Megatron-LM (NVIDIA) introduced TENSOR PARALLELISM — splitting individual weight matrices (e.g. within attention and MLP layers) ACROSS GPUs so that a single layer's computation is distributed, complementing data/pipeline parallelism — and later SEQUENCE PARALLELISM, which additionally shards activations along the SEQUENCE dimension for the portions of the layer not covered by tensor parallelism (layer norm, dropout), further reducing per-GPU activation memory.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.why_it_exists: Data parallelism replicates the whole model per GPU (doesn't help if a single layer is too big); pipeline parallelism splits the model by LAYER across GPUs (helps with model size but each GPU still needs full layers and introduces pipeline bubbles). Tensor parallelism splits WITHIN a layer — necessary when even a single Transformer layer's weight matrices (e.g. a 100B+ model's attention/MLP projections) are too large for one GPU's memory, or when reducing per-GPU compute for a layer is needed to keep pipeline stages balanced. Sequence parallelism addresses a gap: tensor parallelism alone still requires each GPU to hold full-sequence-length activations for non-tensor-parallel ops (layernorm, dropout) — sequence parallelism shards these along the sequence dimension too, for additional activation memory savings.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.how_it_works: TENSOR PARALLELISM for an MLP block (Y = GeLU(XA)B): matrix A is split COLUMN-wise across GPUs (each GPU computes XA_i for its column-shard A_i, producing a shard of the intermediate activation), GeLU is applied elementwise (no communication needed since GeLU is elementwise), then matrix B is split ROW-wise (each GPU computes GeLU(XA_i)B_i using its shard), and the partial results are summed via an ALL-REDUCE to get the final Y — this column-then-row splitting pattern requires only ONE all-reduce per MLP block (and similarly one for attention), minimizing communication. SEQUENCE PARALLELISM: for the LayerNorm/dropout regions between tensor-parallel regions (where activations are otherwise replicated across the TP group), shard the activations along the SEQUENCE dimension across the TP group instead of replicating — requiring additional all-gather/reduce-scatter operations at the boundaries between tensor-parallel and sequence-parallel regions, but reducing the memory each GPU needs for these activations by a factor of the TP degree.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.use_when: Training very large Transformer models (tens to hundreds of billions of parameters) where individual layers exceed single-GPU memory or where balancing pipeline stages requires splitting layer compute — typically combined with data parallelism and pipeline parallelism in '3D parallelism' setups; sequence parallelism is added when activation memory (not just parameter memory) is the binding constraint, especially at long sequence lengths.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.avoid_when: Models small enough that data parallelism (or data + ZeRO/FSDP) alone suffices — tensor parallelism requires fast (typically NVLink-level, within-node) interconnects since it introduces all-reduce communication on EVERY layer's forward and backward pass, making it unsuitable across slow (e.g. cross-node Ethernet) links.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.what_goes_wrong: Tensor parallelism's per-layer all-reduce communication is latency-sensitive — it's typically restricted to GPUs within a single node (connected via NVLink) because the communication frequency (every layer) would be crippling over slower inter-node networks; choosing the TP degree thus often defaults to the number of GPUs per node (e.g. 8), with data/pipeline parallelism handling the across-node scaling.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.real_example: Megatron-LM's tensor parallelism (and its combination with pipeline and data parallelism, '3D parallelism') was used to train GPT-3-scale and larger models (e.g. Megatron-Turing NLG 530B), and the technique — along with sequence parallelism — is now a standard component of large-model training frameworks (used in NVIDIA NeMo, and informing similar implementations in DeepSpeed and torchtitan).

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.what_it_is: Pipeline parallelism splits a model's LAYERS across GPUs (each GPU/'stage' holds a contiguous subset of layers) and processes MULTIPLE MICROBATCHES concurrently in a pipelined fashion. '1F1B' (one-forward-one-backward, from PipeDream/Megatron) is a SCHEDULING strategy that interleaves forward and backward passes of different microbatches to reduce idle time ('pipeline bubbles'); the 'interleaved' (or 'virtual pipeline') schedule further reduces bubbles by having each GPU hold MULTIPLE non-contiguous chunks of layers.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.why_it_exists: Naive pipeline parallelism (process all microbatches' forward passes, then all backward passes — GPipe-style) leaves early stages IDLE while later stages finish, and vice versa during backward — these 'bubbles' waste GPU time proportional to (num_stages - 1) / num_microbatches. 1F1B reduces the PEAK MEMORY (fewer microbatches' activations need to be held simultaneously, since backward passes start earlier) without necessarily reducing bubble time alone; the INTERLEAVED schedule additionally reduces bubble time by giving each GPU work from multiple points in the model, so there's more available work to fill idle slots.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.how_it_works: 1F1B schedule: instead of GPU 1 doing ALL forward passes for microbatches 1..M before any backward pass starts, each GPU alternates — once the pipeline is 'full' (steady state), each GPU does one forward pass for a new microbatch, then one backward pass for an earlier microbatch, repeating — this keeps memory bounded (proportional to the number of pipeline stages, not the number of microbatches) since activations are consumed by backward passes sooner. INTERLEAVED (virtual pipeline) schedule: instead of GPU i holding one contiguous block of L/P layers (for P stages), each GPU holds SEVERAL smaller, non-contiguous chunks (e.g. GPU 1 holds layers [1-2] AND [9-10] in an 8-GPU/16-layer setup) — a microbatch passes through GPU 1's first chunk, then GPU 2's first chunk, ..., then back to GPU 1's second chunk, etc. — this increases the number of pipeline 'stages' from the scheduling perspective (without adding GPUs), reducing the bubble fraction at the cost of more communication rounds per microbatch.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.use_when: Training models where pipeline parallelism is needed (model too large/many layers for tensor parallelism alone, or as the inter-node dimension of 3D parallelism) — 1F1B is essentially always preferred over naive GPipe scheduling; interleaved scheduling is used when bubble overhead remains significant (small number of microbatches relative to pipeline stages) and the extra communication is affordable.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.avoid_when: Very few pipeline stages (P=2) where bubble overhead is inherently small, or when the extra communication rounds of interleaving outweigh bubble reduction on slower interconnects — interleaving trades communication frequency for bubble reduction, a tradeoff that depends on network speed.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.what_goes_wrong: Pipeline bubble fraction is approximately (P-1)/M for P stages and M microbatches with simple 1F1B — if M is small relative to P (e.g. small global batch size split into few microbatches across many stages), bubbles dominate and pipeline parallelism becomes inefficient regardless of scheduling; choosing the microbatch count/size is a key tuning knob alongside the schedule choice.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.real_example: Megatron-LM's interleaved 1F1B schedule was used in training large GPT-style models (e.g. Megatron-Turing NLG 530B) as part of 3D parallelism (pipeline + tensor + data), and the 1F1B schedule (originally from the PipeDream paper) remains the standard baseline pipeline schedule referenced/implemented in essentially all modern large-model training frameworks (DeepSpeed, Megatron, torchtitan).

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.what_it_is: A distributed-training strategy specific to Mixture-of-Experts models: different EXPERT sub-networks (FFN blocks) are placed on different devices, and tokens are routed to the device holding their assigned expert(s) via ALL-TO-ALL communication — a parallelism dimension orthogonal to (and combinable with) data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.why_it_exists: MoE models can have orders of magnitude more total parameters than dense models at the same active-compute budget (e.g. Mixtral 8x7B's ~47B total vs ~13B active) — replicating ALL experts on every GPU (as standard data parallelism would) defeats the memory-efficiency purpose of MoE; expert parallelism instead shards the SET OF EXPERTS across devices (each device holds a subset of experts for each MoE layer), so the model's total parameter memory is divided among devices, while each token's computation is routed to wherever its chosen expert(s) reside.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.how_it_works: For an MoE layer with E experts across G GPUs (each GPU holds E/G experts), the forward pass proceeds: (1) each GPU computes router scores for ITS LOCAL tokens (in the data-parallel/expert-parallel hybrid setup, each GPU initially holds a shard of the token batch); (2) an ALL-TO-ALL communication operation redistributes tokens — each token is sent to the GPU(s) holding its top-k selected expert(s); (3) each GPU computes the FFN for the tokens it received (using its local experts); (4) a second ALL-TO-ALL sends the results back to the originating GPUs, where they're combined (weighted by router probabilities) into each token's output. This double all-to-all (dispatch + combine) is THE characteristic communication pattern of expert parallelism, distinct from the all-reduce (tensor parallelism) or point-to-point (pipeline parallelism) patterns of other strategies.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.use_when: Training/serving MoE models where the number of experts exceeds what fits efficiently on one device, or where distributing experts allows using the aggregate memory of a cluster for a model whose total parameters vastly exceed single-device memory — commonly combined with data parallelism (expert-parallel degree often equals or divides the data-parallel degree) and sometimes tensor parallelism within each expert.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.avoid_when: Small MoE models where all experts fit on each device (in which case standard data parallelism with local expert computation, no all-to-all needed, is simpler) — expert parallelism's all-to-all overhead is only justified when expert SET size genuinely requires distribution.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.what_goes_wrong: All-to-all communication volume depends on TOKEN DISTRIBUTION across experts — if routing is imbalanced (some experts get far more tokens than others, the 'load balancing' problem also relevant to MoE generally), some GPUs become communication/compute bottlenecks while others idle; capacity factors (dropping/padding tokens beyond a per-expert capacity limit) are often used to bound worst-case imbalance at the cost of potentially dropping some tokens' expert computation entirely.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.real_example: Google's GShard and Switch Transformer papers introduced/popularized expert parallelism at scale (Switch Transformer trained models with thousands of experts across large TPU pods using exactly this all-to-all dispatch/combine pattern), and modern open frameworks (DeepSpeed-MoE, Megatron-Core's MoE support) provide expert-parallelism implementations used for training models like Mixtral-scale and DeepSeek-MoE-scale models.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.what_it_is: `torch.compile` (PyTorch 2.0+) is a just-in-time compilation API that speeds up PyTorch models with minimal code changes, built on TWO main components: TorchDynamo (a Python-level JIT that captures PyTorch operations into FX graphs by analyzing/tracing Python bytecode, handling graph breaks for unsupported code) and TorchInductor (a compiler backend that lowers these FX graphs to optimized kernels, generating Triton GPU kernels or C++/OpenMP CPU code).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.why_it_exists: Eager-mode PyTorch executes each operation immediately (Python overhead per op, no cross-op optimization like fusion); prior compilation approaches (TorchScript, `torch.jit.script/trace`) required significant code changes/rewrindo and often failed on dynamic Python control flow. `torch.compile` aims for compilation that's largely TRANSPARENT — works on (most) existing eager PyTorch code with a single decorator/wrapper — by having TorchDynamo handle Python's dynamism gracefully (falling back to eager execution, 'graph breaks', for code it can't trace, rather than failing entirely) while still compiling the traceable portions for speedups via operator fusion, memory planning, and generated kernels.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.how_it_works: TorchDynamo hooks into CPython's frame evaluation API to intercept Python bytecode execution; as the model runs, it traces the sequence of PyTorch tensor operations into an FX GRAPH (a graph IR representing the computation), guarding the compiled graph with assumptions (e.g. tensor shapes/dtypes) that, if violated on a later call, trigger RECOMPILATION. Where Python code can't be traced (e.g. calls to non-PyTorch libraries, complex control flow depending on tensor VALUES), Dynamo inserts a 'graph break' — falling back to eager execution for that portion and resuming graph capture afterward (so compilation is partial but the overall program still runs correctly). The captured FX graphs are passed to TorchInductor, which performs OPERATOR FUSION (combining multiple elementwise/reduction ops into single kernels, reducing memory traffic — similar in spirit to what FlashAttention does specifically for attention, but Inductor does this generally), and generates TRITON kernels (for GPU) or C++/OpenMP (for CPU) — Triton being a Python-like GPU kernel language that compiles to efficient CUDA.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.use_when: Nearly any PyTorch training/inference workload as a 'free' speedup attempt — `torch.compile(model)` with default settings often gives meaningful speedups (commonly 20-50%+ depending on the model) with minimal/no code changes, making it a reasonable default to try.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.avoid_when: Code with heavy data-dependent dynamic control flow or frequent shape changes can suffer from excessive RECOMPILATION (each new shape/condition triggers a new compile, and compilation itself has overhead) — in such cases, `torch.compile`'s overhead may exceed its benefits unless `dynamic=True` (shape-polymorphic compilation) or careful guard management is used; also, debugging compiled code is harder than eager code (error messages/stack traces can be less direct).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.what_goes_wrong: Excessive GRAPH BREAKS (when Dynamo frequently falls back to eager due to untraceable code) limit the scope of fusion/optimization — profiling tools (`torch._dynamo.explain`, TORCH_LOGS env vars) help identify where/why breaks occur; RECOMPILATIONS triggered by changing input shapes (e.g. variable-length sequences without padding to fixed buckets) can cause repeated, costly compilation during training if not anticipated.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.real_example: torchtitan (PyTorch's reference large-model training repo) applies `torch.compile` per-Transformer-block (rather than to the whole model) to balance compilation granularity/recompilation cost against fusion benefits, reporting meaningful throughput improvements for Llama-style pretraining — `torch.compile` adoption is now a standard step in PyTorch performance-tuning guides for both training and inference (e.g. it's a key lever in vLLM and other inference servers too).

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.what_it_is: `torch.export` (PyTorch 2.1+) produces a sound, AHEAD-OF-TIME (AOT) exported graph representation (`ExportedProgram`) of a PyTorch model — a graph WITHOUT graph breaks, suitable for downstream compilation/deployment — and AOTInductor is a backend that compiles such exported graphs into standalone, dependency-free artifacts (e.g. a `.so` shared library) for production inference, without requiring a Python runtime.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.why_it_exists: `torch.compile`/TorchDynamo's just-in-time, graph-break-tolerant approach is great for TRAINING (where flexibility matters and a Python runtime is present), but PRODUCTION INFERENCE often needs: (1) a GUARANTEED full-graph capture (no silent fallback to slow eager code for unexpected inputs), (2) the ability to compile ONCE and deploy the artifact WITHOUT a Python/PyTorch runtime dependency (e.g. for serving in C++ environments, mobile, or embedded). `torch.export` + AOTInductor address these: export produces a complete, graph-break-free representation (raising errors at export time for untraceable code, rather than silently falling back), and AOTInductor compiles it to a self-contained binary artifact.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.how_it_works: `torch.export.export(model, example_inputs)` traces the model (similar tracing machinery to Dynamo, but configured to ERROR on graph breaks rather than fall back) producing an `ExportedProgram` — containing the FX graph, parameters/buffers, and (optionally) dynamic shape specifications (`dynamic_shapes` argument lets certain dimensions vary within specified ranges, producing a graph valid across that shape range rather than a single fixed shape). AOTInductor then takes this `ExportedProgram` and runs TorchInductor's kernel-generation/fusion passes AHEAD OF TIME, emitting compiled kernels plus a lightweight runtime into a shared library (`.so`) that can be loaded and executed from C++ (via `torch::inductor::AOTIModelContainerRunner`) or Python, without needing the full PyTorch JIT/compile machinery at inference time.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.use_when: Production deployment scenarios needing a portable, dependency-minimal compiled artifact — serving from C++ inference servers, embedding models in applications without a Python runtime, or any setting wanting compile-time guarantees (no surprise eager fallbacks) about the deployed model's structure.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.avoid_when: During active model development/training, where `torch.compile`'s flexibility (tolerating graph breaks, dynamic Python) is more valuable than export's strictness — `torch.export` is primarily a DEPLOYMENT-time tool, applied once a model's architecture is finalized.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.what_goes_wrong: Models with genuinely data-dependent control flow that CAN'T be expressed as a single graph (even with `dynamic_shapes`) will fail to export — such models need refactoring (e.g. using `torch.cond` for data-dependent branching in an export-compatible way) before they can be exported/AOT-compiled, which can require non-trivial changes to model code originally written assuming eager flexibility.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.real_example: ExecuTorch (PyTorch's on-device/edge inference runtime) and various production model-serving pipelines use `torch.export` as the entry point for converting trained PyTorch models into deployable artifacts — AOTInductor-compiled `.so` files are used in some of Meta's production recommendation/ranking model inference paths to avoid Python overhead in latency-sensitive serving.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.what_it_is: `torch.distributed.tensor` (DTensor) is PyTorch's native API for representing TENSORS THAT ARE DISTRIBUTED (sharded and/or replicated) across a `DeviceMesh` (a logical grid of devices), with operations on DTensors automatically dispatching the appropriate distributed communication collectives — serving as the unifying abstraction underlying FSDP2, tensor parallelism, and other native PyTorch distributed-parallelism APIs.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.why_it_exists: Prior to DTensor, different parallelism strategies (FSDP, tensor parallelism, pipeline parallelism) each had their OWN ad-hoc ways of representing 'this tensor is split/replicated across devices' — making it hard to COMPOSE strategies (e.g. a tensor that's both FSDP-sharded AND tensor-parallel-sharded along different mesh dimensions) since each system's sharding representation was incompatible with the others. DTensor provides a SINGLE representation (a tensor + a `DeviceMesh` + a list of `Placement`s, one per mesh dimension) that all these strategies can build on, enabling composable N-D parallelism.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.how_it_works: A `DeviceMesh` is an N-dimensional grid of devices (e.g. a 2D mesh of shape [data_parallel_size, tensor_parallel_size]). A `DTensor` wraps a local tensor shard plus metadata: for each mesh dimension, a `Placement` — either `Shard(dim)` (the global tensor is split along `dim` across that mesh dimension), `Replicate()` (each device along that mesh dimension has a full copy), or `Partial()` (each device holds a partial/unreduced contribution, pending a reduction). When an operation (e.g. matmul, addition) is performed on DTensors, PyTorch's dispatcher determines the correct distributed algorithm (e.g. if multiplying a `Shard(1)` tensor by a `Shard(0)` tensor requires an all-reduce of partial results, DTensor inserts that automatically) — so distributed communication emerges from LOCAL tensor operations plus placement-aware dispatch, rather than being manually orchestrated.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.use_when: Building or understanding modern (PyTorch 2.x) native distributed training code — FSDP2 and native tensor-parallel APIs (`torch.distributed.tensor.parallel`) are built on DTensor, so working with these APIs means working with DTensors (e.g. `model.state_dict()` returns DTensors whose `.full_tensor()` or `.to_local()` methods are used to get full/local views).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.avoid_when: Simpler single-strategy parallelism (e.g. plain DDP) where the composability DTensor provides isn't needed — DTensor adds a layer of abstraction/dispatch overhead that's unnecessary if not composing multiple parallelism dimensions.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.what_goes_wrong: DTensor operations that aren't yet supported by a given PyTorch version's dispatch rules can fail or silently fall back to less efficient paths — DTensor support coverage for arbitrary operations/placements has been incrementally expanding across PyTorch 2.x releases, so version compatibility is a practical consideration when relying on specific DTensor-based composability.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.real_example: torchtitan demonstrates DTensor-based 3D parallelism (FSDP2 + tensor parallelism + pipeline parallelism) for Llama-style models, with the `DeviceMesh` explicitly constructed with named dimensions (e.g. 'dp', 'tp', 'pp') and DTensor placements composing across these — illustrating how DTensor unifies what previously required separate, incompatible implementations per parallelism strategy.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.what_it_is: `torch.distributed.checkpoint` (DCP) is PyTorch's native API for saving/loading model and optimizer state in DISTRIBUTED training settings, designed to handle SHARDED state (e.g. FSDP/DTensor-sharded parameters) and support RESHARDING — saving with one parallelism configuration (e.g. 64 GPUs) and loading with a different one (e.g. 8 GPUs), without requiring all-gathering to a single rank.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.why_it_exists: Naive checkpointing of sharded models either requires gathering the FULL model to rank 0 before saving (memory-prohibitive for very large models — defeats the purpose of sharding) or saves each rank's shard separately in a format tightly coupled to that exact parallelism configuration (making it impossible to later load with a different number of GPUs/different sharding). DCP solves both: it saves each rank's local shard directly (no gather-to-rank-0 needed) in a format that records enough metadata (global tensor shapes, each shard's offsets) to allow loading into ANY OTHER sharding configuration — critical for practical workflows like 'train on 512 GPUs, then fine-tune/evaluate on 8 GPUs'.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.how_it_works: When saving, each rank writes its LOCAL shards (of DTensors or other sharded state) to a shared storage location (e.g. a distributed filesystem), along with metadata describing the GLOBAL tensor's shape and how it's partitioned. When loading into a (possibly differently-sharded) model, DCP reads the metadata, determines which saved shards overlap with each loading rank's required shard, and performs the necessary reads/communication to reconstruct each rank's needed portion — effectively a RESHARDING operation performed during load, transparent to the user (`dcp.load(state_dict, checkpoint_id=path)` populates the provided — possibly differently-sharded — state dict in place).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.use_when: Any large-model distributed training run where checkpoints need to be saved/loaded across DIFFERENT numbers of GPUs/nodes (common in practice — training clusters and inference/fine-tuning clusters often differ in size) or where gathering to a single rank for checkpointing is memory-infeasible.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.avoid_when: Small models where a simple `torch.save(model.state_dict())` on rank 0 (after gathering) is feasible and the resharding flexibility isn't needed — DCP's metadata/resharding machinery adds complexity that's unnecessary at small scale.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.what_goes_wrong: Checkpoint I/O at scale (many ranks writing simultaneously) can bottleneck on the underlying STORAGE system's concurrent-write throughput — DCP's design (parallel writes from all ranks) shifts the bottleneck from compute/gather to storage bandwidth, making the choice of storage backend (e.g. a high-throughput distributed filesystem) important for large jobs; checkpoint save/load time can become a non-trivial fraction of training time at the largest scales if not tuned.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.real_example: torchtitan uses `torch.distributed.checkpoint` for fault-tolerant pretraining checkpoints, enabling a training run to be resumed on a different number of GPUs than it was checkpointed on — a practical necessity when cluster allocations change between training sessions for very long pretraining runs.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.what_it_is: NVIDIA Transformer Engine is a library enabling TRAINING (not just inference) of Transformer models using 8-bit floating point (FP8) for the compute-heavy matrix multiplications (in attention and MLP layers), supported natively by Hopper (H100) and newer GPU tensor cores, while maintaining training stability via per-tensor dynamic scaling.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.why_it_exists: FP8 has only 8 bits total (vs 16 for BF16/FP16, 32 for FP32) — using it for matmuls roughly DOUBLES tensor-core throughput and halves memory bandwidth requirements compared to FP16/BF16, a major potential speedup for the dominant cost (matmuls) in Transformer training. But FP8's very limited dynamic range (especially the E4M3 format: 4 exponent bits, 3 mantissa bits) makes naive use prone to overflow/underflow — Transformer Engine provides the scaling infrastructure to use FP8 SAFELY for training, where prior FP8 work was largely inference-only.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.how_it_works: Transformer Engine uses TWO FP8 formats: E4M3 (more mantissa bits, less range — used for forward-pass activations/weights where values are typically better-behaved) and E5M2 (more range, less precision — used for GRADIENTS, which can have larger dynamic range). DELAYED/DYNAMIC SCALING: for each FP8 tensor, a per-tensor scaling factor is maintained, updated based on the recent history of that tensor's value statistics (e.g. tracking the maximum absolute value seen in recent iterations) — values are multiplied by this scale before casting to FP8 (to use the available range fully) and divided after the FP8 matmul (to recover the correct magnitude). The matmul itself accumulates in higher precision (FP32) even though inputs are FP8, limiting accumulation error. This is integrated as drop-in replacements for `nn.Linear`/attention modules (`te.Linear`, etc.) that handle the casting/scaling transparently.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.use_when: Training large models on H100 (or newer, e.g. B100/B200) GPUs where maximizing tensor-core throughput is valuable and the model architecture is primarily Transformer-based (where Transformer Engine's optimized kernels apply) — can give substantial (~30-50%+ in some reports) training speedups over BF16 with comparable final model quality when scaling/recipes are tuned correctly.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.avoid_when: Hardware without native FP8 tensor-core support (pre-Hopper GPUs, e.g. A100) — FP8 matmuls would need to be emulated, losing the throughput benefit; also, models/layers with activation distributions poorly suited to FP8's limited range (without careful per-layer scaling tuning) may see accuracy degradation.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.what_goes_wrong: Even with dynamic scaling, certain layers (e.g. the final layers near the loss, or layers with outlier activations) can be more sensitive to FP8 precision loss — production FP8 training recipes (e.g. as used in DeepSeek-V3's training, which used FP8 for most matmuls but kept certain operations in higher precision) often involve per-layer/per-operation precision decisions rather than uniform FP8 everywhere, requiring careful ablation to avoid quality degradation.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.real_example: DeepSeek-V3's technical report describes an FP8 mixed-precision training framework (built on similar principles to Transformer Engine) as a key factor in its reported training efficiency, using FP8 for the majority of GEMM operations while retaining higher precision for specific sensitive components (e.g. embeddings, certain normalization operations) — illustrating FP8 training moving from 'experimental' to a documented technique behind a frontier-scale model's training efficiency claims.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.what_it_is: A comparison of three reduced-precision floating-point formats used in deep learning: FP16 (1 sign + 5 exponent + 10 mantissa bits — IEEE half precision), BF16 (1 sign + 8 exponent + 7 mantissa bits — 'brain float', same exponent range as FP32 but less mantissa precision), and FP8 (1 sign + 4or5 exponent + 3or2 mantissa bits, in E4M3/E5M2 variants) — differing in their tradeoffs between DYNAMIC RANGE (exponent bits) and PRECISION (mantissa bits).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Dist.why_it_exists: Lower-precision formats reduce memory footprint and increase compute throughput (more values fit in registers/caches, tensor cores process more elements per cycle), but risk numerical issues (overflow, underflow, insufficient precision for small gradient updates) — the choice among FP16/BF16/FP8 is fundamentally a tradeoff between these efficiency gains and the numerical-stability risks, with each format occupying a different point on the range-vs-precision spectrum.
