3|🟡 T2 🔬 Training at Scale|Training at S.why_it_exists: Practically, most PyTorch models written in idiomatic eager-mode style leave significant performance on the table due to kernel-launch overhead and unfused elementwise operations — `torch.compile` was designed so that EXISTING code (not rewritten for a specific compiler) can often benefit with just a wrapping call, making compilation accessible to practitioners without requiring deep compiler knowledge.
3|🟡 T2 🔬 Training at Scale|Training at S.how_it_works: `model = torch.compile(model)` (or `torch.compile(model, mode=...)` for different optimization presets — `default`, `reduce-overhead` for CUDA-graph-based reduction of launch overhead, or `max-autotune` for more aggressive, longer-compile-time kernel search). The first call with a given input shape triggers compilation (slow); subsequent calls with the SAME shape reuse the compiled artifact (fast). Practical workflow considerations: (1) compile the model BEFORE the training loop, not inside it (avoid recompiling every step); (2) for models with variable input shapes (e.g. variable-length sequences), either pad to fixed buckets to avoid recompilation, or use `dynamic=True` for shape-polymorphic compilation; (3) check `TORCH_LOGS=graph_breaks` or `torch._dynamo.explain(model)(*inputs)` to diagnose excessive graph breaks limiting fusion opportunities; (4) for large models, compiling per-Transformer-block (rather than the whole model) can reduce compilation time and recompilation blast-radius.
3|🟡 T2 🔬 Training at Scale|Training at S.use_when: As a default first step for ANY new PyTorch training/inference pipeline on PyTorch 2.x — low cost to try, often meaningful gains.
3|🟡 T2 🔬 Training at Scale|Training at S.avoid_when: Rapid prototyping/debugging phases where compilation overhead (and harder-to-read compiled stack traces) slows down iteration — many practitioners develop in eager mode, then add `torch.compile` once the model architecture stabilizes.
3|🟡 T2 🔬 Training at Scale|Training at S.what_goes_wrong: The most common practical complaint is unexpected RECOMPILATION storms — e.g. if batch size or sequence length varies every step without `dynamic=True`, each new shape triggers a fresh (slow) compilation, potentially making training SLOWER overall than eager mode; the fix is either fixing shapes (padding/bucketing) or explicitly enabling dynamic shape support.
3|🟡 T2 🔬 Training at Scale|Training at S.real_example: HuggingFace Transformers and torchtitan both document `torch.compile` as a standard recommended flag/step in their training scripts, with specific guidance on per-block compilation for large models and shape-handling for variable-length sequence data — reflecting its status as a near-default practical optimization rather than a specialized technique.

3|🟡 T2 🔬 Training at Scale|Training at S.what_it_is: JAX is a NumPy-like array computing library (Google) built around FUNCTIONAL transformations — `jit` (just-in-time compilation via XLA), `grad` (automatic differentiation), `vmap` (automatic vectorization/batching), and `pmap`/`shard_map` (parallelization across devices) — composable as function transformations rather than object-oriented APIs; Flax and Equinox are neural-network libraries built on JAX, differing in how they handle PARAMETERS within JAX's purely-functional paradigm (Flax historically separates parameters from model definition via explicit `params` dicts/PyTrees; Equinox represents models as PyTrees directly, closer to PyTorch's `nn.Module` ergonomics).
3|🟡 T2 🔬 Training at Scale|Training at S.why_it_exists: PyTorch's object-oriented, stateful `nn.Module` design (parameters as mutable attributes) doesn't fit JAX's functional-programming model (pure functions, no hidden state, transformations like `grad`/`vmap`/`jit` operate on functions). JAX's appeal is that its COMPOSABLE TRANSFORMATIONS make certain patterns very natural — e.g. `vmap(grad(loss_fn))` automatically gives per-example gradients (useful for differential privacy or meta-learning), or `pmap`/`shard_map` for data/model parallelism compose with `jit`/`grad` without special-casing. Flax and Equinox provide neural-network-building ergonomics on top while preserving (to varying degrees) this functional composability.
3|🟡 T2 🔬 Training at Scale|Training at S.how_it_works: In JAX, a model's PARAMETERS are just data (PyTrees — nested dicts/lists/tuples of arrays), and the model's FORWARD PASS is a pure function `forward(params, x) -> y` with no internal state. `jax.jit` traces this function once per input-shape/dtype signature and compiles it via XLA (Google's linear-algebra compiler, also used by TPUs) to fused, optimized code. `jax.grad(loss_fn)` returns a NEW function computing gradients via automatic differentiation, which can itself be `jit`-ed or `vmap`-ed. Flax's `nn.Module` (newer Flax NNX, or older Flax Linen) provides a familiar class-based way to DEFINE architectures, but parameter initialization returns a separate PyTree of parameters passed explicitly to the forward function — maintaining the pure-function contract JAX transformations require. Equinox represents the whole model (architecture + parameters) as a single PyTree, allowing `model = eqx.tree_at(...)` style updates and arguably more PyTorch-like ergonomics while remaining a valid JAX PyTree (so `jit`/`grad`/`vmap` work directly on model objects).
3|🟡 T2 🔬 Training at Scale|Training at S.use_when: Research requiring heavy use of JAX's transformation composability (per-example gradients, custom parallelism via `pmap`/`shard_map`, second-order optimization requiring nested `grad`), or TPU-centric workloads (JAX/XLA has historically had the strongest TPU support) — much of Google DeepMind's research codebase (e.g. for Gemini-family models) is JAX-based.
3|🟡 T2 🔬 Training at Scale|Training at S.avoid_when: Teams with existing PyTorch expertise/infrastructure and no specific need for JAX's functional-transformation composability — PyTorch's larger community, more extensive pretrained-model ecosystem (HuggingFace), and more familiar OO-style API make it the pragmatic default for most applied work; the functional paradigm has a real learning-curve cost.
3|🟡 T2 🔬 Training at Scale|Training at S.what_goes_wrong: The functional/pure-function discipline that gives JAX its composability also means common 'stateful' patterns (in-place updates, Python-side mutable counters/RNGs) require explicit handling (e.g. JAX's RNG keys must be explicitly split and threaded through function calls, since there's no global random state) — code ported naively from PyTorch/NumPy without adapting to this discipline produces subtle bugs (e.g. reusing an RNG key giving identical 'random' values across calls).
3|🟡 T2 🔬 Training at Scale|Training at S.real_example: Google DeepMind's large-scale research (including much of the work behind Gemini and earlier large models like PaLM/Chinchilla) is built on JAX, often with Flax for model definitions — and the broader JAX ecosystem (Optax for optimizers, Orbax for checkpointing) is the TPU-centric counterpart to PyTorch's CUDA-centric ecosystem, relevant context when discussing why a research lab's codebase might be JAX- vs PyTorch-based.

3|🟡 T2 🔬 Training at Scale|Training at S.what_it_is: Triton (OpenAI, open-source) is a Python-embedded language and compiler for writing custom GPU kernels at a higher level of abstraction than raw CUDA — programmers write kernels using NumPy-like operations on BLOCKS of data (tiles), and Triton's compiler handles memory-coalescing, shared-memory allocation, and thread/warp scheduling automatically, while still achieving performance competitive with hand-tuned CUDA for many kernels.
3|🟡 T2 🔬 Training at Scale|Training at S.why_it_exists: Writing efficient CUDA kernels requires expertise in low-level GPU details (memory hierarchies, thread/warp/block organization, shared memory bank conflicts) that most ML researchers/engineers lack — but PyTorch's built-in operators don't cover every custom operation a new research idea might need (e.g. a novel attention variant, a fused activation+normalization). Triton lets practitioners write custom kernels in Python-like syntax (operating on tiles/blocks, similar to how one might think about NumPy operations on array slices) while Triton's compiler generates GPU code with much of the low-level optimization that would otherwise require manual CUDA expertise.
3|🟡 T2 🔬 Training at Scale|Training at S.how_it_works: A Triton kernel is a Python function decorated with `@triton.jit`, operating on PROGRAM IDs (analogous to CUDA's block/thread indices, but at a coarser, block-of-elements granularity) and using `tl.load`/`tl.store` for memory access with explicit pointer arithmetic and masking (for handling boundary conditions when data size isn't a multiple of block size). Within a kernel, operations on loaded BLOCKS (e.g. a 2D tile of a matrix) use NumPy-like syntax (`tl.dot` for matmul, elementwise ops, reductions) — Triton's compiler handles the mapping of these block-level operations to efficient GPU instructions, including automatic use of shared memory/registers and coalesced memory access patterns. Triton kernels are JIT-compiled (with autotuning over block-size/configuration choices via `@triton.autotune`) the first time they're called with a given input signature.
3|🟡 T2 🔬 Training at Scale|Training at S.use_when: Implementing custom fused operations not available in standard libraries (FlashAttention itself is implemented in Triton in some versions; custom normalization/activation fusions, custom MoE routing kernels) where writing raw CUDA would be too slow/error-prone for the team, but a standard PyTorch op composition would leave performance on the table due to lack of fusion.
3|🟡 T2 🔬 Training at Scale|Training at S.avoid_when: When an existing, well-optimized kernel (in PyTorch core, cuDNN, or a library like FlashAttention) already covers the needed operation — writing a custom Triton kernel is only worth the effort when there's a genuine gap in available optimized implementations.
3|🟡 T2 🔬 Training at Scale|Training at S.what_goes_wrong: Triton abstracts away SOME but not all GPU details — getting good performance still requires understanding concepts like block size selection (too small wastes parallelism, too large can exceed shared memory/register limits) and memory access patterns; `@triton.autotune` helps by searching over configurations, but autotuning adds compilation-time overhead and the search space/heuristics still require some GPU-architecture awareness to set up well.
3|🟡 T2 🔬 Training at Scale|Training at S.real_example: `torch.compile`'s Inductor backend GENERATES Triton kernels as its compiled output for GPU targets — meaning every speedup from `torch.compile` on a GPU is, under the hood, Triton code that Inductor wrote automatically; FlashAttention-2's official Triton implementation (alongside the hand-written CUDA version) is also a commonly-referenced example of a complex, performance-critical kernel implemented in Triton.

3|🟡 T2 🔬 Training at Scale|Training at S.what_it_is: Composer (MosaicML, now part of Databricks) is a PyTorch training library/framework focused on packaging EFFICIENCY techniques (many of the 'training recipe' tricks — gradient checkpointing, mixed precision, various optimizers/schedules, algorithmic speedup methods like progressive resizing or selective backprop) as composable, easily-toggleable components, with an emphasis on reproducible, cost-efficient training recipes for LLMs and other large models.
3|🟡 T2 🔬 Training at Scale|Training at S.why_it_exists: Many individual efficiency techniques (each potentially giving a few percent speedup or memory savings) exist scattered across papers/implementations with inconsistent APIs — Composer's value proposition was providing a CURATED, BENCHMARKED collection of such techniques with a consistent API, plus pre-built 'recipes' (combinations of techniques validated together) for common model types, aimed at reducing the cost of large-scale training runs (MosaicML's business was selling efficient training infrastructure/recipes before being acquired by Databricks).
3|🟡 T2 🔬 Training at Scale|Training at S.how_it_works: Composer wraps the PyTorch training loop with an `Algorithm` abstraction — each efficiency technique (e.g. `BlurPool`, `ChannelsLast`, `MixUp`, `SeqLengthWarmup`, `GradientClipping` variants) is implemented as an Algorithm that can hook into different points of the training loop (before/after forward, before/after backward, etc.) and be toggled on/off via configuration, allowing systematic ABLATION of which combination of techniques gives the best cost/quality tradeoff for a given model/dataset. Composer also provides its own Trainer abstraction integrating with FSDP, mixed precision, and various distributed strategies.
3|🟡 T2 🔬 Training at Scale|Training at S.use_when: Teams wanting a curated starting point of 'known-good' efficiency techniques with empirical benchmarks for a given model class, especially if building on MosaicML's published recipes (e.g. for training LLMs or ResNets cost-efficiently) — relevant historical/practical context when discussing the ecosystem of 'efficient training' tooling around 2022-2023.
3|🟡 T2 🔬 Training at Scale|Training at S.avoid_when: Projects already built on a different established framework (raw PyTorch + FSDP, DeepSpeed, torchtitan, HuggingFace Trainer/Accelerate) where adopting Composer would mean a significant framework migration for benefits that may now be available natively (many of Composer's individual techniques have since become standard/available directly in PyTorch or other frameworks).
3|🟡 T2 🔬 Training at Scale|Training at S.what_goes_wrong: As with any specialized framework, depending on Composer ties a project to its abstractions/APIs and release cadence — teams should weigh the curated-recipe convenience against the lock-in/migration cost, especially as the broader PyTorch ecosystem has absorbed many individual techniques (e.g. `torch.compile`, native FSDP) that originally motivated using a wrapper framework.
3|🟡 T2 🔬 Training at Scale|Training at S.real_example: MosaicML's MPT (MosaicML Pretrained Transformer) model series was trained using Composer, with MosaicML publishing detailed cost/time benchmarks (e.g. 'train a GPT-3-quality model for $X in Y days') as part of demonstrating the efficiency-recipe value proposition — these published recipes were frequently cited as reference points for LLM pretraining cost estimates around 2023.

3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_it_is: StreamingLLM (Xiao et al. 2023) is a technique enabling pretrained LLMs (trained with finite context windows) to generate text over effectively UNBOUNDED-length streams without fine-tuning, by combining a fixed-size SLIDING WINDOW of recent tokens' KV cache with a small number of retained initial tokens — 'attention sink' tokens — whose KV entries are NEVER evicted.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.why_it_exists: Naively applying a sliding window (evicting the oldest tokens' KV cache once a length limit is reached, keeping only the most recent W tokens) causes a sudden PERPLEXITY SPIKE/collapse once the first tokens are evicted — the authors discovered this happens because the FIRST FEW TOKENS of a sequence receive disproportionately large attention scores from ALL subsequent tokens regardless of their semantic content (an 'attention sink' phenomenon, likely because softmax requires attention scores to sum to 1, and early tokens — visible to all positions due to causal masking — become a convenient 'dump' for excess attention). Evicting these sink tokens removes something the model has learned to rely on, breaking generation.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.how_it_works: StreamingLLM's KV cache retains: (1) a small fixed number of 'sink' tokens (e.g. the first 4 tokens of the sequence — these are kept FOREVER regardless of how long generation continues) and (2) a sliding window of the most recent W tokens (evicting older non-sink tokens as new ones arrive). Position information is handled by using POSITIONS WITHIN THE CACHE (not original sequence positions) for rotary/relative position embeddings — i.e., the cached tokens are treated as if contiguous, with the sink tokens always at the earliest cache positions and the sliding window tokens at relative positions after them, regardless of their true original positions in the (arbitrarily long) stream. This requires NO FINE-TUNING — it's purely an inference-time KV-cache management strategy that works with already-pretrained models, enabling stable perplexity over streams of millions of tokens with constant memory and latency.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.use_when: Long-running streaming/conversational applications (chatbots that run indefinitely, continuous monitoring/summarisation of live streams) where constant memory/latency per generated token is required and full retention of all context isn't necessary (the model effectively 'forgets' middle content beyond the window, retaining only the sink tokens + recent window).
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.avoid_when: Tasks requiring the model to recall/reference specific information from ARBITRARY points in a long context (not just recent + the very start) — StreamingLLM explicitly trades away access to the 'middle' of long contexts for unbounded-length stability; for tasks needing full-context recall, use actual long-context models (with Ring Attention / FlashAttention) or retrieval-augmentation instead.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.what_goes_wrong: StreamingLLM does NOT extend the model's effective context/knowledge — it only prevents the perplexity COLLAPSE from naive cache eviction, allowing stable (but not necessarily 'long-context-aware') generation; content evicted from the sliding window is genuinely inaccessible to the model afterward, a frequently-misunderstood limitation.
3|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Fron.real_example: The 'attention sink' discovery from StreamingLLM has informed subsequent KV-cache management and quantisation schemes (many libraries now special-case the first few tokens, avoiding aggressive quantisation/eviction for them) — and the technique itself is used in some long-running local-inference chat applications (e.g. via llama.cpp's StreamingLLM-inspired cache management options) to support indefinite conversation length on memory-constrained hardware.
